cards.name: Xia
cards.description: Xia is the first dynasty in the traditional account of Chinese history. Later books name its kings, but no royal records from their own time have been securely identified. Its familiar dates are therefore much less certain than those of the later Shang.
cards.note: 2070–1600 BCE is a conventional, approximate chronology, not a securely documented sequence of reigns. Erlitou has not been proven to be Xia.
cards.catalogNote: 2070–1600 BCE is one modern reconstructed chronology, not securely established exact dates. Xia's identification with excavated cultures and the historical status of its early rulers remain debated. Display as approximate/traditional.

sections.title: The evidence at Erlitou
sections.text: Excavations at Erlitou reveal a major early Bronze Age centre, with large buildings for powerful families and workshops requiring skilled workers. People there could gather considerable wealth and labour. Whether they called their kingdom Xia is another question. The place and broad dates fit some later accounts, but that alone cannot identify its rulers. The settlement is real; its connection with Xia remains debated.

sections.title: Why later rulers told the story
sections.text: Later accounts describe Xia losing power because its rulers failed to govern well. Shang then takes its place. This gave later generations a way to explain why one ruling family could rightfully replace another. The tradition may preserve memories of an older world, while also expressing what later writers believed a ruler should do.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Early China · Erlitou and the search for Xia

dateReview.note: 2070–1600 BCE is one modern reconstructed chronology, not securely established exact dates. Xia's identification with excavated cultures and the historical status of its early rulers remain debated. Display as approximate/traditional. Existing UI already labels the date approximate; preserve its fuller description.

image.alt: A pottery vessel with a long spout and three pointed legs.
image.caption: An Erlitou pottery jue in Luoyang Museum. Archaeological evidence for Erlitou does not by itself establish the names or reigns of the Xia kings.

cards.name: Shang
cards.description: Shang sites preserve large settlements and elaborate bronze vessels. At Anyang (安阳), writing on bones and turtle shells records the concerns of late Shang kings. The earlier walled centre at Zhengzhou (郑州) shows how much work rulers could organize, though the dates and identities of the earliest Shang rulers are less secure.
cards.note: About 1600–1046 BCE is the conventional range. Late Shang writing is much more securely documented than the dynasty’s precise beginning.
cards.catalogNote: Museum chronology supports approximately 1600–1046 BCE; early boundaries are reconstructions. 'First archaeological state' is misleading because earlier complex societies are archaeologically known.

sections.title: Bronze, ancestors and power
sections.text: Making large bronze vessels required metal, fuel and highly skilled workers. Rulers used the vessels in offerings and feasts that displayed rank and honoured powerful ancestors. Their beauty depended on a ruling family’s ability to command resources. Large tombs reveal a harsher side of that power: people were also killed in human sacrifices.

sections.title: What the writing tells us
sections.text: The inscriptions bring us close to royal decisions, but mostly record what troubled the king and the people who interpreted signs for him. They tell us much less about ordinary households. Archaeology helps fill those gaps and reveals other Bronze Age centres beyond the court’s reach. Shang territory should not be confused with the borders of China today.

sourceLabels.https://asia.si.edu/whats-on/exhibitions: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art · Anyang
sourceLabels.https://faculty.risd.edu/bcampbel/Dematt: Paola Demattè · Early Chinese dynasties and Zhengzhou archaeology

dateReview.note: Museum chronology supports approximately 1600–1046 BCE; early boundaries are reconstructions. 'First archaeological state' is misleading because earlier complex societies are archaeologically known. Existing UI already labels the date approximate; preserve its fuller description.

image.alt: Bronze vessel forms arranged in a reconstructed tomb chamber.
image.caption: A reconstructed display of Fu Hao’s tomb at Yinxu, photographed in 2007. It interprets the archaeological burial and must not be mistaken for original grave goods still lying in their excavated positions.

cards.name: Western Zhou
cards.description: After defeating Shang, Zhou rulers claimed that Heaven had given them the right to govern: the Mandate of Heaven. Their power depended on regional lords and influential families. Land grants and family ties helped hold this order together, though it did not work identically everywhere.
cards.note: 1046 BCE is a widely used conquest date, but early Zhou chronology remains debated. “Feudal” is an imperfect comparison, not an exact match to medieval Europe.
cards.catalogNote: Approximately 1046–771 BCE follows the Met. The reconstructed start should not be presented as unquestionably exact.

sections.title: Promises cast in bronze
sections.text: A lord receiving an appointment or reward could have it recorded on a bronze vessel used in ceremonies for ancestors. The inscription celebrated the king’s favour and helped the recipient’s descendants claim their place. Family relationships mattered, but warfare, marriage and service also bound lords to the court. The king needed these alliances to exercise power at a distance.

sections.title: Explaining the conquest
sections.text: Stories of the Zhou founders gave later rulers and noble families respected ancestors to follow. They also explained how overthrowing Shang could be justified: a ruling family might lose Heaven’s support. This argument served a dynasty born through conquest. As conditions changed, later generations retold the founding story to support their own claims about good government.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Constance Cook · Scribes, cooks and artisans

dateReview.note: Approximately 1046–771 BCE follows the Met. The reconstructed start should not be presented as unquestionably exact. Existing UI already labels the date approximate; preserve its fuller description.

image.credit: Gary Lee Todd, Ph.D. · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: An ancient bronze vessel with two handles on a square pedestal.
image.caption: The Li gui, an early Western Zhou bronze whose inscription records the conquest of Shang. The vessel is evidence close to the event, rather than a later portrait of its protagonists.

cards.name: Eastern Zhou
cards.description: The Zhou royal court moved east in 770 BCE. Kings kept their respected title, but regional rulers increasingly controlled their own armies, taxes and decisions. The Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods describe successive parts of this long era of competition.
cards.note: 770–256 BCE dates the Eastern Zhou royal house. Warring States politics continues beyond its fall to 221 BCE; the two spans describe different things.
cards.catalogNote: 770–256 BCE: 770 marks King Ping's move to Luoyi; 256 is the conventional end of the Zhou royal house. Warring States continues beyond this dynasty's end.

sections.title: Stronger states around a weaker king
sections.text: Rival courts developed ways to collect taxes, recruit soldiers and settle disputes. The Zhou king could lose power while government elsewhere became more forceful. Officials, teachers and military advisers travelled between courts seeking support for their ideas. Competition brought destructive wars, but also new ways to organize armies and govern larger territories.

sections.title: Competing ideas of good rule
sections.text: Rulers and thinkers still appealed to Zhou ceremonies and admired figures from the past. They disagreed about what those examples meant. Confucian and Mohist teachings, among others, grew in this world of rival answers. There was no single philosophy shared by everyone. Later labels make the arguments look more neatly divided than they were when teachers and their followers first debated them.

sourceLabels.https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/shang-a: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Shang and Zhou bronze cultures

dateReview.note: 770–256 BCE: 770 marks King Ping's move to Luoyi; 256 is the conventional end of the Zhou royal house. Warring States continues beyond this dynasty's end.

image.alt: A miniature bronze building containing musicians and other figures.
image.caption: A Spring and Autumn-period bronze model of a building with performers. Elite ceremony and entertainment accompanied the competition between regional courts.

cards.name: Late Warring States
cards.description: The Zhou royal family lost its rule in 256 BCE, but the rival kingdoms continued fighting. Qin defeated its remaining major rivals in 230–221 BCE. These years belong to the Warring States period; they are not a separate dynasty.

sections.title: Keeping armies supplied
sections.text: Qin needed more than able commanders to win repeated wars. Farming households supplied grain and workers; officials arranged transport and deliveries between regions. Documents excavated at Liye help reveal these networks. Behind military victories lay the daily work of offices that moved supplies and kept track of responsibilities. Without that work, armies could not keep campaigning.

sections.title: A victory that was not guaranteed
sections.text: The other kingdoms defended their own rulers and formed alliances to survive. Qin’s eventual victory can make their defeat seem inevitable, but they had different possible futures in view. Conquest ended their independent courts. It did not immediately erase regional customs, languages or loyalties. The new empire had to govern people whose lives had developed under separate states.

cards.note: 256–221 BCE covers the years after the Zhou royal house fell. The full Warring States period began earlier, and Qin’s conquests involved several campaigns.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Early China · Qin logistics and financial administration
sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin%27s_wa: Wikipedia · Qin%27s wars of unification (reference overview)

dateReview.note: 256–221 BCE is explicitly editorial, not a claimed dynasty. Final conquests 230–221 match the scholarly article. Keep its note.

image.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Small bronze figures of armed warriors.
image.caption: Warring States bronze warriors, photographed in a museum. These are period objects, not portraits of particular generals or a reconstruction of a named battle.

cards.name: Qin
cards.description: In 221 BCE, Qin defeated its major rivals and created an empire governed through appointed officials. The dynasty fell in 206 BCE, but later rulers kept many of its methods. Its government lasted far longer in practice than its ruling family did.
cards.note: 221–206 BCE dates the empire; Qin existed as a state for centuries before it. Descriptions of identical rule across every locality overstate what survives in the evidence.
cards.catalogNote: 221–206 BCE is the standard museum range for the imperial Qin dynasty, not the longer history of the Qin state.

sections.title: Making a large empire work
sections.text: Common measures, written records and official procedures helped officials compare goods and carry out orders across long distances. They could also help trade. For rulers, these standards made it easier to collect resources and direct people. Excavated records show many offices handling routine transfers. Even a powerful emperor depended on officials doing this work in local communities.

sections.title: The burden on households
sections.text: Military campaigns, construction and compulsory service demanded much from ordinary families. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, struggles over succession and rebellion broke the dynasty. Later Han writers stressed Qin’s cruelty, and their accounts need to be read alongside excavated evidence. Han’s continued use of Qin methods shows how much survived the collapse, despite the sharp criticism of its rulers.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Early China · Qin logistics and financial administration

dateReview.note: 221–206 BCE is the standard museum range for the imperial Qin dynasty, not the longer history of the Qin state.

image.alt: Rows of terracotta soldiers and a horse in a museum display.
image.caption: Terracotta figures from the First Emperor’s mausoleum complex. Their differentiated faces and equipment belong to a coordinated funerary project, not a surviving photograph of the Qin army.

cards.name: Han
cards.description: Han rulers rebuilt an empire after the wars that destroyed Qin. Its history includes Western Han, the interruption of Wang Mang (王莽)’s Xin dynasty, and the restored Eastern Han. Across these centuries, government changed, classical learning grew and connections across Eurasia expanded.
cards.note: 206 BCE marks Liu Bang (刘邦) becoming king of Han; 202 BCE marks his imperial accession. Xin interrupted Han rule in 9–23 CE and appears separately.

sections.title: Sharing and gathering power
sections.text: Some regions were governed by appointed officials; others were kingdoms held by members of the imperial family. Disputes over these arrangements gradually increased the court’s power. Farming households supplied much of the tax income and labour. Officials still needed local knowledge and the help of influential families to turn orders from the emperor into action.

sections.title: Life behind the fine objects
sections.text: Han tombs preserve textiles, lacquerware and images of farms, servants and entertainments. They show what wealthy people valued, along with signs of the work supporting their lives. Learning from ancient texts became more important in government, but punishment and inherited privilege remained powerful. The familiar story of a cruel Qin followed by a kind Han overlooks both the methods they shared and disagreements within Han itself.

sourceLabels.https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/han-dyn: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Han dynasty
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Cambridge History of China · Structure and practice of Han government

dateReview.note: 206 BCE–220 CE museum envelope is supported; Xin interruption and 202 imperial accession are already explained. Description saying dynasty encompassed Xin should become: The overview spans Western Han, the intervening Xin regime, and Eastern Han.

image.alt: A monumental stone horse standing above a fallen figure.
image.caption: A horse trampling a Xiongnu figure at Huo Qubing’s mausoleum. The monument expresses a Han victory narrative and should be read as imperial commemoration.

cards.name: Xin
cards.description: Wang Mang (王莽) replaced Han in 9 CE and founded the Xin dynasty. He tried to change landholding, slavery, currency and the government’s role in the economy, claiming to restore an ideal ancient order. Rebellion ended his reign in 23 CE. Further warfare followed before Han rule was restored.
cards.catalogNote: 9–23 CE follows the Met chronology for Wang Mang's dynasty.

sections.title: Old ideals, disruptive changes
sections.text: Invoking the past allowed Wang Mang (王莽) to argue for sweeping reforms. But his measures disturbed powerful interests and familiar ways of doing business. Repeated changes to money created a practical problem: issuing a new currency did not ensure that people could or would use it. Officials needed the ability to carry out reforms, and the public needed reasons to trust them.

sections.title: A reign under pressure
sections.text: Floods drove people from their homes and deepened rural hardship. These disasters added to resistance and difficulties carrying out policy. The reforms’ failure had several causes. Calling Wang Mang (王莽) a modern socialist is also misleading: his model was an ancient society with fixed ranks. Later Han histories judged a ruler their own dynasty had replaced.

cards.note: 9–23 CE dates the Xin regime. The scale and implementation of individual reforms are debated; later Han histories were written within the dynasty that supplanted him.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Cambridge History of China · Wang Mang and Later Han

dateReview.note: 9–23 CE follows the Met chronology for Wang Mang's dynasty.

image.credit: Prof. Gary Lee Todd · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A bronze coin shaped like a knife with a round head.
image.caption: Knife-shaped money associated with Wang Mang’s monetary reforms. Its deliberately archaic form makes the appeal to antiquity tangible.

cards.name: Age of Division
cards.description: Between Han and Sui, rival courts ruled different parts of China. Wars drove migration, while powerful families and religious communities carried practices and learning across borders. The Age of Division is a name for this period of several competing governments.
cards.note: 220–581 is the overview frame; Sui’s conquest of the southern Chen occurred in 589.

sections.title: Government continued across the divide
sections.text: Successor states employed officials and kept methods inherited from earlier rulers. Their kings and emperors argued over who deserved to rule the empire. Even when no court controlled it all, the idea of imperial rule remained powerful. Political borders did not bring all learning, trade or government work to a halt.

sections.title: New regional centres
sections.text: Migration helped reshape society around the lower Yangtze (长江) River. In the north, courts maintained military and religious ties with Inner Asia. These regions developed their own centres of power and culture. People living through these changes did not know that a future dynasty would reunite much of the country. Their choices involved the rival courts and opportunities of their own time.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Cambridge History of China · Literature, 317–649

dateReview.note: 220–581 is a declared editorial Han-to-Sui foundation frame. Political division continued until Chen conquest in 589, already stated in the note; neither date should be presented as the only periodization.

image.credit: Auckland War Memorial Museum Tāmaki Paenga Hira · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A dark clay model of a saddled horse.
image.caption: An unglazed pottery horse attributed to the Wei dynasty, in Auckland Museum. A funerary object offers material evidence alongside the dynastic chronicles.

cards.name: Sui
cards.description: The Sui dynasty began in 581 and conquered the southern Chen dynasty in 589, bringing north and south under one court. Its rulers built the transport and government systems needed to hold this large territory together. Their demands also helped turn people against them.
cards.note: 581–618 follows the conventional dynastic span. Some scholarship ends its main political narrative in 617; southern conquest occurred in 589.
cards.catalogNote: 581–618 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

sections.title: Connecting north and south
sections.text: Winning territory was only the first step. Officials needed records of households, ways to collect grain and reliable routes for moving supplies and armies. The canal network connected regions that had spent generations under different rulers. Sui government also drew on practices inherited from those earlier states; reunification did not mean that every district immediately worked in the same way.

sections.title: The cost of imperial ambition
sections.text: Canal construction and repeated campaigns against Goguryeo in 612–614 demanded labour and supplies from communities. The same power that made enormous projects possible could place unbearable pressure on the people supporting them. Sui lasted only until 618, but later dynasties inherited important parts of its government and transport network. Their usefulness outlived the court that built them.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Arthur Wright · The Sui Dynasty
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: David Graff · The Reach of the Military: Tang

dateReview.note: 581–618 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

image.alt: An elaborately carved stone funerary bed displayed in a museum.
image.caption: The tomb furnishings of Yu Hong, who died in 592, in the Shanxi Museum. Their imagery offers evidence for the Sogdian and Iranian connections within Sui elite society.

cards.name: Tang
cards.description: The Tang ruled China for close to three centuries, taking power in 618 after the collapse of the [[id:sui|Sui]] (隋朝 Suícháo), which had [[id:reunification|reunified the country in 589]] following almost four hundred years of division. Chinese tradition treats the Tang as the high point of imperial China in both politics and culture, and the dynasty's territorial reach in the 660s was the largest of any Chinese state before the Manchu [[id:qing|Qing]].
cards.catalogNote: 618–907 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

sections.title: Frontier origins
sections.text: The ruling Li (李 Lǐ) family came from the militarised northwest frontier, where Chinese officials had intermarried for generations with Turkic and Xianbei (鲜卑 Xiānbēi) steppe nobility, a world shaped by the [[id:catalog-R_NS_NORTHERN_WEI|Northern Wei]]. This mattered in practice. Emperor Taizong (太宗 Tàizōng, born Li Shimin 李世民 Lǐ Shìmín, r. 626–649), who took the throne after [[id:xuanwu-gate|killing two brothers at the Xuanwu Gate]] and forcing his father's abdication, accepted the steppe title Heavenly Khagan (天可汗 Tiān Kèhán) in 630 after defeating the Eastern Turks. He governed as Chinese emperor and as khan of a nomadic confederation at once, and his [[id:zhenguan-government|Zhenguan era]] became the model of good government invoked by every later dynasty. Tang armies held protectorates deep into Central Asia until defeat by the Abbasids at [[id:talas|Talas]] (怛罗斯 Dáluósī) in 751 checked further westward expansion.

sections.title: Government
sections.text: Administratively the Tang built on Sui foundations and produced the model that most later dynasties worked from. The [[id:tang-code|Tang Code]] (唐律疏议 Tánglǜ Shūyì) of 653 was the most influential legal document in East Asian history, adopted in modified form by Japan, Korea and Vietnam. Government ran through three departments and six ministries (三省六部 sān shěng liù bù). Officials were recruited partly through written civil service examinations (科举 kējǔ), [[id:sui-examinations|begun under the Sui]], though the great aristocratic clans retained most senior posts throughout the dynasty. Land was distributed under the equal-field system (均田制 jūntiánzhì) and the army raised through rotating militia service (府兵制 fǔbīngzhì), both of which broke down in the eighth century.

sections.title: A world capital
sections.text: [[id:chang-an|Chang'an]] (长安 Cháng'ān), the capital, held roughly a million people within a walled grid, and both Nara and Heian-kyō in Japan were laid out in imitation of it. Sogdian and Persian merchants, Japanese and Korean students, and Zoroastrian, Manichaean and Nestorian Christian communities all had a presence there, and a stele erected in 781 records the Christian mission. [[id:catalog-E_BUD_SPREAD|Buddhism]] reached its greatest institutional strength, supported by pilgrim-scholars such as [[id:xuanzang-return|Xuanzang]] (玄奘 Xuánzàng), who travelled to India between 629 and 645 and returned with several hundred texts. Steppe habits persisted in elite society, and [[id:tang-women-riding|aristocratic women rode horses, hunted and played polo]] with a freedom that later dynasties withdrew. Roughly 48,900 poems by some 2,200 Tang authors survive, and the work of [[id:li-bai-du-fu|Li Bai (李白 Lǐ Bái) and Du Fu (杜甫 Dù Fǔ)]] became the standard against which later Chinese poetry was measured.

sections.title: Wu Zetian
sections.text: [[id:wu-zhou|Wu Zetian]] (武则天 Wǔ Zétiān), who entered the palace as a concubine of Taizong and later became consort to his son Gaozong (高宗 Gāozōng), governed in his name during his illness and in 690 declared her own Zhou dynasty (周朝 Zhōucháo). She ruled as emperor in her own right until 705, the only woman ever to do so, and expanded examination recruitment against the interests of the established aristocracy.

sections.title: The rebellion and after
sections.text: The [[id:an-lushan|rebellion of the frontier general An Lushan]] (安禄山 Ān Lùshān), which began in 755 during the long reign of Emperor Xuanzong (玄宗 Xuánzōng, r. 712–756, whose [[id:kaiyuan-era|Kaiyuan era]] is remembered as the dynasty's peak) and was not suppressed until 763, permanently altered the dynasty. Registered population fell from about 52.9 million in 754 to about 16.9 million in 764, a figure that reflects administrative collapse as much as mortality, though the human cost was enormous by any measure. Afterwards provincial military governors (节度使 jiédùshǐ) held effective autonomy, the court financed itself through a [[id:two-tax|new twice-yearly tax]] (两税法 liǎngshuìfǎ) from 780, and palace eunuchs controlled the imperial armies while the bureaucracy consumed itself in [[id:niu-li-disputes|factional struggle]]. State [[id:huichang|suppression of Buddhism]] under Emperor Wuzong (武宗 Wǔzōng) in 845 closed thousands of monasteries and marked a broader turn against foreign influence. The [[id:huang-chao|rebellion of Huang Chao]] (黄巢 Huáng Cháo) sacked Chang'an in 881, and in 907 the warlord Zhu Wen (朱温 Zhū Wēn) [[id:tang-end|deposed the last emperor]] and founded the [[id:catalog-R_FIVE_LATER_LIANG|Later Liang]] (后梁 Hòu Liáng), opening the [[id:five-dynasties|Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period]] (五代十国 Wǔdài Shíguó).

sections.title: The centre of gravity moves south
sections.text: The rebellion also accelerated a permanent shift in where China's people and wealth sat. Tang power rested on the Guanzhong basin (关中 Guānzhōng) around Chang'an and the Central Plains (中原 Zhōngyuán) around Luoyang (洛阳 Luòyáng), the old Yellow River heartland. A clear majority of households registered in the census of 742 were northern. The wars of the eighth century, and then the devastation of the ninth, drove sustained migration south across the Huai River into the Yangtze (长江 Chángjiāng) valley, and [[id:southward-economic-shift|by the Song the majority of the population lived in the south]]. Wet-rice agriculture in the lower Yangtze yielded far larger surpluses than the millet and wheat farming of the north, and the [[id:sui-grand-canal|Grand Canal]] (大运河 Dà Yùnhé), dug at ruinous cost by the Sui, carried that surplus upriver to feed the capitals. After 755 the court survived on southern grain and on a salt monopoly administered from the Huai region, which by the 780s supplied more than half of its cash revenue. Yangzhou (扬州 Yángzhōu), where the canal met the Yangtze, became the wealthiest commercial city in the empire, and Guangzhou (广州 Guǎngzhōu) carried a seaborne trade with Arab and Persian merchants substantial enough that a massacre of foreign residents there during the Huang Chao rebellion was recorded as far away as Iraq. The two-tax reform of 780, which assessed land and property rather than registered adults, was an admission that the old northern system of allotted fields and counted persons no longer described the country.

sections.title: Why the Tang matters
sections.text:
Historians describe the passage from the late Tang into the [[id:song|Song]] as the hinge between medieval and early modern China, an argument first framed by the Japanese scholar Naitō Konan and known as the Tang-Song transition (唐宋变革 Táng-Sòng biàngé). The aristocratic clans that had held the senior offices throughout the Tang were broken by the rebellions of the ninth century, and the Song governed instead through a gentry class made by examination. The capital never returned to Chang'an. The Song ruled from Kaifeng (开封 Kāifēng) and later Hangzhou (杭州 Hángzhōu), both chosen for their access to the canal and the southern economy. Political power had followed the grain.

The Tang reputation as a golden age was largely formed after the fact, by writers of the ninth century onward who understood themselves to be living in the aftermath of something greater. Later dynasties, with north China or the whole country under non-Chinese rule for much of the following millennium, came to treat the Tang as the last great native dynasty. That reading sits awkwardly with the frontier and steppe origins of the Tang ruling house itself.

image.caption: Tang administration and protectorates in 661. In this modern reconstruction, dark red marks civil administration, the middle shade marks Anxi military administration, and pale red marks briefly controlled protectorates. Control varied across these regions and over time.

sectionImages.alt: Ink painting of a white horse tethered to a post, surrounded by collectors’ seals and inscriptions.
sectionImages.caption: Night-Shining White, attributed to Han Gan, c. 750. The painting depicts a horse belonging to Emperor Xuanzong; later collectors added seals and inscriptions.
sectionImages.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · accession 1977.78

sectionImages.alt: A glazed ceramic two-humped camel carrying a decorated saddle.
sectionImages.caption: A Tang sancai glazed ceramic camel, photographed in Xi’an’s Bell Tower Museum. Camels carried goods along the Silk Road, the network connecting China with Central Asia and lands farther west. Sogdian and Persian merchants helped bring textiles, metalwork, and new fashions into Tang cities. This figure evokes that commercial world and the cosmopolitan tastes of Tang society: foreign people, goods, and styles became familiar subjects for Chinese craftspeople.
sectionImages.credit: Gary Todd · Wikimedia Commons · photograph 2011

sectionImages.alt: Painted wooden female attendant wearing a long dress and a short jacket.
sectionImages.caption: This painted wooden attendant wears the high-waisted dress and short jacket fashionable at the Tang court. The Met associates its survival with the dry regions of the Silk Roads. Trade also influenced elite fashion: fitted sleeves, short tunics, and riding boots reflected Central Asian tastes. Late seventh to early eighth century.
sectionImages.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Gift of Enid A. Haupt, 1997 · 1997.442.7.2

sectionImages.alt: A broken ceramic bowl base with a dragon medallion and patches of green, amber, and pale glaze.
sectionImages.caption: Made in China and excavated at Nishapur in Iran, this Tang bowl fragment shows how far Chinese ceramics travelled. Its dragon medallion survives beneath a three-colour glaze. Local potters drew inspiration from imported Chinese wares. Late seventh to first half of the eighth century.
sectionImages.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Rogers Fund, 1938 · 38.40.274

sectionImages.alt: Close view of the stone Vairocana Buddha’s head, upper body, and carved halo at Fengxian Temple, Longmen.
sectionImages.caption: Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple, Longmen Grottoes, completed in 675. A surviving example of Buddhist sculpture from the Tang imperial court’s era of patronage. Photograph taken in 2009.
sectionImages.credit: Gary Todd · Wikimedia Commons

sectionImages.caption: Older and later canal courses connect the Yellow River and Yangtze regions. This composite map explains transport geography; it is not a map of a single year or of migration routes.

cards.name: Wu Zetian (武则天)’s Zhou dynasty
cards.description: In 690, Wu Zetian (武则天) took the imperial title and founded her own Zhou dynasty, interrupting [[id:tang|Tang rule]]. A woman occupying the emperor’s position broke established expectations. Keeping that position required a working government, loyal supporters and ways to persuade others that her rule was legitimate.

sections.title: Choosing officials
sections.text: Wu expanded recruitment through examinations, opening opportunities beyond established court connections. Successful candidates could owe their advancement to her support. This did not mean that ability alone determined promotion: she also favoured relatives and sought the prestige of aristocratic family connections. New routes into office worked alongside older forms of privilege.

sections.title: Poetry and court connections
sections.text: Her support for writers made the court an important place to seek recognition. Access was uneven, and writers formed new poetic communities as they pursued opportunities or faced exclusion. Poetry belonged to this world of friendships, patronage and political ambition. Wu’s government depended on the relationships around her as well as on her own unusual position.

cards.name: Five Dynasties
cards.description: Between Tang’s fall in 907 and Song’s foundation in 960, five dynasties succeeded one another in the north. Some regional states lasted much longer. Military commanders could make and unmake emperors, but government did not start again from nothing with each new ruling family.
cards.note: 907–960 concerns the five northern dynasties. The wider regional division extends beyond those dates.
cards.catalogNote: 907–960 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

sections.title: Armies and personal loyalty
sections.text: Commanders depended on relationships with their troops and on access to money and supplies. These ties could help a ruler take power, then allow another commander to overthrow him. Offices, armies and regional centres often survived a change of dynasty, even when the people at the top changed quickly.

sections.title: The foundations of Song
sections.text: Later Zhou strengthened its military and government and expanded its territory before Song was founded. Song inherited that work and continued the struggle to bring regional states under one court. The year 960 therefore marks a new dynasty, not an instant end to division. Reunification depended on campaigns and negotiations that continued after the Five Dynasties period.

cards.name: Song
cards.description: The Song (宋 Sòng) dynasty ruled much of China from 960 to 1279. Its era brought government-issued paper money, movable-type printing and celebrated landscape painting. Founded by Emperor Taizu (太祖 Tàizǔ), it reunited much of a divided China before losing the north in 1127; its southern court survived until the Mongol conquest.

sections.title: Taizu founds the dynasty
sections.text:
In 960, an army commander seized the throne from a child emperor. His name was Zhao Kuangyin (赵匡胤 Zhào Kuāngyìn), better known as Emperor Taizu (r. 960–976). Backed by his troops, he forced the ruler of Later Zhou (后周 Hòu Zhōu) to abdicate and founded the Song.

China had been divided since the fall of the [[id:tang|Tang]] (唐 Táng). In the north, military leaders repeatedly overthrew one another; in the south, rival kingdoms ruled independently. Later Zhou was the last of the northern regimes in this [[id:five-dynasties|Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period]] (五代十国 Wǔdài Shíguó). When its emperor died in 959, his young son inherited the throne. Taizu took power the following year.

From his capital at Kaifeng (开封 Kāifēng), Taizu conquered several southern kingdoms and brought their tax revenues under Song control. His brother and successor, Emperor Taizong (太宗 Tàizōng, r. 976–997), completed the remaining conquests and submissions by 979. Reuniting much of China took the two emperors nearly twenty years.

Taizu knew that another general could overthrow him in turn. He and his successors put civilian officials in charge of regional government, brought strong military units into the central army and rotated commanders. Generals had less freedom to build the personal armies that had brought earlier rulers to power.

sections.title: Northern Song and Southern Song
sections.text:
The Northern Song (北宋 Běi Sòng, 960–1127) ruled from Kaifeng over much of northern and southern China. It shared the wider region with powerful neighbours: the Khitan-ruled [[id:liao|Liao]] (辽 Liáo) to the north and the Tangut-ruled [[id:western-xia|Western Xia]] (西夏 Xī Xià) to the northwest. Song campaigns failed to recover all the northern lands its rulers claimed. Agreements with [[id:chanyuan|Liao in 1005]] and Xia in 1044 brought peace in return for annual payments.

Hoping to regain northern territory, Song joined the Jurchen-ruled [[id:jurchen-jin|Jin]] (金 Jīn) in an attack on Liao. Jin then turned against Song. Its armies [[id:jingkang|captured Kaifeng in 1127]] and took both the reigning emperor and his father prisoner.

Another member of the imperial family took the throne as Emperor Gaozong (高宗 Gāozōng, r. 1127–1162). His court fled south and, after years on the move, settled at Hangzhou (杭州 Hángzhōu). Officially called Lin'an (临安 Lín'ān), it became the capital in 1138.

The Southern Song (南宋 Nán Sòng, 1127–1279) was the same dynasty ruling from a new capital. It had lost the north, but retained populous southern lands with productive farms and busy markets. Their wealth sustained the court and its armies for another century and a half. A peace agreement with Jin in 1141–42 recognised the division, although Song rulers continued to hope for recovery of the north.

sections.title: Governing through educated officials
sections.text:
Song emperors relied increasingly on officials selected through the civil examinations (科举 kējǔ). Candidates studied classical texts and practised the writing required for government service. Passing could win a government post and bring status to a whole family. Parents invested in schooling and books to give their sons that chance.

Years of study were expensive. Families already connected to government could afford better preparation and had other routes into office. Women could study and teach their children, but could not sit the examinations or enter the civil service.

Civilian officials also supervised a large professional army. Paying soldiers and defending the borders put heavy demands on the treasury. From 1069, [[id:song-wang-anshi|Wang Anshi]] (王安石 Wáng Ānshí), supported by Emperor Shenzong (神宗 Shénzōng), introduced reforms that included government loans to farmers, changes to labour obligations and local militia training. He hoped to help farming households and increase government revenue. Opponents disputed how the reforms worked and whom they helped. The struggle over his policies outlasted his years in office.

sections.title: Rice, paper money and sea trade
sections.text:
New rice varieties helped feed the growing towns. Early-ripening, drought-resistant Champa rice from Southeast Asia could grow in places less suited to older varieties. Farmers also extended irrigation and brought more land into cultivation. More food supported a larger population, while farming families sold surplus crops and specialised in products such as tea and silk. The [[id:southward-economic-shift|south's economic expansion]] was already well advanced before the court moved there in 1127.

Song merchants and officials developed new ways to pay for this trade. In Sichuan (四川 Sìchuān), merchants used paper notes to avoid carrying heavy iron coins. In 1023, the government set up an office to issue [[id:song-paper-money|paper currency]]. Paper notes could carry a large value without the weight of metal, although coins remained in use.

Large ships carried Chinese ceramics, silk and books overseas. Magnetic compasses helped sailors navigate, and watertight compartments limited the spread of water through a damaged hull. Taxes on maritime commerce supplied government revenue. Southern Song also maintained a powerful navy, which fought for a state increasingly dependent on its rivers and coast.

sections.title: Movable type and gunpowder weapons
sections.text:
Bi Sheng (毕昇 Bì Shēng) developed movable type in the 1040s. Printers could arrange individual clay characters to make a page, then reuse them for another text. Woodblock printing, in which a whole page was carved on a block, remained more widely used. The larger expansion of printing put examination guides, religious works and practical manuals within reach of more readers.

Gunpowder acquired new military uses during the Song. Armies used [[id:song-gunpowder|gunpowder incendiary weapons]], including grenades thrown by catapults, and military manuals recorded recipes for making the powder. These weapons spread fire during sieges. Song's enemies also acquired its technology, so inventions could give an advantage without guaranteeing victory.

sections.title: Landscape painting and Confucian learning
sections.text:
Song painters made mountains, rivers and forests the main subjects of major works. In a monumental landscape by Fan Kuan (范宽 Fàn Kuān), towering peaks dwarf the travellers below. Ink and brushwork could suggest rock, mist and distance on a hanging scroll. Landscape painting became one of the best-known achievements of Chinese art.

Potters produced ceramics for a wide market. Cizhou (磁州 Cízhōu) was known for black-and-white stoneware, including vases decorated with carved peonies. Similar wares were made elsewhere in northern China. Merchants carried bowls, dishes and vases from regional workshops to buyers across China and overseas.

Confucian scholars reconsidered how people should learn and live. [[id:song-zhu-xi|Zhu Xi]] (朱熹 Zhū Xī) helped establish academies and taught that study should shape personal conduct and family responsibilities. His commentaries on the Four Books (四书 Sìshū), a collection of Confucian texts, brought earlier teachings into an influential programme of moral education. His ideas faced opposition in his lifetime before gaining official support.

sections.title: Mongol conquest and what continued
sections.text:
The Mongols conquered Southern Song after decades of war. Chinese soldiers, sailors and engineers helped their armies besiege cities and fight on the rivers. The fall of the stronghold of Xiangyang (襄阳 Xiāngyáng) in 1273 opened an invasion route into the south. Hangzhou surrendered in 1276, but surviving members of the imperial family continued resistance. Their final naval defeat in 1279 ended Song rule.

Southern China became part of the Mongol [[id:yuan|Yuan]] (元 Yuán) dynasty. Song books remained in use, and later rulers adopted Zhu Xi's interpretations of the Confucian classics for the civil examinations. Students continued to study his work long after the dynasty that produced it had fallen.

dateReview.note: 960–1279 is secure; the 1127 division and incomplete territorial unification are correctly noted.

cards.name: Yuan
cards.description: The Yuan (元 Yuán) dynasty was [[id:early-yuan|founded by Kublai Khan in 1271]]. Its Mongol rulers conquered southern China in 1279 and governed a reunited China until 1368. Yuan China was connected to trade across Asia and produced celebrated plays, paintings and [[id:yuan-blue-white|blue-and-white porcelain]], while Mongols retained privileges over their conquered subjects.
cards.catalogNote: 1271 dates the Yuan dynastic name, 1279 the final Song conquest. 1368 ends Yuan rule from Beijing, not all subsequent Mongol or Northern Yuan rule.

sections.title: Kublai founds the Yuan
sections.text:
Kublai inherited a war of conquest that had begun before his birth. His grandfather, Genghis Khan, united the Mongols under his leadership in 1206 and launched campaigns across Asia. After Genghis died, his successors destroyed the [[id:jurchen-jin|Jin]] (金 Jīn) dynasty in 1234 and took control of northern China. The [[id:song|Song]] (宋 Sòng) continued to rule the south.

Kublai became great khan in 1260 after a disputed succession. He wanted the wealth of southern China to support his armies, court and nobles. Taking its cities required fleets and siege weapons, as well as cavalry. Chinese soldiers, shipbuilders and engineers helped the Mongols fight across rivers and break through fortified towns.

In 1271, Kublai gave his state the Chinese dynastic name Yuan. He adopted Chinese court ceremonies and government offices to rule the lands his family had conquered. His capital, [[id:catalog-C_BEIJING_YUAN|Dadu]] (大都 Dàdū), was built at present-day Beijing (北京 Běijīng). He also kept a summer court at Shangdu (上都 Shàngdū), where hunting and life on the grasslands remained part of imperial routine.

Kublai was both a Mongol khan and an emperor of China. The government he built preserved Mongol authority while drawing on Chinese officials and institutions to collect taxes and administer the country.

sections.title: Conquest, expansion and rival khans
sections.text:
The Yuan declaration came eight years before the conquest of Song was complete. After a long siege, Xiangyang (襄阳 Xiāngyáng) fell in 1273. Its capture opened the way into the south. The Song capital at Hangzhou (杭州 Hángzhōu) surrendered in 1276, and the last Song resistance ended in 1279. Northern and southern China were once again under one dynasty.

Kublai tried to extend his power overseas. Fleets attacked Japan in 1274 and 1281, but both invasions failed. The second fleet suffered devastating storm damage. These campaigns consumed ships, men and money without bringing Japan under Yuan rule.

The other Mongol rulers across Asia did not all obey Kublai. Separate khanates governed territories farther west, including Persia and southern Russia, and rival Mongol princes fought one another. Yuan China belonged to this wider Mongol world, but its emperor did not directly govern every Mongol conquest.

Kublai died in 1294. His successors kept the dynasty in power for another seventy-four years, although struggles within the ruling family repeatedly disrupted the court. Emperors could be removed by coups or assassination. Officials and commanders had to navigate these changes of ruler as well as run the government.

sections.title: Government and unequal status
sections.text:
The Yuan retained ministries responsible for taxes, appointments, justice and public works. Provincial offices carried out orders beyond the capital. Mongol overseers helped keep these officials answerable to the ruling group.

A person's background affected their prospects. Mongols enjoyed the greatest privileges. The court also recruited Central Asians and other outsiders, often giving them positions of authority over Chinese subjects. People from the former Jin territories and those from the conquered Song south were treated differently in appointments and law. Southern Chinese generally faced the greatest disadvantages.

The state also assigned many families hereditary occupations. A military household had to supply soldiers; an artisan household owed skilled work to the government. These duties passed to later generations. Families that could not meet them sometimes fled rather than remain registered where officials could find them.

The civil examinations (科举 kējǔ), which had been an important route into Song government, returned in the early fourteenth century. Quotas favoured Mongols and other privileged groups, and examinations filled only a small share of official posts. Educated men also found work as clerks, teachers and doctors. Some refused to serve the conquerors, while others entered government hoping to protect their communities.

sections.title: Canals, ports and journeys across Asia
sections.text:
Dadu needed grain from the productive south. The Yuan extended the [[id:sui-grand-canal|Grand Canal]] (大运河 Dà Yùnhé) north to the capital and also transported supplies by sea. Floods and silt repeatedly blocked the canal, so officials had to switch between routes. Keeping the court supplied required ships, repairs and labour on a large scale.

At [[id:song-quanzhou|Quanzhou]] (泉州 Quánzhōu), foreign merchant communities traded through a busy seaport. Ships carried Chinese ceramics to buyers around the Indian Ocean. The Yuan also continued the use of [[id:song-paper-money|paper currency]] inherited from earlier dynasties, including arrangements to exchange old Song notes for Yuan money.

Mongol rulers welcomed merchants and recruited officials from distant lands. Travellers carried knowledge as well as goods: Persian and Indian astronomy and mathematics reached China, while Chinese technologies travelled west. Marco Polo's account introduced European readers to wealthy Chinese cities and the use of paper money.

Some people travelled by choice; others were moved by force. Mongol conquerors took skilled workers from captured cities and sent them far from home to serve their rulers. The same connections that offered merchants new customers could mean compulsory service for an artisan.

[[id:yuan-religions|Religious communities]] also crossed these routes. Buddhists, Muslims and Christians lived under Yuan rule alongside Chinese religious traditions. Kublai especially favoured Tibetan Buddhism. Patronage was unequal, and his support for Buddhists could come at the expense of their Daoist rivals.

sections.title: Plays, paintings and porcelain
sections.text:
The Yuan was a major age of [[id:yuan-drama|Chinese drama]]. Plays combined spoken dialogue with songs, commonly arranged in four acts. Their subjects included love, family conflict and injustice. Performances could reach audiences who would never read a literary text.

Guan Hanqing (关汉卿 Guān Hànqīng) wrote The Injustice to Dou E (窦娥冤 Dòu É yuān), about a widow wrongly condemned to death. She confesses to a murder to save her mother-in-law from torture.

Painting offered another form of expression. Zhao Mengfu (赵孟頫 Zhào Mèngfǔ), a descendant of the Song imperial family, became a Yuan official and an influential painter and calligrapher. Some former friends condemned his decision to serve the Mongols. Yuan scholar-painters used brushwork to express personal taste and feeling, and studied older paintings as models. Later collectors eagerly sought their work.

Potters at Jingdezhen (景德镇 Jǐngdézhèn) made blue-and-white porcelain by painting cobalt designs beneath a transparent glaze. The surviving David Vases have dragons around their bodies and elephant-head handles. Their inscriptions date them to 1351 and record a gift to a Daoist temple.

sections.title: Rebellion and the Ming takeover
sections.text:
In the dynasty's final decades, floods, famine and epidemics added to the hardships of taxation and compulsory labour. Court disputes weakened the government's response. The [[id:red-turbans|Red Turban rebellions]] (红巾军 Hóngjīnjūn) spread as rebel leaders gathered followers among people who had lost their livelihoods. Forced river work in 1351 helped fuel the unrest.

Zhu Yuanzhang (朱元璋 Zhū Yuánzhāng), a poor young man who had spent time in a Buddhist monastery, joined the rebels. He built his own army and defeated rival leaders. In 1368 he founded the [[id:ming|Ming]] (明 Míng) dynasty, and his forces took Dadu. The Yuan emperor fled north with his court.

The loss of China did not end the ruling family's claims or its power in Mongolia. Yuan rulers and their successors continued there, while the Ming inherited parts of the government they had displaced. Military and artisan families still owed hereditary service under the new dynasty.

cards.name: Ming
cards.description: The Ming (明 Míng) dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644 after overthrowing [[id:yuan|Mongol rule]]. Its emperors built [[id:catalog-C_BEIJING_MING|Beijing’s]] (北京 Běijīng) imperial palace and much of today’s Great Wall (长城 Chángchéng). Growing trade and population supported a flourishing market for porcelain, silk and books before rebellion and conquest ended the dynasty.
cards.catalogNote: 1368–1644 is the main Ming court convention. Southern Ming successors survived after Beijing fell.

sections.title: Zhu Yuanzhang founds the Ming
sections.text:
Zhu Yuanzhang (朱元璋 Zhū Yuánzhāng), the founding Hongwu emperor (洪武 Hóngwǔ, r. 1368–1398), came from a poor farming family. After famine and disease killed his parents, he entered a Buddhist monastery and spent time begging for food. In 1352 he joined the [[id:red-turbans|Red Turban rebels]] (红巾军 Hóngjīnjūn), one of several movements fighting the Mongol-led Yuan (元 Yuán) dynasty.

The Yuan government was losing control as disasters and rebellion spread. Zhu built an army, recruited advisers and captured Nanjing (南京 Nánjīng) in 1356. From this base, he defeated rival rebel leaders. In January 1368 he proclaimed the Ming dynasty. His forces took the Yuan capital later that year, and the Mongol emperor fled north. Further campaigns brought remaining territories under Ming control.

Hongwu wanted farming households to provide dependable taxes and service to the state. He registered land and families, and assigned hereditary duties to soldiers and craftsmen. A military family, for example, had to keep supplying a soldier across generations.

He also concentrated power in his own hands. In 1380 he executed his chief minister and [[id:hongwu-chancellor|abolished the chancellorship]], leaving the ministries directly answerable to the emperor. Purges killed thousands of officials and their associates. Later rulers relied on senior secretaries to manage the paperwork, but the founder’s system gave no single minister an independent position above the others.

sections.title: Yongle’s capital and ocean voyages
sections.text:
Hongwu’s death in 1398 brought his grandson to the throne. The new emperor soon faced a rebellion led by his uncle Zhu Di (朱棣 Zhū Dì), an experienced commander based in the north. After a civil war, Zhu Di seized Nanjing in 1402 and became the Yongle emperor (永乐 Yǒnglè, r. 1402–1424).

Yongle made Beijing the main capital in 1421. There he built the Forbidden City (紫禁城 Zǐjìnchéng), the palace compound used by China’s emperors for the next five centuries. The [[id:sui-grand-canal|Grand Canal]] (大运河 Dà Yùnhé) carried grain from the south to feed the northern court and its troops. Nanjing remained a secondary capital.

Yongle also sent fleets into the Indian Ocean under [[id:zheng-he|Zheng He]] (郑和 Zhèng Hé), a Muslim [[id:catalog-E_MING_EUNUCH_1|eunuch]] who served as a naval commander. Seven expeditions between 1405 and 1433 visited ports across Southeast Asia and as far as East Africa. They carried gifts and brought foreign envoys to the Ming court, where rulers could acknowledge the emperor’s authority through tribute missions.

The last voyage sailed after Yongle’s death. Later emperors stopped these costly expeditions. Chinese merchants continued sailing overseas, although [[id:ming-maritime-conflict|government restrictions]] often put their trade outside the law.

sections.title: The northern frontier
sections.text:
Expelling the Yuan court had not removed the Mongol armies beyond China’s northern border. Ming rulers fought campaigns, negotiated trade and built defences to deal with them. In 1449, a Ming emperor led an expedition north and was [[id:tumu-crisis|captured at Tumu]] (土木 Tǔmù). The court installed another emperor, and the dynasty survived the defeat.

Much of the familiar brick-and-stone Great Wall dates from the Ming. Watchtowers passed warnings along the frontier, while garrisons guarded fortified passes. Earlier dynasties had built walls too, but the Ming defences were extensive new works and reconstructions. They required continuing supplies, repairs and soldiers.

The coast posed different problems. Restrictions on private sea trade encouraged smuggling, and armed raiders attacked coastal settlements. The government relaxed the overseas trade ban in 1567. Throughout the dynasty, officials had to decide which contacts to permit and which to fight.

sections.title: Silver, crops and a larger population
sections.text:
By the later Ming, merchants linked farming regions, workshops and cities through busy markets. Some communities specialised in cotton cloth, others in silk or sugar. Women spun and wove at home, supplying textiles that merchants sold far from the villages where they were made.

China’s population grew substantially. Estimates place it at roughly 60–80 million near the dynasty’s beginning and 150–200 million toward its end, although some estimates are higher. These are reconstructions rather than reliable census totals. Late in the dynasty, new crops from the Americas, including maize and sweet potatoes, allowed farmers to cultivate some land poorly suited to established crops.

Foreign buyers paid for Chinese silk and porcelain with silver. Supplies came from Japan and, through [[id:manila-silver|Manila in the Philippines]], from mines in the Spanish Americas. This trade connected Chinese producers to markets across the Pacific as well as the Indian Ocean.

Silver also became central to taxation. Reforms extended under [[id:zhang-juzheng|Zhang Juzheng]] (张居正 Zhāng Jūzhèng) in the late sixteenth century combined many taxes and labour obligations into payments in silver. Officials could then pay workers instead of summoning households for compulsory service. Farmers who sold produce for copper coins still had to obtain the silver needed for their taxes.

sections.title: Books, learning and new ideas
sections.text:
The civil service examinations (科举 kējǔ) again became the main route into government. Families invested in teaching boys the classical texts on which they would be tested. Provincial quotas helped spread opportunities beyond the richest and best-educated regions, although success remained difficult.

Printers sold books to a growing market. Long novels drew on stories that performers had told for generations. [[id:ming-journey-west|Journey to the West]] (西游记 Xīyóu jì) followed a Buddhist pilgrim and his magical companions, including the Monkey King, on their journey to India. Romance of the Three Kingdoms (三国演义 Sānguó yǎnyì) turned the struggles after the [[id:han|Han]] (汉 Hàn) dynasty into an extended tale of rival rulers and warriors.

[[id:ming-wang-yangming|Wang Yangming]] (王阳明 Wáng Yángmíng) challenged the idea that moral understanding depended on years of scholarly investigation. He argued that people possessed an innate knowledge of right and wrong, which they had to put into practice. Knowing how to honour one’s parents, for example, meant acting accordingly in daily life.

Contacts with European missionaries brought exchanges in astronomy, mathematics and geography. Matteo Ricci worked with Chinese scholars, and his [[id:ricci-world-map|Chinese-language world map of 1602]] included the Americas. Some educated readers welcomed this learning while rejecting the missionaries’ religious claims.

sections.title: Porcelain for the court and the world
sections.text:
Jingdezhen (景德镇 Jǐngdézhèn) supplied porcelain to the imperial court and to buyers at home and overseas. Workshops divided the work of shaping, decorating and firing vessels among specialised workers. Imperial orders demanded particular shapes and designs, and pieces that failed inspection could be deliberately smashed.

Blue-and-white wares had cobalt decoration beneath a clear glaze. Potters also made brightly coloured enamelled pieces. A surviving jar from the Jiajing reign (嘉靖 Jiājìng, 1522–1566) combines blue dragons with stylised characters for longevity. It was made at Jingdezhen in an imperial workshop. Other kilns produced wares for sale across the world.

sections.title: Rebellion and the Qing conquest
sections.text:
In the early seventeenth century, the Ming faced mounting military costs while drought, famine and epidemics devastated communities. Tax revenues fell, soldiers went unpaid, and rebel armies gained recruits. The court also fought an expanding Manchu state in the northeast.

In 1644, [[id:li-zicheng-beijing|Li Zicheng]] (李自成 Lǐ Zìchéng) captured Beijing with a rebel army. The Chongzhen emperor (崇祯 Chóngzhēn) killed himself. The Ming commander Wu Sangui (吴三桂 Wú Sānguì) then allied with the Manchus against Li. Their forces defeated the rebels, and the Manchu-led [[id:qing|Qing]] (清 Qīng) took the capital.

The conquest continued after 1644. Members of the Ming ruling family maintained rival courts in the south, collectively known as the [[id:southern-ming|Southern Ming]] (南明 Nán Míng). The last of these emperors was killed in 1662. The Qing kept Beijing as their capital and continued to govern from the Forbidden City.

cards.name: Qing
cards.description: The Qing (清 Qīng) was China’s last imperial dynasty, ruling from 1644 to 1912. [[id:early-qing|Founded by the Manchus before their conquest of China]], it built an enormous empire and governed a rapidly growing population. Its final decades brought foreign invasions, civil wars and reforms that preceded the founding of [[id:republic|a republic]].
cards.catalogNote: 1644–1912 is valid for rule from Beijing. The Qing dynastic name was proclaimed in 1636; the emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912, after the revolution began in 1911.

sections.title: A dynasty built before the conquest
sections.text:
The Qing began with a state northeast of [[id:ming|Ming]] (明 Míng) China. Nurhaci (努尔哈赤 Nǔ'ěrhāchì), a Jurchen leader, united neighbouring communities through alliances and conquest. His Eight Banners (八旗 bāqí) organised soldiers together with the families, farmers and craftspeople who supported them. In 1616, he declared a dynasty called Later Jin (后金 Hòu Jīn).

His son Hong Taiji (皇太极 Huáng Tàijí) expanded this state, recruited Chinese officials and soldiers, and adopted the dynastic name Qing in 1636. The Manchus therefore entered the struggle for China with an established army and government. They could offer defeated Ming commanders positions in a new regime.

The opportunity came in 1644. [[id:li-zicheng-beijing|Li Zicheng]] (李自成 Lǐ Zìchéng) captured [[id:catalog-C_BEIJING_QING|Beijing]] (北京 Běijīng), and the last Ming emperor killed himself. The Ming general Wu Sangui (吴三桂 Wú Sānguì) allied with the Manchus against Li. Qing forces took the capital under Dorgon (多尔衮 Duō'ěrgǔn), regent for the child Shunzhi emperor (顺治 Shùnzhì).

Victory at Beijing began decades of conquest. [[id:southern-ming|Southern Ming]] (南明 Nán Míng) courts continued to resist. The order that men shave the front of their heads and wear a long plait became a public test of submission; resistance brought severe punishment, including massacres. Under the [[id:kangxi-rule|Kangxi emperor]] (康熙 Kāngxī), the Qing defeated a major rebellion by former allied commanders in 1681 and conquered the Zheng family’s regime in Taiwan (台湾 Táiwān) in 1683.

sections.title: The eighteenth-century empire
sections.text:
Kangxi and his successors Yongzheng (雍正 Yōngzhèng) and Qianlong (乾隆 Qiánlóng) presided over the Qing’s greatest expansion. Their empire included Mongolia, Tibet and [[id:qing-inner-asia|Xinjiang]] (新疆 Xīnjiāng), far beyond the territory the Ming had governed. By the time Qianlong formally retired in 1796, the Qing had become one of the largest empires in world history.

These conquests were costly and sometimes devastating. The destruction of the Dzungar state in the 1750s included mass killing. Garrisons and settlement helped secure the conquered lands, but distant territories required continuing military expenditure.

The emperors governed this varied empire through different institutions. Chinese provinces retained officials trained in the classical tradition. Mongol nobles and Tibetan religious authorities had their own relationships with the throne. Manchu identity, language and banner privileges remained important at court.

The population and economy were immense. Historical estimates for 1820 put China at more than a third of the world’s population and about a third of global economic output, making it the world’s largest economy.

sections.title: More people, more trade
sections.text:
China’s population roughly doubled during the eighteenth century, from about 150 million in 1700 to 300 million or more by 1800. Recovery from warfare, longer periods of peace and the cultivation of more land helped sustain this growth. Maize and sweet potatoes could grow in places poorly suited to rice, supporting settlement in uplands and frontier districts.

Merchants connected specialised producing regions with distant customers. Farming families also spun and wove textiles, combining work on the land with goods for sale. Tea, silk and porcelain reached overseas buyers. European ships traded under restrictions, with their commerce concentrated at Guangzhou (广州 Guǎngzhōu), also known as Canton.

Prosperity did not reach everyone equally. By the mid-nineteenth century, the population exceeded 400 million. As the population grew, farms became smaller, while settlers cleared hillsides that were vulnerable to erosion. More people depended on small plots and supplementary work, leaving households exposed when harvests failed.

sections.title: Books and skilled crafts
sections.text:
The civil service examinations (科举 kējǔ) kept classical learning central to education and official careers. Successful candidates could enter government, while families invested years in preparing sons for fiercely competitive examinations.

The Qing court collected art and commissioned paintings, porcelain, jade and other decorative works. European enamelling materials and techniques reached court workshops in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Chinese craftspeople developed new colours for decorating porcelain, metal and glass. Glass was also shaped into vessels in its own right, including Qianlong-period vases.

Imperial sponsorship also shaped the written record. The [[id:qing-siku|Siku Quanshu]] (四库全书 Sìkù quánshū) project assembled a vast collection of books in the late eighteenth century. The same undertaking enabled officials to identify and suppress writings considered hostile to the dynasty. Collecting knowledge and controlling its circulation went together.

Commercial publishing offered readers fiction as well as scholarship. Cao Xueqin (曹雪芹 Cáo Xuěqín) wrote most of [[id:red-chamber|Dream of the Red Chamber]] (红楼梦 Hónglóu mèng), a novel following the fortunes of a wealthy household. Its characters negotiate marriage, family duty and the unequal relationships between masters and servants. The completed novel appeared in print in 1791 and became one of China’s best-known literary works.

sections.title: Foreign wars and civil rebellion
sections.text:
In the nineteenth century, the Qing faced military challenges it struggled to contain. British traders sold opium grown in India into China despite Chinese prohibitions. In 1839, the official Lin Zexu (林则徐 Lín Zéxú) confiscated opium stocks. Britain [[id:catalog-E_QING_OPIUM|went to war]], using naval forces the Qing could not effectively resist.

The [[id:nanking|Treaty of Nanjing]] (南京 Nánjīng) ended the First Opium War in 1842. China ceded Hong Kong Island (香港岛 Xiānggǎng Dǎo), paid an indemnity and opened five ports to British trade. Further defeat in the [[id:catalog-E_QING_OPIUM2|Second Opium War]] expanded foreign access and privileges.

At the same time, the [[id:catalog-E_QING_TAIPING|Taiping Rebellion]] (太平天国 Tàipíng Tiānguó, 1850–1864) devastated large parts of China. Its leader, Hong Xiuquan (洪秀全 Hóng Xiùquán), claimed a divine mission and established a rival capital at Nanjing. To defeat the rebels, Qing officials raised regional armies whose soldiers depended on particular commanders. The dynasty survived, but provincial military leaders gained influence and huge areas needed rebuilding.

sections.title: Attempts to strengthen the state
sections.text:
From the 1860s, the [[id:catalog-E_QING_SSM|Self-Strengthening Movement]] (洋务运动 Yángwù yùndòng) established arsenals, shipyards and schools for foreign languages and technical learning. Officials sought weapons and practical knowledge that would help defend the empire. [[id:catalog-E_QING_SJ|Defeat by Japan in 1894–1895]] exposed continuing weaknesses; the peace settlement ceded Taiwan and imposed another heavy indemnity.

The Guangxu emperor (光绪 Guāngxù) supported [[id:catalog-E_QING_100D|wider reforms in 1898]], but the Empress Dowager Cixi (慈禧 Cíxǐ) intervened and stopped the programme. In 1900, her court backed the anti-foreign [[id:catalog-E_QING_BOXER|Boxer movement]] (义和团 Yìhétuán). Foreign armies invaded Beijing, and the settlement imposed further financial burdens.

After this disaster, the court introduced extensive changes. New schools taught modern subjects, new armies received different training, and the [[id:qing-exams-end|old examinations ended in 1905]]. Provincial assemblies followed in 1909. These measures created organised groups with expectations of political influence, while promises of a constitution moved too slowly for many reformers.

sections.title: The throne gives way to a republic
sections.text:
[[id:catalog-E_QING_1911|An army mutiny at Wuchang]] (武昌 Wǔchāng) on 10 October 1911 helped set off a revolution. Provinces declared independence from the Qing court. Negotiations between imperial officials, military commanders and revolutionaries brought the dynasty to an end.

On 12 February 1912, the child emperor [[id:abdication|Puyi]] (溥仪 Pǔyí) abdicated. The Republic of China (中华民国 Zhōnghuá Mínguó) replaced the imperial throne, ending a system of dynastic rule that had lasted more than two thousand years.

The republic inherited claims to the Qing’s vast territories, along with its debts and powerful regional armies. Removing the emperor did not establish a strong national government. The struggle over who would govern China continued under the new republic.

cards.name: Republic of China (mainland period)
cards.description: The Republic of China (中华民国 Zhōnghuá Mínguó) replaced imperial rule in 1912. Its mainland years brought struggles to unite the country, new schools and cultural movements, [[id:war-japan|war with Japan]], and [[id:civil-war|civil war]]. Communist victory in 1949 drove the Nationalist government to [[id:roc-taiwan|Taiwan]] (台湾 Táiwān), where the Republic of China continued.
cards.catalogNote: 1 January 1912 is the republic’s founding. 1949 ends this mainland-period card, not the existence of the ROC government, which relocated to Taiwan. Qing abdication followed on 12 February 1912.

sections.title: Sun Yat-sen and the new republic
sections.text:
Sun Yat-sen (孙中山 Sūn Zhōngshān) became provisional president at Nanjing (南京 Nánjīng) on 1 January 1912. He had spent years organising against the [[id:qing|Qing]] (清 Qīng) dynasty and raising support among Chinese communities overseas. His aim was a republic whose government would represent the nation and make China strong enough to resist foreign domination.

Sun had been abroad when the [[id:catalog-E_QING_1911|revolution of 1911]] began. An army uprising spread into a revolt by provinces against the Qing court. The revolutionaries could establish a government in the south, but they lacked the military strength to impose its authority across China.

The strongest northern commander was Yuan Shikai (袁世凯 Yuán Shìkǎi), a former Qing official. Sun agreed to give up the presidency if Yuan secured the [[id:abdication|emperor’s abdication]] and supported a republic. The last emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912, and Yuan succeeded Sun later that year. The republic began through this settlement between revolutionaries and the old regime’s military leadership.

Parliamentary elections followed, but Yuan suppressed his opponents and concentrated power in his own hands. His attempt to become emperor in 1915–1916 provoked resistance. He abandoned the plan and died in 1916, leaving competing commanders to struggle over his army and government.

sections.title: A country divided among armies
sections.text:
During the [[id:warlord-era|warlord period]] (军阀 jūnfá), regional commanders controlled troops and made or broke alliances. A government remained in Beijing (北京 Běijīng), but it could not reliably command the provinces. Controlling the capital gave a military faction foreign recognition without guaranteeing control of the country.

Repeated campaigns disrupted farming, trade and travel. Banditry led communities to organise their own defences. Some cities still supported expanding industries, newspapers and universities. Political fragmentation and cultural experimentation occurred together.

Foreign powers retained privileges inherited from treaties with the Qing. These included control of concessions in important cities and exemptions from Chinese courts. Ending such privileges became a cause shared by students, merchants and competing political movements.

sections.title: The Nationalists reunite much of China
sections.text:
Sun’s Nationalist Party, or Kuomintang (国民党 Guómíndǎng, KMT), sought to defeat the warlords and end foreign privileges. With Soviet assistance, it strengthened its party organisation and army. Members of the [[id:ccp-founding|Chinese Communist Party]] (中国共产党 Zhōngguó Gòngchǎndǎng, CCP), founded in 1921, joined this alliance while retaining their own organisation.

Sun died in 1925. Chiang Kai-shek (蒋介石 Jiǎng Jièshí) led the Northern Expedition (北伐 Běifá), launched in 1926. Military victories and agreements with regional commanders brought much of China under Nationalist authority by 1928. The government ruled from Nanjing, though powerful regional armies remained.

The alliance broke apart during the advance. In 1927, Chiang’s forces and allies killed Communists and labour activists in Shanghai (上海 Shànghǎi). Further purges drove surviving Communists underground or into rural bases. The campaign to unite China also began a prolonged struggle between the Nationalists and Communists.

During the Nanjing decade, the government worked to improve banking, currency, roads and communications. It recovered some rights to set tariffs and reduced foreign privileges. The Nationalists restricted political opposition and governed through party rule. Military spending and continuing conflict limited what they could achieve.

sections.title: New writing, education and women’s rights
sections.text:
The New Culture Movement (新文化运动 Xīn Wénhuà Yùndòng) challenged ideas about education, family authority and China’s future. The journal that became New Youth (新青年 Xīn Qīngnián), founded in 1915, promoted science, political change and writing closer to everyday speech. Reformers wanted readers to express new ideas without mastering the old classical literary language first.

[[id:lu-xun|Lu Xun]] (鲁迅 Lǔ Xùn) used this form of writing in A Madman’s Diary (狂人日记 Kuángrén rìjì), published in 1918. Its narrator imagines a society of cannibals, turning a disturbing story into an attack on cruel social conventions. Fiction became a way to question the authority of families and elders as well as governments.

On 4 May 1919, [[id:catalog-E_MOD_MAY4|students in Beijing protested]] against the Versailles settlement’s transfer of German privileges in Shandong (山东 Shāndōng) to Japan. Demonstrations spread, joined by strikes and boycotts. The May Fourth Movement (五四运动 Wǔsì yùndòng) brought questions of culture and national independence into the same public struggle.

Schools and universities trained teachers, engineers, doctors and other professionals. More women entered education, journalism and paid work. The Nationalists’ civil code in the 1930s gave daughters inheritance rights and expanded women’s rights in marriage and divorce. Many rural families knew little of these laws, and custom often outweighed them.

In Shanghai, publishing, cinema and manufacturing created new jobs and audiences. Factory workers, including many women and girls, endured long hours and poor conditions. The opportunities celebrated in magazines were far beyond the reach of much of the population.

sections.title: The Communists build rural bases
sections.text:
Mao Zedong (毛泽东 Máo Zédōng) and other Communist leaders organised peasants in areas beyond firm Nationalist control. Land redistribution, armed forces and local party networks helped them recruit supporters. Internal purges and coercion also shaped these bases.

Nationalist campaigns forced the Communists to abandon their main southern base in 1934. The [[id:catalog-E_MOD_LONG_MARCH|Long March]] (长征 Chángzhēng), the main Communist army’s retreat in 1934–1935, cost them many lives but preserved a core of troops and leaders. Mao gained authority during these struggles. The party later established its headquarters at Yan’an (延安 Yán’ān) in the northwest.

sections.title: War with Japan
sections.text:
Japan seized Manchuria (满洲 Mǎnzhōu) in 1931 and established a dependent state there. Full-scale war spread across China in 1937. Nationalist armies fought major battles, including a prolonged defence of Shanghai. When Japanese forces captured Nanjing in December, they massacred civilians and disarmed soldiers and committed widespread rape.

The Nationalist government eventually made Chongqing (重庆 Chóngqìng), far inland, its wartime capital. Officials and industries moved away from occupied areas. Repeated bombing, shortages and difficult supply routes made continued resistance costly.

Nationalists and Communists agreed to cooperate against Japan, but mistrust and armed clashes persisted. The Nationalists fought large conventional campaigns while Communist forces expanded guerrilla bases behind Japanese lines. Both drew recruits, food and labour from communities already suffering under invasion and war.

China became an Allied power in the wider Second World War. Foreign supplies helped sustain its forces; roads and air routes through neighbouring countries were important because Japan controlled many coastal approaches. Chinese and American troops working along the Ledo Road formed part of this effort to restore an overland supply route.

Japan’s surrender in 1945 ended the invasion, but left China devastated. Millions had died, many more had fled their homes, and farms and factories had been destroyed. The government had won a place among the victors while exhausting much of its strength.

sections.title: Civil war and the move to Taiwan
sections.text:
Negotiations failed to produce a lasting settlement between the Nationalists and Communists. By 1946, full-scale civil war had resumed. The two sides fought for cities, railways and the resources needed to supply their armies.

The Nationalists began with larger forces and American support, but military defeats, corruption, harsh conscription and runaway inflation eroded their position. The Communists combined military organisation with rural mobilisation and land reform. Their campaigns brought support from many villagers, alongside coercion against people who resisted.

Decisive Communist victories in 1948–1949 destroyed major Nationalist armies. On 1 October 1949, Mao proclaimed the [[id:prc|People’s Republic of China]] (中华人民共和国 Zhōnghuá Rénmín Gònghéguó) in Beijing. The Nationalist government withdrew to Taiwan.

The Republic of China continued there, with its own government and armed forces. Fighting continued across the Taiwan Strait. The rival governments carried their competing claims into the decades that followed.
