image.credit: Anonymous Tang printers; commissioned by Wang Jie · British Library
image.alt: A printed Buddhist assembly above columns of Chinese text.
image.caption: The frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra dated 868, now in the British Library. Its survival makes the relationship between devotion, sponsorship, and woodblock reproduction unusually concrete. The 868 object uses woodblock printing; it must not be mistaken for a surviving example of Bi Sheng’s later movable type.

cards.name: Treaty of Chanyuan (澶渊)
cards.description: In 1005, Song and Liao agreed to end a period of frontier warfare. Song promised annual payments of silver and silk, and the two courts recognized one another’s imperial standing. The settlement made coexistence possible without either side conquering the other.
cards.catalogNote: Mid-January 1005 oath exchange follows the winter campaign of 1004; use 1005 in converted Common Era chronology.

sections.title: The cost of peace
sections.text: Annual payments were easy to criticize, but war also required money for armies and garrisons and disrupted livelihoods along the border. The treaty offered a way to secure the frontier through negotiation. Accepting another emperor meant placing practical limits on each court’s claims to supreme authority.

sections.title: A durable but changeable agreement
sections.text: Repeated embassies and more predictable relations followed. Rivalry and border disputes did not vanish, and the agreement depended on a changing regional balance of power. Song later allied with Jin against Liao, helping overturn the order that the treaty had supported. A century of relative peace was a significant achievement, but it did not make the settlement permanent.

cards.note: 1005 uses the converted common-era year; the agreement followed the winter campaign of 1004. Peace was relative, not the absence of every frontier dispute.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Paul Jakov Smith · The fragility of the Chanyuan peace

dateReview.note: Mid-January 1005 oath exchange follows the winter campaign of 1004; use 1005 in converted Common Era chronology.

image.alt: A seated portrait of Song emperor Zhenzong in formal robes.
image.caption: A traditional portrait of Emperor Zhenzong, whose government concluded the Chanyuan agreement with Liao in 1005. It is court portraiture, not a depiction of the negotiations, and the Commons record gives no artist or date.

cards.name: Fall of Kaifeng (开封)
cards.description: Jin forces captured Kaifeng (开封) in 1127. They took Emperor Qinzong (宋钦宗), the retired Emperor Huizong (宋徽宗) and members of the Song court north as prisoners. Northern Song ended, but a surviving prince established a new Song court that same year.
cards.catalogNote: 1127 dates Northern Song's fall and imperial captivity, at the culmination of the 1126–1127 crisis.

sections.title: An alliance backfires
sections.text: Song had joined the rising Jin against Liao, hoping to recover territory. Once Liao was defeated, Song faced a more dangerous neighbour. Removing an old rival had also removed a state that stood between Song and another expanding power. The earlier alliance left Song in a much more difficult position.

sections.title: Rebuilding in the south
sections.text: Officials and refugees carried skills, possessions and memories south. A new court drew on the region’s existing economic strength to rebuild government. The captive emperors complicated the new ruler’s claim to authority, and recovering the north remained a charged political issue. Southern Song preserved the dynasty while changing its territory, resources and relationship with its northern enemy.

cards.note: 1127 marks Kaifeng (开封)’s fall and the emperors’ captivity after campaigns in 1125–1127. Song continued in the south until 1279.

dateReview.note: 1127 dates Northern Song's fall and imperial captivity, at the culmination of the 1126–1127 crisis.

image.credit: Emperor Huizong of Song (1082–1135) · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Cranes circling above a palace roof in a painted sky.
image.caption: Auspicious Cranes, associated with Emperor Huizong of Song. The courtly vision of an auspicious capital is particularly revealing when read alongside the political disaster of 1127.

cards.name: Ming Voyages
cards.description: Zheng He (郑和)’s first fleet departed in 1405. It began seven Ming-sponsored expeditions that continued until 1433, linking the imperial court with ports across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean. The fleets eventually reached the East African coast, travelling along routes already used by merchants and sailors.

sections.title: Gifts, trade and military power
sections.text: The ships carried envoys, gifts and commercial goods, as well as troops. The expeditions displayed the emperor’s wealth and power and sometimes intervened in local conflicts. Their journeys depended on existing knowledge of navigation and the port communities they visited. These were ambitious state voyages through a connected maritime world.

sections.title: The court ended the voyages; maritime trade continued
sections.text: The Ming court eventually stopped funding these enormous official expeditions as its spending priorities changed. Chinese merchants continued to travel and trade by sea after the fleets ended. The date on this card, 1405, marks the first departure; it does not date the whole series of voyages.

cards.note: 1405 marks the first departure; the seven-expedition programme extended to 1433. The largest ship-size claims remain contested and are not used here.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Journal of Chinese History · Official voyages and private sailings

dateReview.note: 1405 is the first departure. The existing note appropriately explains the seven-voyage sequence through 1433.

image.alt: A tall stone slab with three blocks of inscriptions.
image.caption: The Galle trilingual inscription associated with Zheng He, dated 1409. Chinese, Tamil, and Persian texts place maritime diplomacy within several religious and linguistic worlds.

cards.name: Treaty of Nanking (南京)
cards.description: The Treaty of Nanking (南京) ended the First Opium War in 1842. The Qing ceded Hong Kong (香港) Island to Britain, agreed to pay a large sum of money and opened five ports to British trade and residence. The settlement gave lasting force to demands made through military pressure.

sections.title: From one treaty to a wider system
sections.text: Later agreements added foreign privileges, including arrangements that placed foreigners outside parts of Qing legal authority. Other powers sought similar treatment. These terms accumulated over time. They affected where foreigners could live and trade, which courts could judge disputes and how officials dealt with foreign residents. The later provisions should be distinguished from the original 1842 treaty.

sections.title: Trade on imposed terms
sections.text: Chinese merchants had traded overseas long before the war. The treaty changed the terms on which foreign powers could demand access to Chinese ports. Britain used military victory to secure commercial and territorial concessions. Qing government continued, but its control over foreign activity was reduced. The treaty itself did not legalize the opium trade.

cards.note: 1842: Treaty of Nanking (南京). Extraterritoriality was elaborated in subsequent agreements; the treaty did not itself legalize the opium trade.

sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/milestones/183: U.S. Office of the Historian · Opium War and treaty system

dateReview.note: 1842 is confirmed for the treaty; the distinction between this treaty and subsequent privileges is appropriate.

image.alt: A silver coin stamped with several small Chinese marks.
image.caption: A Mexican Spanish dollar dated 1796, bearing Chinese merchant chop marks. This later coin illustrates the long-lived silver trade, not a coin documented on the first Manila galleon. The nineteenth-century treaty imposed an indemnity denominated in silver dollars; this 1796 coin is a comparable circulating monetary object, not a coin from the payment.

cards.name: End of Imperial China
cards.description: On 12 February 1912, the child emperor Puyi (溥仪) abdicated and Qing rule ended. The Republic of China had already been founded on 1 January. Negotiations among revolutionaries, the court and military leaders brought the monarchy to an end, following the uprising of 1911.

sections.title: A settlement backed by military power
sections.text: Yuan Shikai (袁世凯) commanded forces essential to the court’s survival. Sun Yat-sen (孙中山) agreed to give up the provisional presidency in his favour as part of the settlement. The new republic therefore depended partly on men who had gained power under the Qing. Its civilian leaders still faced the problem of controlling armies and the commanders who led them.

sections.title: A new government, a longer transition
sections.text: Abdication ended the dynasty, but changing the institutions and habits of government took longer. The republic promised citizenship and representative government while officials and military leaders competed for authority. Under the settlement, Puyi (溥仪) continued to live in the Forbidden City until 1924. His departure from power and his departure from the palace were separate events.

sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/countries/chin: U.S. Office of the Historian · Recognition and diplomatic relations
sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/historicaldocu: U.S. diplomatic documents · Abdication and republican transition, 1912

cards.note: Qing abdication: 12 February 1912. The Republic was founded earlier, on 1 January 1912. Puyi (溥仪) remained in the Forbidden City until 1924.

dateReview.note: Qing abdication occurred on 12 February 1912, after the ROC provisional government was established on 1 January.

image.credit: George Grantham Bain Collection · Library of Congress
image.license: Public domain in the United States
image.alt: Three-year-old Puyi wearing formal court clothing and a hat.
image.caption: Puyi at age three in 1909, during his reign as the Xuantong emperor. He abdicated in February 1912 at age six, ending Qing rule.

cards.name: Yu founds Xia (legendary tradition)
cards.description: Later tradition describes Yu founding Xia as the beginning of dynastic rule. The familiar date of 2070 BCE comes from a reconstructed chronology. No contemporary document confirms a foundation in that year, so this event belongs to a tradition whose details remain uncertain.
cards.note: 2070 BCE is traditional and uncertain. This is not an asserted archaeological identification of Xia or an independently dated coronation.

sections.title: Earning the right to rule
sections.text: In the story, Yu restores a habitable world after terrible flooding. His service to people gives him the right to govern. Power then passes to his son, introducing rule by a hereditary family. Later thinkers could use this tension to ask a lasting question: should a ruler choose the most capable successor, or should the office stay in the family?

sections.title: Searching for traces
sections.text: Excavated settlements, elite buildings and evidence of ancient floods can help reconstruct the world in which these stories developed. They cannot establish that a named hero founded a dynasty in a particular year. Connecting a flood deposit, a settlement and a much later account requires evidence for each connection. Xia’s archaeological identity remains unsettled.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Early China · Erlitou and the search for Xia

dateReview.note: 2070 BCE is a reconstructed Xia boundary, not an independently verified event. Existing approx and note disclose uncertainty. Prefer an undated legendary card; if a plotted reference is required, preserve the qualifier visibly and never treat it as a factual coronation date.

cards.catalogNote: No historically verified founding year. Existing 2070 BCE derives from the selected Xia reconstruction, not independent evidence of Yu founding a dynasty. Do not display it as an exact dated event. Numeric year is retained solely as an editorial placement for compatibility; it is not an asserted historical date.

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A rubbing of a carved figure holding an implement.
image.caption: A Han-period stone relief representing Yu the Great. It records how later generations remembered Yu, not his appearance or an eyewitness account of flood control.

cards.name: Yu the Great (大禹) (legendary figure)
cards.description: Yu the Great (大禹) is a legendary hero remembered for controlling a catastrophic flood and bringing order to the land. Later traditions place him before or at the founding of Xia. His position in this early period does not give us a verified birth date.
cards.note: Yu is legendary; no verified dates are known. His identity and connection with particular floods are not securely established.

sections.title: A ruler working with water
sections.text: Stories describe Yu channelling rivers and opening passages. He earns authority through practical work for a wider community. Later rulers could draw on this example when explaining their own water projects and duties. If managing water was part of a ruler’s responsibility, failure could also become a judgment on his government.

sections.title: The limits of the evidence
sections.text: Different accounts of Yu were assembled long after the events they describe. Geological evidence can identify ancient floods, but cannot name the person who responded to them. Yu’s identity and lifetime remain uncertain. His influence on later political and religious life is much easier to trace: generations used his story to think about service, leadership and the difficult relationship between people and water.

sourceLabels.https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/6: Oxford Handbook of Chinese Archaeology · Geoarchaeology and flood myths

dateReview.note: 2100 BCE has no verified birth/activity basis. Existing text acknowledges this, but a date label alone can mislead. Recommended date display is Unknown (legendary); numeric 2100 may serve only as explicitly editorial placement, never as historical date.

cards.catalogNote: 2100 BCE is not a verified birth or activity date. No exact lifetime should be assigned. Keep as an undated legendary figure or use a separately labelled editorial placement. Numeric year is retained solely as an editorial placement for compatibility; it is not an asserted historical date.

image.credit: Xie Sui · National Palace Museum / Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A painted landscape showing Yu directing workers during flood-control efforts.
image.caption: Xie Sui’s Qing-period painting imagines Yu directing flood-control work. Made millennia after the legendary age, it records a later visual tradition rather than the historical appearance of Yu or the flood.

cards.name: Zhou conquest of Shang
cards.description: King Wu (周武王)’s defeat of Shang became the founding victory of Zhou. Bronze inscriptions and later books preserve memories of the conquest, although its exact date remains disputed. Rebellion and further campaigns, associated with the Duke of Zhou (周公), followed the first victory.
cards.note: 1046 BCE is a widely used conventional date. The subsequent consolidation is not compressed into a claim that the entire Zhou order began on one day.

sections.title: Building a new ruling order
sections.text: Zhou rulers had to reward allies and decide how to deal with the people who had served Shang. They kept some Shang ceremonies and drew on useful specialists. Changing the ruling family did not erase everything the old court had built. The new dynasty needed relationships and places of authority that could survive beyond the battlefield.

sections.title: Why Heaven could change sides
sections.text: Later accounts explain Shang’s defeat by saying its rulers lost virtue and Heaven’s favour passed to Zhou. This made rebellion against a king acceptable when he no longer deserved to govern. The same argument could later be turned against other rulers. The conquest became both an event in political history and a story through which generations debated the duties of government.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Early China · Zhou royal memory and bronze inscriptions

dateReview.note: 1046 BCE is a widely adopted reconstructed date for the Zhou conquest, not universally agreed. Display c. 1046 BCE.

cards.catalogNote: 1046 BCE is a widely adopted reconstructed date for the Zhou conquest, not universally agreed. Display c. 1046 BCE.

image.alt: A standing ruler in ceremonial robes, identified as King Wu of Zhou.
image.caption: A later painting traditionally identified as King Wu, the Zhou ruler associated with the conquest of Shang. It is an imagined dynastic portrait, not a contemporary likeness or a picture of the battle.

cards.name: Zhou
cards.description: Zhou began with a royal network built after the conquest of Shang. Over nearly eight centuries, it changed into a world of competing kingdoms around a weakened king. Western and Eastern Zhou name two phases of the royal house, whose power and circumstances changed greatly.
cards.note: 1046–256 BCE dates the royal dynasty using the timeline’s convention. Its fall precedes the conclusion of Warring States politics in 221 BCE.

sections.title: A respected title, less control
sections.text: As the king’s reach shrank, Zhou titles, ceremonies and ancestors still carried weight. Powerful regional rulers could seek recognition from a court that could no longer reliably command their armies. Respect for the royal house helped shape relationships even after much of its practical power had passed elsewhere.

sections.title: An example for later teachers
sections.text: Later thinkers described Zhou as a model of good government. They used its poems, rituals and stories to answer problems in their own time. Different teachers selected different lessons, so the Zhou past was continually interpreted. What later generations called the Zhou ideal was shaped by those arguments as well as by the institutions of the early dynasty.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Early China · Zhou royal memory and bronze inscriptions

dateReview.note: Approximately 1046–256 BCE follows the Met chronology. The beginning is reconstructed; 256 BCE is the conventional end of Zhou royal rule.

cards.catalogNote: Approximately 1046–256 BCE follows the Met chronology. The beginning is reconstructed; 256 BCE is the conventional end of Zhou royal rule.

image.credit: originally by Qiang, an official who lived in ~917/15 to 900 BC · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A rubbing of tightly ordered columns of bronze-script characters.
image.caption: A rubbing of the inscription inside the Shi Qiang pan, a Western Zhou ritual basin. Its account of royal and family ancestors shows political memory being cast into bronze. The inscription predates the Gonghe regency and provides context for Western Zhou royal memory, not a record of that regency.

cards.name: Spring and Autumn Period
cards.description: During the Spring and Autumn period, strong regional rulers competed to lead alliances while still seeking recognition from the Zhou king. The Five Hegemons, or leading lords, traditionally include Duke Huan of Qi (齐桓公) and Duke Wen of Jin (晋文公). Lists differ over the other three.
cards.note: 770–481 BCE is the dating used here. Other accounts use 476/475 BCE and other boundaries; 481 BCE does not mark a universal change in government.

sections.title: Alliances and ceremonies
sections.text: Marriages, visits and sworn agreements helped rulers establish rank and obligations. Ceremonies were part of political competition, even when participants broke their promises. A lord’s knowledge of the proper forms could give him influence. These leading lords headed competing states; they did not replace Zhou with a single new dynasty.

sections.title: An uneven change
sections.text: Fighting within noble families and wars between states gradually shifted power. Larger states developed more direct ways to govern their territories, alongside older family privileges. The transition to the Warring States period happened unevenly. The dates used to divide the periods help organize the history, but cannot mark one moment when every community’s government changed.

sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_and: Wikipedia · Spring and Autumn period (reference overview)
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Constance Cook · Scribes, cooks and artisans
sourceLabels.https://ctext.org/fengsutongyi/huang-ba/: Chinese Text Project · Fengsu Tongyi on the Five Hegemons

dateReview.note: 770–481 BCE is a supported scholarly convention. This is a historical period, not a regime; alternatives use 479, 476, or 475 as endpoint.

cards.catalogNote: 770–481 BCE is a supported scholarly convention. This is a historical period, not a regime; alternatives use 479, 476, or 475 as endpoint.

image.alt: An ornamented bronze chariot axle hub from the Spring and Autumn period.
image.caption: A bronze chariot fitting from the Spring and Autumn period. Chariots belonged to elite warfare and display, although one surviving fitting cannot represent every state or campaign in the period.

cards.name: Warring States Period
cards.description: Larger states absorbed weaker neighbours during the Warring States period. Seven became the main rivals: Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei. Other states also survived, and the seven did not all emerge at once.
cards.note: 481 BCE is the start used here; 475 BCE and 403 BCE are other common boundaries. These dates mark different ways of dividing the period, not rival dates for one event. The seven main states were not the only ones.

sections.title: Drawing households into war
sections.text: Rulers registered families, collected taxes and required military service. Farming and effective local government supplied armies that could conquer more land. These methods differed between states. Inherited privilege, ceremonies and local interests continued to matter, even as governments gained more direct control over ordinary people’s work and service.

sections.title: Competing ideas about restoring order
sections.text: Thinkers offered rival answers to the violence around them. Some stressed moral education, others care for all people, strong institutions or rewards and punishments. Their disagreements addressed practical problems of cooperation and rule. Later writers grouped these arguments into schools, but the texts within each group could differ. Teachers also depended on supporters who helped their ideas travel between courts.

sourceLabels.https://www.persee.fr/doc/befeo_0336-151: Bulletin de l’École française d’Extrême-Orient · Ritual origins of Warring States
sourceLabels.https://www.zgbk.com/ecph/words?ID=13597: Encyclopedia of China · Seven Warring States

dateReview.note: 481–221 BCE is an explicit Met chronology, not an error to 'fix' solely because another chronology uses 475 or 403. It is periodization rather than a single founding event.

cards.catalogNote: 481–221 BCE is an explicit Met chronology, not an error to 'fix' solely because another chronology uses 475 or 403. It is periodization rather than a single founding event.

image.credit: Gary Todd · National Museum of China / Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A bronze tally in the shape of a crouching tiger, inscribed with Chinese characters.
image.caption: A tiger-shaped bronze tally associated with Chu and used to authorize travel through courier stations. It offers material evidence for administration within one Warring States polity, not a picture of the period’s wars.

cards.name: Sun Tzu (孙子) (traditional c. 500 BCE)
cards.description: The Art of War, attributed to Sunzi (孙子), examines how information, preparation and advantage affect warfare. Its thirteen chapters consider when to fight and how to conserve resources. The text and its later influence are better documented than the life of its traditional author, Sun Wu (孙武).
cards.note: Ca. 500 BCE remains a conventional reference, not a secure birth or composition date. The text’s formation and authorship are debated; Han tomb manuscripts establish early circulation.

sections.title: Winning without wasting strength
sections.text: A long campaign or costly siege could weaken a ruler even if his army won. Intelligence and deception offered ways to act with less risk. The text treats restraint as a practical military choice. It accepts warfare while asking commanders to avoid unnecessary losses and expense.

sections.title: A text people argued with
sections.text: Other early thinkers, including Xunzi (荀子), questioned deception on moral and practical grounds. Ancient Chinese writers did not all share one view of strategy. Modern adaptations sometimes turn sayings from the Art of War into business advice. Its advice addressed rulers and armies facing supply limits, uncertainty and the cost of war.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Early China · Sunzi and Xunzi on deception

dateReview.note: 500 BCE is only a traditional approximate placement associated with King Helu's reign. Sunzi's historicity and authorship are contested; the surviving Art of War must not be assigned a proven composition date of 500 BCE. Existing UI already labels the date approximate; preserve its fuller description.

cards.catalogNote: 500 BCE is only a traditional approximate placement associated with King Helu's reign. Sunzi's historicity and authorship are contested; the surviving Art of War must not be assigned a proven composition date of 500 BCE.

image.alt: Rows of inscribed bamboo slips laid out for display.
image.caption: Bamboo slips of the Art of War excavated at Yinqueshan in 1972. The Han-period manuscript is a material witness to the text’s transmission, not Sun Tzu’s own handwriting.

cards.name: Alexander the Great
cards.description: Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE) conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire and led Macedonian armies into Central Asia and northwestern South Asia. He lived during China’s Warring States period, but his campaigns did not reach China.
cards.note: 356–323 BCE gives Alexander’s lifespan. His Asian campaigns began in 334 BCE. He did not invade China.

sections.title: After Alexander’s death
sections.text: When he died in 323 BCE, his commanders fought over his empire and founded successor kingdoms. Those later societies helped develop Hellenistic culture through their cities, royal support and exchanges with regional traditions. The empire broke apart, but the movement of artistic ideas and practices continued under its successors.

sections.title: Two histories in the same century
sections.text: Alexander and Warring States rulers faced some similar problems: feeding armies, securing support from powerful people and governing conquered populations. Similarities make comparison useful, but do not prove contact or influence. Connections between the Mediterranean, Central Asia and China grew through many later intermediaries. Placing Alexander here helps locate Chinese history within a wider world without suggesting that every contemporary event was directly connected.

sourceLabels.https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/art-of-: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Hellenistic art and its contexts

dateReview.note: Use the securely recorded biographical range 356–323 BCE for the existing Alexander subject. The former 330 BCE point was an editorial campaign reference, not inherently an erroneous event date. Do not rename the subject to Persepolis solely to justify that anchor.

cards.catalogNote: 330 BCE is a campaign reference, not a biographical date. Keep it only as an explicitly approximate editorial marker. Alexander lived 356–323 BCE; a biographical range is preferable when the display supports ranges.

image.credit: Ancient mosaic, artist unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A mosaic portrait of an armoured young man.
image.caption: A detail of the Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii, made centuries after Alexander’s campaigns. The Roman mosaic is a later representation of the Macedonian conqueror.

cards.name: Qin and Han government
cards.description: Qin created an empire in 221 BCE. After civil war, Han rulers rebuilt it and adapted many Qin methods. Looking at the two dynasties together shows how government practices could survive a change of ruling family, even when policies and circumstances changed.
cards.note: 221 BCE–220 CE is an analytical grouping with the Xin interruption included. It is neither a dynasty nor a claim that later imperial history followed an inevitable path.

sections.title: The daily work of empire
sections.text: Officials registered households, kept legal records and arranged the movement of goods. At the local level, they turned imperial commands into decisions about taxes, compulsory service and disputes. The emperor held the highest authority, but needed these offices and their staff to reach ordinary families. Surviving documents show how much imperial rule relied on routine work.

sections.title: An ambition later rulers inherited
sections.text: Later dynasties repeatedly sought to govern one empire, even after periods of division. Qin and Han offered examples of how such rule might work. Their methods were adapted to changing military needs, tax income and society. The persistence of that ambition did not mean uninterrupted unity: rival states could all claim a right to the same imperial inheritance.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Cambridge History of China · Structure and practice of Han government
sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government: Wikipedia · Government of the Han dynasty (reference overview)

dateReview.note: 221 BCE–220 CE is an editorial umbrella for Qin and Han, including intervening conflicts and Xin; not one continuous regime. Stored duration 441 is coordinate subtraction; elapsed historical years are 440 because BCE/CE has no year zero.

cards.catalogNote: 221 BCE–220 CE is an editorial umbrella for Qin and Han, including intervening conflicts and Xin; not one continuous regime. Stored duration 441 is coordinate subtraction; elapsed historical years are 440 because BCE/CE has no year zero.

image.credit: Gary Lee Todd, Ph.D. · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Both sides of a round bronze coin with a square central hole.
image.caption: A Qin banliang coin. Its denomination and form illustrate the monetary standards associated with imperial consolidation, while actual circulation remained a practical administrative task.

cards.name: Western Han
cards.description: Western Han combined districts governed by appointed officials with kingdoms held by royal relatives. Emperor Wu (汉武帝), who reigned 141–87 BCE, expanded campaigns against the Xiongnu and sent diplomatic missions west. These commitments helped connections later called the Silk Roads grow, while increasing the costs of government.
cards.note: 206 BCE–9 CE is the conventional range used here. Liu Bang (刘邦) became emperor in 202 BCE. Institutions and territorial reach changed substantially during Western Han.

sections.title: Keeping powerful allies in check
sections.text: Giving supporters kingdoms helped the early rulers secure their position. Those kingdoms could later threaten the court. After the rebellion of seven kingdoms in 154 BCE, the emperor further reduced their independence. Arrangements that had rewarded allies after conquest became problems for later rulers seeking firmer control.

sections.title: Taxes, monopolies, and the cost of expansion
sections.text: Emperor Wu (汉武帝)’s armies and frontier activity required continuing supplies and money. Government monopolies and other ways of raising revenue provoked disagreement. Support for classical learning accompanied these policies without replacing law or military force. Critics could object to the burden on households while still supporting imperial government. Debate about good rule included the practical question of what people should have to pay.

sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of: Wikipedia · History of the Han dynasty (reference overview)
sourceLabels.https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/han-dyn: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Han dynasty

dateReview.note: 206 BCE–9 CE is the standard museum convention, beginning with Liu Bang's kingship; 202 BCE marks his imperial accession and is used by other historians. Duration 215 is coordinate subtraction; elapsed historical years 214.

cards.catalogNote: 206 BCE–9 CE is the standard museum convention, beginning with Liu Bang's kingship; 202 BCE marks his imperial accession and is used by other historians. Duration 215 is coordinate subtraction; elapsed historical years 214.

image.alt: A human-shaped burial suit assembled from rectangular jade plaques joined with wire.
image.caption: A Western Han jade burial suit made for an elite tomb. It provides evidence for wealth, craftsmanship and funerary belief at the top of society, not a representative view of ordinary Han life.

cards.name: Eastern Han
cards.description: Liu Xiu (刘秀) proclaimed a restoration of Han in 25 CE and ruled from Luoyang (洛阳). Civil war had changed alliances and local power, so bringing back the Han name did not restore everything that had existed before. The dynasty lasted until 220 CE, with commanders increasingly controlling its final decades.
cards.note: 25–220 CE dates the restored dynasty; Liu Xiu (刘秀)’s reunification continued after 25. War between regional powers preceded formal abdication in 220.

sections.title: Rival groups at the imperial court
sections.text: Imperial relatives, empresses’ families, eunuchs and officials competed for access to the ruler. Appointments linked palace struggles to supporters and resources outside it. Powerful local families supplied knowledge and influence that the court needed, but could not always control. These relationships affected how government worked far beyond the palace.

sections.title: Life beyond the final wars
sections.text: The dynasty’s collapse can overshadow two centuries of writing, skilled production and contact between regions. Ban Zhao (班昭)’s historical work and Zhang Heng (张衡)’s technical inquiries belong to this longer history. The final breakdown raises a separate question: how did the court lose its ability to manage succession, armed commanders and competing interests? Earlier achievements did not vanish because that political order eventually failed.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Cambridge History of China · Wang Mang and Later Han

dateReview.note: 25–220 CE follows the Met chronology; restoration in 25 is distinct from the earlier Gengshi claimant 23–25.

cards.catalogNote: 25–220 CE follows the Met chronology; restoration in 25 is distinct from the earlier Gengshi claimant 23–25.

image.credit: Ancient Chinese artists of the late Eastern Han period · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Women in flowing robes depicted in a tomb mural.
image.caption: Women in an Eastern Han mural at Dahuting. Tomb painting preserves elite representations of social life; it does not describe every household or woman’s experience.

cards.name: Qin weights and measures
cards.description: In 221 BCE, the First Emperor ordered common weights and measures across the new empire. Standard weights carrying the decree survive. They show one practical part of Qin’s wider effort to bring conquered territories under a common government.
cards.note: 221 BCE dates the weights-and-measures edict. Other standardization measures developed over time; they were not all completed that year.

sections.title: Agreeing on an amount
sections.text: Officials and traders needed to know whether two quantities were equivalent. A government standard could reduce uncertainty in trade and tax collection. The inscription on a weight also announced imperial authority. An everyday transaction could therefore put the emperor’s rule into practice far from the court.

sections.title: An order still needed people to follow it
sections.text: A decree cannot prove that every district immediately used the same measures. Qin records show local offices handling transfers and keeping accounts within a larger system. Standards had to reach those offices and be used in daily work. The same caution applies to official writing: common written forms did not make everyone speak alike. Unification involved continuing work across a varied population.

sourceLabels.https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/441/: UNESCO · Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

dateReview.note: The specific weights-and-measures edict is dated 221 BCE, not 220. Other standardization measures were a process; narrowing the label provides a defensible single year.

cards.catalogNote: The specific weights-and-measures edict is dated 221 BCE, not 220. Other standardization measures were a process; narrowing the label provides a defensible single year.

image.alt: Twelve incised seal-script characters on a rectangular stone.
image.caption: A Qin-period stone inscription in small-seal script. Such inscriptions show the political use of a standardized written form without implying that everyday writing immediately became uniform.

cards.name: Classical learning and Han government
cards.description: In 136 BCE, Emperor Wu (汉武帝) gave official support to the study of the Five Classics, a group of ancient texts used to discuss learning and government. He founded an imperial academy in 124 BCE. These steps strengthened classical learning at court without making other teachings disappear.
cards.note: 136 BCE marks official promotion of the Five Classics. The imperial academy followed in 124 BCE; neither step imposed one exclusive teaching everywhere.

sections.title: Learning could open a door to office
sections.text: Knowledge of classical texts helped people take part in government and find examples for court decisions. It could also support criticism. A learned official might argue that a ruler’s spending or treatment of the people fell short of respected ancient models. Court support gave these debates a recognized place in political life.

sections.title: Government kept several traditions
sections.text: Calling this a complete victory for Confucianism oversimplifies Han rule. Courts continued to use administrative law, punishment and other intellectual traditions. Some specialists also interpreted relationships between human affairs and the wider universe. Certain texts and teachers became more influential, but their meanings remained contested. Han government was shaped by this mixture, rather than by one exclusive doctrine.

Lee Ting-mien · The “victory of Confucianism” reconsidered
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Early China · Ban Gu and Han political thought

dateReview.note: 136 BCE marks official promotion of the Five Classics in Han education and scholarship. The imperial academy followed in 124 BCE. These are distinct milestones in a gradual development, not the simultaneous adoption of one exclusive ideology.

cards.catalogNote: 130 BCE has no specific event support.136 BCE is a documented milestone in official promotion of the Five Classics. Formation of state Confucianism was gradual, not a single adoption event.
cards.pinyin: rú xué yǔ hàn dài zhèng zhì

image.alt: Fragments of an Eastern Han stone slab carved with lines of classical Chinese text.
image.caption: Fragments of the Eastern Han stone classics. They are later than Emperor Wu’s initiatives, but show the continuing effort to establish authoritative versions of texts used in education and government.

cards.name: Zhang Qian (张骞)'s first western mission
cards.description: Zhang Qian (张骞) set out on his first western mission in 138 BCE, seeking allies for the Han court in Central Asia. His reports gave Han rulers information about distant peoples, resources and possible diplomatic partners. Earlier exchanges and the people living along the routes had already made long-distance travel possible.
cards.note: Zhang Qian (张骞)’s first mission is commonly dated 138–126 BCE; some sources use 139 BCE for departure.

sections.title: Looking for allies
sections.text: The Han court wanted allies against the Xiongnu. Its envoys gathered information about distant peoples and resources while carrying gifts. Merchants used opportunities created by these political relationships, though wars could also obstruct movement. Trade and diplomacy developed within the same world as military rivalry.

sections.title: Many routes and many hands
sections.text: Goods could pass through several owners along changing routes. Travellers needed water, food grown at oases and arrangements with local authorities. The later name Silk Road can make this seem like one highway, although many routes and commodities were involved. The communities between large empires kept these connections working; no single traveller created them all.

dateReview.note: 138 BCE is the selected conventional departure date for Zhang Qian’s first western mission, commonly dated 138–126 BCE. A UNESCO overview uses 139 BCE for departure. Earlier trade and later exchanges make this a mission milestone, not the creation of the Silk Roads.

cards.catalogNote: 130 BCE is unsupported as a precise 'Silk Road expansion' event.138 BCE dates Zhang Qian's departure in the UNESCO education publication; another UNESCO overview uses 139 BCE. Trade routes predated and developed after this mission.

image.alt: A weathered rammed-earth watchtower in a dry desert landscape.
image.caption: Remains of a Han watchtower near Dunhuang. The modern photograph shows the material infrastructure behind frontier surveillance and long-distance movement.

cards.name: Buddhism comes to China
cards.description: Travellers, merchants and religious teachers brought Buddhism into the Han world from South and Central Asia. The date around 50 CE is approximate. Evidence becomes clearer during the first and second centuries CE, especially with the translation of Buddhist teachings into Chinese.
cards.note: About 50 CE represents early contact, not a verified introduction year. The familiar imperial dream story is a later tradition, not a contemporary arrival record.

sections.title: Finding words for new ideas
sections.text: Translators had to explain rebirth, liberation from suffering and disciplined religious life using unfamiliar languages and existing Chinese words. This involved choices and discussion. An Shigao (安世高), a translator active in the second century, gives us a firmer historical reference than a single story about Buddhism’s arrival.

sections.title: Communities grew gradually
sections.text: Buddhist practitioners at one centre do not prove that the wider population shared their beliefs. Support from rulers also varied. Religious communities needed patrons, teachers and continuing contact across borders. Later stories placed Buddhism within Chinese imperial history, while the religion spread through the slower work of translating, teaching and sustaining communities.

sourceLabels.https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/ex: University of Washington · Buddhism on the Silk Routes
sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_: Wikipedia · Silk Road transmission of Buddhism (reference overview)

dateReview.note: 50 CE is an editorial midpoint for the first century, not an attested arrival year. Precise introduction is unknown; earlier contacts are possible. Retain year 50 only when displayed explicitly as first-century approximation. Existing UI already labels the date approximate; preserve its fuller description.

cards.catalogNote: 50 CE is an editorial midpoint for the first century, not an attested arrival year. Precise introduction is unknown; earlier contacts are possible. Retain year 50 only when displayed explicitly as first-century approximation.

image.alt: The modern entrance gate of White Horse Temple near Luoyang.
image.caption: The modern entrance to White Horse Temple, traditionally connected with the early transmission of Buddhism to China. The surviving complex is much later and cannot by itself verify the temple’s first-century foundation story.

cards.name: Terracotta Army (c. 210 BCE)
cards.description: Thousands of terracotta soldiers, horses and other figures form part of the First Emperor’s enormous burial complex. Construction began before Qin unified the rival kingdoms and continued into the end of his reign. The date 210 BCE marks his death, rather than the making of every figure.
cards.note: 210 BCE is a commemorative endpoint. UNESCO dates the beginning of the mausoleum project to 246 BCE; the warriors were discovered in 1974.

sections.title: An army for the afterlife
sections.text: The soldiers belong to a much larger complex of burial facilities and supporting structures. Together they express an ambition to continue imperial command after death. Making them required organized production, transport and skilled labour. The finished figures let us see some of the work behind the emperor’s plans.

sections.title: What remains unknown
sections.text: Faces and equipment vary, while repeated parts reveal organized manufacture. A distinctive face does not necessarily portray a particular living soldier. The central burial chamber remains unexcavated, so later descriptions of its contents are not archaeological observations. The objects reveal much about craftsmanship and representations of military life, while leaving questions about individual figures and the burial itself unanswered.

sourceLabels.https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/441/: UNESCO · Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

dateReview.note: 210 BCE is the emperor's death/burial reference, not exact construction date for every statue. Existing explanation is correct; approx flag should match.

cards.catalogNote: Around 210 BCE is a conventional art-historical date associated with the First Emperor's burial. Manufacture occurred over time; this is not a precise creation day/year for every figure.

image.alt: Rows of excavated terracotta soldiers standing in the First Emperor’s burial complex.
image.caption: Pit 1 of the First Emperor’s terracotta army. The modern view includes excavated and restored figures, so it is evidence of the burial project rather than the army’s original finished appearance.

cards.name: Wei
cards.description: Cao Pi (曹丕) became emperor in 220, and Cao Wei controlled much of northern China. He inherited the military and farming arrangements built under Cao Cao (曹操). The Sima family gradually took real power before founding Jin in 266.
cards.note: 220–265 is one conventional dating for Wei. The Jin accession falls in 266 in common Gregorian chronologies.

sections.title: Food for an army
sections.text: Agricultural colonies supplied soldiers and helped organize displaced people and land. Farming was closely tied to the demands of war. A court needed more than a large area on a map: grain and revenue had to be collected and moved reliably. These arrangements helped sustain Wei’s military strength.

sections.title: Power inside the government
sections.text: Senior offices, army commands and positions governing on an emperor’s behalf gave powerful families ways to gather influence. The Sima family’s rise came through Wei’s own government. The dynasty was eventually replaced from within, rather than simply defeated by an outside enemy. Keeping the imperial title did not ensure that the Cao rulers still controlled the offices and armies supporting it.

dateReview.note: 220–265 follows the museum chronology.

cards.catalogNote: 220–265 follows the museum chronology.

image.credit: Attributed to Yan Liben · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A later painted image of Cao Pi seated in court dress.
image.caption: A later painting traditionally identified as Cao Pi, founder of Wei. Its attribution and date do not make it a verified likeness of the third-century ruler.

cards.name: Shu
cards.description: Liu Bei (刘备)’s court in Sichuan (四川) claimed to restore Han rule. Zhuge Liang (诸葛亮) helped govern Shu and led northern campaigns against Wei in 228–234. Mountain routes and limited resources restricted those ambitions. Wei conquered Shu in 263.
cards.note: 221–263 dates Shu Han as an imperial court. Literary portrayals are later interpretations, not direct transcripts of campaigns.

sections.title: Protected by the mountains, limited by them
sections.text: Sichuan (四川) had productive farmland and approaches that could be defended. The same difficult terrain made it hard to supply armies sent beyond Shu’s home territory. Claiming descent from Han could attract support, but could not remove the cost of mobilizing a smaller population. Geography offered protection while limiting prolonged expansion.

sections.title: Zhuge Liang (诸葛亮) in history and stories
sections.text: Later plays and fiction made Zhuge Liang (诸葛亮) famous for extraordinary foresight and ingenious plans. His historical work also involved recruiting people, organizing government and keeping the state able to fight. The northern expeditions were sustained military efforts under difficult conditions. His later reputation grew from that service, but fictional feats cannot be read as direct accounts of the campaigns.

sourceLabels.https://www.chinaknowledge.de/History/Di: Ulrich Theobald · Three Kingdoms military organization

dateReview.note: 221–263 follows the museum chronology.

cards.catalogNote: 221–263 follows the museum chronology.

image.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A pottery musician seated with an instrument.
image.caption: A Shu-period pottery musician. Courtly and funerary culture continued in Sichuan during the political and military rivalry of the Three Kingdoms. The musician belongs to Shu material culture; it is not an image of Zhuge Liang or his northern campaigns.

cards.name: Wu
cards.description: The Sun family built Wu around the lower Yangtze (长江) River. Sun Quan (孙权) became king in 222 and claimed the imperial title in 229. Wu outlasted both Shu and Wei, until Jin conquered it in 280.
cards.note: 222 marks kingship; 229 marks the imperial title. Both conventions describe stages of a longer consolidation.

sections.title: Ruling with local families
sections.text: Military leaders needed the support of powerful families whose estates and followers provided resources. Marriages and official appointments helped connect them to the court. These ties did not erase their independent influence. Wu’s rulers governed through agreements with people who already held power in the region, and those relationships could produce conflict as well as cooperation.

sections.title: The cost of expansion
sections.text: As Wu extended control into hill regions, it drew communities into taxation and military service. Official accounts might describe this as bringing order or developing productive land. For the people affected, it could mean being forced under a new authority. Growth in the southern economy therefore came with burdens on communities whose experience is harder to see in court records.

sourceLabels.https://www.chinaknowledge.de/History/Di: Ulrich Theobald · Three Kingdoms military organization

dateReview.note: 222–280 follows the museum chronology.

cards.catalogNote: 222–280 follows the museum chronology.

image.credit: PHG at English Wikipedia · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A green-glazed ceramic jar with elaborate figures around its top.
image.caption: An Eastern Wu ceramic jar. The object illustrates the regional production and burial culture of the lower Yangtze during the Three Kingdoms.

cards.name: Fall of Han
cards.description: In 220, Cao Pi (曹丕) accepted the Han emperor’s abdication and founded Wei. Han’s control had already weakened over many years. Cao Cao (曹操) had built a powerful military government while keeping the emperor and issuing decisions in his name.
cards.note: 220 dates the formal end of Han; the breakdown of effective central rule began earlier.

sections.title: The emperor’s name still mattered
sections.text: Controlling the emperor allowed Cao Cao (曹操) to authorize appointments and campaigns without immediately replacing Han. The abdication later gave Cao Pi (曹丕) a claim to a lawful transfer of rule. The ceremony presented the new dynasty as legitimate to officials and rivals. Possessing military power and being accepted as the rightful ruler were connected, but different, problems.

sections.title: Several successors to Han
sections.text: Shu and Wu developed their own courts and claims after the transfer. Han’s methods of government and imperial language remained useful to several rival states. The dynasty’s formal end did not make its inheritance disappear. The date 220 marks the end of the Han ruling house within a division of power that had already advanced much further on the ground.

sourceLabels.https://www.chinaknowledge.de/History/Di: Ulrich Theobald · Three Kingdoms political history

dateReview.note: 220 marks the end of Eastern Han; long political fragmentation preceded formal abdication.

cards.catalogNote: 220 marks the end of Eastern Han; long political fragmentation preceded formal abdication.

image.alt: A Qing-period illustration of Emperor Xian of Han wearing court robes.
image.caption: A Qing-period illustration of Emperor Xian, whose abdication in 220 ended the Han dynasty. It is an imagined portrait produced many centuries later.

cards.name: Battle of Red Cliffs
cards.description: At Red Cliffs in winter 208–209 CE, forces associated with Sun Quan (孙权) and Liu Bei (刘备) stopped Cao Cao (曹操)’s advance along the Yangtze (长江). Cao Cao (曹操) controlled the Han emperor and dominated the north. His defeat allowed southern rivals to survive while Han still formally existed.
cards.note: 208 CE is the conventional battle date; the campaign extends into winter 208–209. Troop totals, the exact location and several familiar tactics are disputed.

sections.title: Fighting on the river
sections.text: Naval experience mattered, along with disease, supplies and the difficulty of campaigning far from familiar ground. The defeat stopped Cao Cao (曹操) from immediately extending northern dominance southward. It did not create the [[Three Kingdoms]] in one day. Wei, Shu and Wu emerged through later campaigns and competing claims to rule.

sections.title: The battle in later stories
sections.text: Fiction turned Red Cliffs into a setting for brilliant plans and memorable personalities. Surviving historical accounts support a more limited picture, and several famous tricks remain disputed. Those later stories shaped how people remembered the battle, especially its lessons about loyalty and intelligence. They need to be distinguished from evidence of what the armies actually did.

sourceLabels.https://www.usni.org/magazines/naval-his: US Naval Institute · The Flaming Ships of Red Cliffs
sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_: Wikipedia · Battle of Red Cliffs (reference overview)
sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_the: Wikipedia · End of the Han dynasty (reference overview)

dateReview.note: 208 CE follows Rafe de Crespigny's scholarly chronology. Winter of Jian'an 13 overlaps 208–209 in Julian conversion. Parent Eastern Han is correct; the formal Three Kingdoms period starts 220.

cards.catalogNote: 208 CE follows Rafe de Crespigny's scholarly chronology. Winter of Jian'an 13 overlaps 208–209 in Julian conversion. Parent Eastern Han is correct; the formal Three Kingdoms period starts 220.

image.alt: Red Chinese characters carved into a riverside rock face.
image.caption: The inscribed cliff at a site traditionally associated with Red Cliffs. This modern view shows a landscape of commemoration, not archaeological proof of the battle’s exact location.

cards.name: Western Jin
cards.description: The Sima family founded Western Jin after gradually taking power within Wei. Jin conquered Wu in 280 and briefly ended the Three Kingdoms division. Later conflicts among imperial princes and military leaders weakened the court, which lost Luoyang (洛阳) and then Chang’an (长安).
cards.note: 266–316 dates Western Jin. Luoyang (洛阳) fell in 311; the final western court at Chang’an (长安) fell in 316.

sections.title: A takeover built through service
sections.text: The Sima family gained offices and military commands before changing the imperial title. Its rise had therefore begun long before Jin’s formal founding. The new rulers inherited Wei’s officials and resources, along with relationships that were difficult to manage. A new dynastic name did not settle every contest for power.

sections.title: Reaching ordinary households
sections.text: Changes in farming settlements and the landholdings of powerful families affected what the court could demand. To collect labour and military service, officials needed household records and cooperation from local intermediaries. The struggles between princes were part of this wider problem. A government also needed reliable access to the people and resources that supported its armies.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cam: Cambridge History of China · Western Jin

dateReview.note: 266–316 is supported with calendrical qualification: Cambridge explicitly gives 265 or 266 for the foundation. Retain 266.

cards.catalogNote: 266–316 is supported with calendrical qualification: Cambridge explicitly gives 265 or 266 for the foundation. Retain 266.

image.alt: A tall Western Jin celadon funerary jar crowded with modeled figures and buildings.
image.caption: A Western Jin hunping, or funerary jar, covered with figures and architectural forms. It provides evidence for burial practice and ceramic production, not a direct account of Jin reunification or collapse.

cards.name: Western Jin loses Chang’an (长安)
cards.description: Chang’an (长安) fell in 316, ending the remaining Western Jin court. Luoyang (洛阳) had already fallen in 311. These successive defeats displaced political leaders and helped shift power between northern and southern centres.
cards.note: 316 is the end of Western Jin, not all Jin rule. Ancient descriptions of devastation are not reliable modern demographic totals.

sections.title: A collapse in stages
sections.text: The court lost effective control over territory and resources before its final defeat. Cities, armies and communities experienced the breakdown at different times. The date 316 makes a clear endpoint for Western Jin, but the fighting and displacement formed a longer sequence. Ancient accounts of devastation also cannot be treated as reliable modern population counts.

sections.title: Jin continued in the south
sections.text: Sima Rui (司马睿)’s southern government kept the Jin name. It needed support from families who had fled the north and influential families already established in the south. Ancestry helped its claim, but cooperation made rule possible. The fall of the western court was therefore also part of the formation of a different Jin society and government around the Yangtze (长江).

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cam: Cambridge History of China · Western Jin
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Cambridge History of China · Eastern Jin

dateReview.note: 316 is the fall of Western Jin at Chang’an; Eastern Jin continued in the south.

cards.catalogNote: 316 is the fall of Western Jin at Chang’an; Eastern Jin continued in the south.

image.alt: A green-glazed ceramic jar with a small spout.
image.caption: An Eastern Jin celadon jar. It reflects the material culture of the southern court’s period, rather than portraying a particular political event.

cards.name: Buddhism expands in China (c. 350)
cards.description: Buddhist texts and communities existed in China before the fourth century. During the Age of Division, more translations, images and support from patrons helped Buddhism grow in different regions. About 350 is a reference point for this gradual, uneven expansion.
cards.note: 350 is approximate and represents broader fourth-century expansion, not Buddhism’s first arrival in China.

sections.title: The work behind a growing religion
sections.text: Translators and readers kept texts in use. Patrons and craftspeople paid for and made images. Monasteries needed resources and protection. Buddhism took root through these relationships within local society, with different results in different regions. Its growth involved continuing work by communities, rather than the simple arrival of a complete set of foreign beliefs.

sections.title: Negotiating with rulers
sections.text: Monks’ religious duties and claims to a distinct status raised practical questions for governments. Who should pay taxes, perform service or show allegiance to a ruler? Court support did not settle every tension. Buddhism’s expansion included negotiations and conflicts as well as devotion, intellectual exchange and the creation of art.

sourceLabels.https://www.metmuseum.org/ja/essays/chin: Denise Patry Leidy · Chinese Buddhist Sculpture
sourceLabels.https://soas-repository.worktribe.com/ou: Antonello Palumbo · Buddhism and the Chinese state

dateReview.note: 350 is an illustrative midpoint for fourth-century growth, not a dated introduction or single event.

cards.catalogNote: 350 is an illustrative midpoint for fourth-century growth, not a dated introduction or single event.

image.alt: A carved Northern Wei stone stele showing a Buddhist triad and attendant figures.
image.caption: A Northern Wei Buddhist triad stele. It is later than the card’s approximate 350 reference point, but records the spread of Buddhist images and patronage in northern China.

cards.name: Sui and Tang
cards.description: Sui and Tang together span the rebuilding of a united empire and nearly three centuries of change. Tang inherited northern military and government traditions from Sui, along with a territory that had recently been reunited.
cards.note: 581–907 groups two successive dynasties, Sui and Tang.

sections.title: An inherited foundation
sections.text: The change of dynasty in 618 brought new rulers and priorities, while useful offices and practices continued. Governing a large empire still meant appointing officials, collecting resources and moving grain and armies. Both dynasties relied on many of the same offices and governing practices.

sections.title: A changing empire
sections.text: The An Lushan Rebellion (安史之乱) transformed Tang government. New military commands and ways of collecting taxes changed the relationship between the court and the provinces. Later Tang rulers worked within arrangements very different from those of early Sui. Across this long period, institutions survived by changing, rather than operating in one fixed form.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Arthur Wright · The Sui Dynasty
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: David Graff · The Reach of the Military: Tang

dateReview.note: 581–907 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

cards.catalogNote: 581–907 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

image.alt: The brick Giant Wild Goose Pagoda rises above trees in Xi’an.
image.caption: The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda was founded in Tang Chang’an in 652 to house Buddhist texts brought from India. This 2018 photograph shows the repaired and rebuilt monument, not its seventh-century appearance.

cards.name: Muhammad’s first revelation
cards.description: Islamic tradition dates Muhammad’s first revelations to 610. The migration to Medina, known as the Hijra, followed in 622. The early Muslim community grew through several stages before the later expansion of Muslim-ruled states.
cards.note: 610 is the traditional date of the first revelation, not the arrival of Islam in China.

sections.title: A growing community
sections.text: Religious belief developed alongside new political relationships and institutions. Later expansion brought Muslim communities into contact with other regions and traditions. Forms of government and material culture changed through those encounters; the whole process cannot be assigned to a single founding year.

sections.title: Later connections with China
sections.text: Trade and diplomacy eventually connected Muslim societies with Chinese ports and courts. These connections developed after the first revelations. The seventh century saw important changes across Eurasia, but 610 is not a date for the arrival of Islam in China.

sourceLabels.https://www.metmuseum.org/fr/essays/the-: Metropolitan Museum of Art · The Birth of Islam
sourceLabels.https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/c: Encyclopaedia Iranica · Persian settlements in China

dateReview.note: 610 refers to the first revelation in Islamic tradition, not a single date encompassing Islam’s rise.

cards.catalogNote: 610 refers to the first revelation in Islamic tradition, not a single date encompassing Islam’s rise.
cards.pinyin: yī sī lán jiào xīng qǐ

image.alt: A parchment manuscript page with Arabic writing.
image.caption: A page of the early Qurʾanic Ṣanʿāʾ manuscript, with underlying writing revealed through imaging. It is evidence for early textual transmission, not an image of the revelation of 610.

cards.name: Dadu (大都), the Yuan capital
cards.description: In 1272, Kublai Khan (忽必烈)’s northern capital received the name Dadu (大都). He had proclaimed the Yuan dynasty the year before. Planning and construction of the city had already begun.
cards.note: 1272 is the Dadu (大都) naming milestone. It is distinct from the Yuan dynastic proclamation in 1271 and from earlier capital construction.

sections.title: Between China and Mongolia
sections.text: The capital connected the emperor’s Chinese farming territories with his Mongol power base. Its court and monumental layout expressed ambitions that reached across both worlds. Governing from a permanent city did not mean abandoning the northern relationships on which Mongol power depended.

sections.title: Supplying an imperial city
sections.text: Officials, guards, artisans and visiting envoys needed food and materials. Transport from productive regions mattered as much as walls and palaces. The court brought people with different skills and backgrounds together, although some moved under obligations imposed by conquest. Dadu (大都)’s grandeur rested on this continuing movement of people, supplies and expertise.

sourceLabels.https://www.metmuseum.org/exhibitions/li: Metropolitan Museum · The World of Khubilai Khan

dateReview.note: Recommend 1272 for Dadu naming/capital milestone instead of preserving a 1271 foundation-context marker. Current explanatory note is honest, but its date refers to the wider dynasty rather than this capital event.

cards.catalogNote: 1271 dates adoption of the dynastic name Yuan; 1272 dates the Dadu name and capital milestone. Construction and use as a political center began earlier, so this is not Beijing's first establishment as a capital.
searchAliases: Dadu named as the Yuan capital

image.alt: A schematic plan compares the footprint of Yuan Dadu with later Beijing walls.
image.caption: A modern diagram comparing Yuan Dadu’s plan with the later Ming and Qing capital. It helps locate the Yuan city within Beijing, but it is a schematic reconstruction rather than a Yuan-period map.

cards.name: Beijing (北京) becomes the Ming capital
cards.description: The Yongle (永乐) Emperor moved the Ming court from Nanjing (南京) to Beijing (北京) in 1421. The Forbidden City had been completed the year before. Beijing (北京) was his former power base and stood close to the northern frontier. Nanjing (南京) remained a secondary capital with its own government offices.
cards.note: 1421 marks the court’s transfer to Beijing (北京). The Forbidden City was completed in 1420. Beijing (北京) had also been a capital under earlier dynasties, notably the Yuan.

image.alt: The Forbidden City’s north gate, with red walls, golden tiled roofs and visitors in the foreground.
image.caption: The Forbidden City’s north gate, photographed in 2006. The surviving palace reflects centuries of rebuilding after the Ming capital moved here.

sections.title: Beijing (北京)’s military and political advantages
sections.text: Beijing (北京) brought the emperor closer to the armies defending the northern frontier and the Mongol powers beyond it. Yongle (永乐) had seized the throne in civil war, and his earlier base now became the centre of imperial government. The choice combined military concerns with the ruler’s own position. It changed where power was concentrated without removing Nanjing (南京)’s importance.

sections.title: A capital supplied from the south
sections.text: Moving the court did not move the empire’s richest farmland with it. The capital and its soldiers depended on grain brought from southern regions. The restored Grand Canal, together with storage and shipping arrangements, helped keep those supplies moving. Beijing (北京)’s growth as an imperial capital depended on the labour and harvests of people living far from its walls.

sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emp: Yongle Emperor · capital relocation and supply

dateReview.note: 1420 dates palace completion and preparations; formal transfer occurred in Yongle 19, 1421. Avoid permanent capital, since later governments used other capitals.

cards.catalogNote: 1420 dates palace completion and preparations; formal transfer occurred in Yongle 19, 1421. Avoid permanent capital, since later governments used other capitals.
cards.pinyin: yǒng lè qiān dū běi jīng

cards.name: Beijing (北京) Becomes the Qing Capital
cards.description: Qing forces entered Beijing (北京) in 1644. Li Zicheng (李自成)’s rebels had already captured the city, and the Ming emperor had died. The Qing made the former Ming capital their own, eight years after proclaiming their dynasty in the northeast.
cards.note: 1644 marks Beijing (北京)’s conquest and adoption as Qing capital. It is distinct from the 1636 dynastic foundation and from the later completion of territorial consolidation.

sections.title: Taking over the imperial capital
sections.text: The palaces, offices and ceremonies of Beijing (北京) helped the new rulers claim the authority of emperors. They presented themselves as successors to the Ming while criticizing its failures. Familiar institutions helped officials and residents deal with the new court. The ruling family had changed, but much of the machinery and symbolism of imperial government remained useful.

sections.title: The war continued elsewhere
sections.text: Possession of Beijing (北京) gave the Qing an important centre of government. Ming princes and loyalist armies still resisted in the south, and the conquest continued. The Qing also retained military and political arrangements developed before taking the city. Its move to Beijing (北京) was a major turning point within a longer expansion, rather than the moment when every region accepted its rule.

sourceLabels.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition: Wikipedia · Transition from Ming to Qing

dateReview.note: 1644 dates the Qing court's move to Beijing; Qing was proclaimed in 1636, and territorial conquest continued after 1644.

cards.catalogNote: 1644 dates the Qing court's move to Beijing; Qing was proclaimed in 1636, and territorial conquest continued after 1644.

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A painted portrait of Dorgon in formal court robes.
image.caption: A seventeenth-century portrait of Dorgon. The regent’s image accompanies the Qing conquest of Beijing in 1644, which was distinct from the dynasty’s foundation in 1636.

cards.name: Ming Palace Eunuchs
cards.description: Eunuchs served inside the Ming palace, but some also became military commanders, administrators and imperial envoys. Their responsibilities expanded under the Yongle (永乐) Emperor and later rulers. Access to the emperor could give a palace attendant influence far beyond the imperial household.
cards.note: Circa 1403–1424 is the Yongle (永乐) reign era, used here to show an expansion of eunuch roles. Yongle (永乐) took power in 1402. The change developed over time.

sections.title: A second route to the emperor
sections.text: An emperor could give trusted attendants tasks that would otherwise pass through regular officials. This offered another source of information and another way to issue orders. It also gave attendants opportunities to control access and promote supporters. Palace service became part of a wider struggle over who could advise the ruler and carry out his decisions.

sections.title: Different people, different roles
sections.text: Zheng He (郑和) led overseas expeditions; Wei Zhongxian (魏忠贤) later built a powerful court network that persecuted opponents. Their shared status as eunuchs does not explain their different careers. Scholar-officials often wrote hostile accounts of eunuch power, while also competing with them for influence. Each career is best understood through the responsibilities and powers the emperor granted.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cam: Cambridge History of China · Ming institutional history

dateReview.note: The exact 1400 marker is unsupported. Proposed circa 1403 is an editorial anchor for expansion under Yongle: accession 1402, reign era 1403–1424. This was a continuing institutional process, not a single decree.

cards.catalogNote: The exact 1400 marker is unsupported. Proposed circa 1403 is an editorial anchor for expansion under Yongle: accession 1402, reign era 1403–1424. This was a continuing institutional process, not a single decree.
searchAliases: Expansion of eunuch power in Ming government
cards.pinyin: míng dài huàn guān quán lì

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: An emperor seated in a yellow robe and black headdress.
image.caption: A formal portrait of the Yongle emperor. It provides a courtly image of the ruler associated with the transfer of the Ming capital to Beijing and Zheng He’s voyages. The emperor’s portrait provides context for palace service and imperial delegation; it does not depict a eunuch.

cards.name: Wei Zhongxian (魏忠贤)’s Court Power
cards.description: Wei Zhongxian (魏忠贤) gained exceptional influence during the Tianqi (天启) emperor’s reign. He used access to the palace and allies among officials to build a powerful network. In 1624, the official Yang Lian (杨涟) publicly denounced him. Persecution of critics associated with the Donglin movement followed.
cards.note: 1624 is the inherited focal year of confrontation, not the beginning of all Wei’s influence. His fall and death came in 1627. Hostile accounts of his early life require caution.

sections.title: Power through access
sections.text: The ability to influence what the emperor heard could affect appointments and careers across government. Wei relied on officials outside the palace as well as other attendants. Some joined his network, while others resisted or tried to work around it. His power grew through these connections and the emperor’s protection, rather than through one formal title.

sections.title: A change of emperor
sections.text: Tianqi (天启) died in 1627. Under the new Chongzhen (崇祯) emperor, Wei lost his protection and his position collapsed. His fall showed how closely his influence had depended on favour at court. It also followed years of harm to opponents. The 1624 date marks a major confrontation during his rise; his fall and death came three years later.

dateReview.note: 1624 is a supported focal year: Yang Lian's memorial denouncing Wei is dated Tianqi 4. Wei's influence began earlier; major persecutions followed in 1625–1626 and his fall and death in 1627.

cards.catalogNote: 1624 is a supported focal year: Yang Lian's memorial denouncing Wei is dated Tianqi 4. Wei's influence began earlier; major persecutions followed in 1625–1626 and his fall and death in 1627.

image.alt: Several painted porcelain cups displayed together.
image.caption: Porcelain teacups from the Tianqi reign, 1621–1627. These are objects from the period of Wei Zhongxian’s influence, not evidence that he personally commissioned them.

cards.name: First Opium War
cards.description: In 1839, Qing commissioner Lin Zexu (林则徐) moved to suppress the illegal opium trade. Conflict with Britain followed. British naval and land forces, including troops from India, attacked coastal and river positions. The war ended in 1842 with the Treaty of Nanking (南京).
cards.note: 1839–1842 includes the initial clashes; 1840–1842 is also used for the main expedition. The 1842 treaty did not itself legalize opium or establish all later foreign privileges.

sections.title: Opium, tea and overseas trade
sections.text: Merchants used opium grown in British India to help finance purchases of Chinese tea. This trade connected Indian production, Chinese buyers and British demand. Qing efforts to stop the imports challenged a profitable business while confronting the damage caused by addiction. Britain intervened militarily and pressed for wider access to Chinese markets.

sections.title: The terms of defeat
sections.text: British forces advanced along the Yangtze (长江) toward Nanjing (南京). The resulting treaty opened five ports, required payments and ceded Hong Kong (香港) Island to Britain. Later agreements added further foreign privileges. These concessions limited the Qing government’s control over foreign activity. The treaty did not itself legalize opium. The dates 1839–1842 include the initial clashes; some accounts use 1840 for the main British expedition.

sourceLabels.https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/first-chin: National Army Museum · First China War
sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/milestones/183: U.S. Office of the Historian · Opium War and treaty system
