image.alt: The entrance and grounds of a royal tomb complex.
image.caption: The Yongling tomb of Wang Jian, founder of Former Shu, photographed in 2010. The site provides a specific Chengdu setting for the kingdom’s royal culture.

cards.name: Wuyue
cards.description: The Qian family governed Wuyue in the lower Yangtze (长江) region from 907 to 978. Regional wealth, diplomacy and religious support helped it outlast many neighbouring states. Its final submission to Song was negotiated.
cards.note: 907–978 dates Wuyue. Its final submission to Song was negotiated, not a violent conquest.

sections.title: Recognition and local control
sections.text: Wuyue accepted titles and recognition from northern courts while preserving substantial control at home. This arrangement offered another route to survival besides claiming authority over the whole empire. Diplomatic compromise could protect the ruling family and the resources of its region.

sections.title: Changing religious support
sections.text: Early rulers supported a range of Buddhist and Daoist institutions. Under the last king, support became more concentrated on particular Chan Buddhist lineages. Religious life developed through changing relationships between rulers and communities, rather than a single policy maintained unchanged for the whole dynasty.

sourceLabels.https://doi.org/10.21313/hawaii/97808248: Benjamin Brose · Buddhist institutions in Wuyue

image.caption: An official document issued in 922 by Qian Liu of Wuyue to the monk Sikuang. The surviving text connects regional sovereignty with the administration of Buddhist institutions.

cards.name: Chu (Ma Chu)
cards.description: Ma Yin (马殷)’s Chu ruled from Hunan (湖南) and drew income from regional production and trade, including tea. The Ma family’s court ended in 951, but some local commanders continued to hold power afterward.
cards.note: 907–951 covers Ma Chu’s broader state history; 927 is a later kingdom milestone used in some chronologies. Autonomous rule in Hunan (湖南) continued beyond the Ma court’s fall in 951.

sections.title: Tea across borders
sections.text: Tea connected growers and merchants with customers and courts beyond Chu. Income from this trade helped sustain the state alongside diplomacy with stronger neighbours. Political division did not sever commercial routes; a regional government could depend on exchange across its borders.

sections.title: After the Ma family
sections.text: The end of the ruling house did not immediately bring all of Hunan (湖南) under another state’s administration. Local leaders kept parts of Hunan (湖南) autonomous after the Ma court fell in 951.

image.alt: Cash coins associated with Southern Chu are displayed in the Shanghai Museum.
image.caption: Coins displayed in the Shanghai Museum and catalogued on Commons with Southern Chu coinage. They provide material evidence for regional money, although the photograph’s record does not identify each coin in view.

cards.name: Min
cards.description: The Wang family’s Min state developed in Fujian (福建), drawing resources partly from coastal trade. Conflict within the ruling house divided it before its conventional end in 945. Some local centres continued under separate leaders.
cards.note: 909–945 is the conventional dynastic span. Some local port rulers survived the fragmentation of the Wang court.

sections.title: A trading coast still needed government
sections.text: Sea routes brought opportunities, but rulers also needed to govern inland districts, maintain support and manage succession within the family. Commercial resources could strengthen a court without protecting it from internal conflict. Min’s troubles grew within a region that remained connected to maritime exchange.

sections.title: Different local endings
sections.text: Ports and districts did not all change rulers at the same moment. Some local authorities survived the Wang court’s fragmentation. The disappearance of the Min dynastic name therefore marks one political ending, rather than an immediate break in every community’s institutions.

image.caption: The tomb of Wang Shenzhi, the ruler who established the Min kingdom in Fujian. This 2023 photograph shows the surviving memorial site, which has been altered since the tenth century.

cards.name: Southern Han
cards.description: Southern Han ruled from Guangzhou (广州) and participated in sea trade and regional commerce. Its surviving coins and tax records reveal some of the everyday work behind a regional imperial court.
cards.note: 917–971 dates Southern Han. Archaeological finds are selective evidence, not a complete statistical record of trade.

sections.title: Coins and salt taxes
sections.text: Lead coins were issued in Guangzhou (广州) from 917. Silver ingots wrapped in receipts record salt-tax payments, including the metal’s weight and purity. Such details show officials keeping track of the value they collected. These finds reveal particular practices, even though they cannot tell us the size of the whole economy.

sections.title: Ruling a coastal state
sections.text: The court claimed imperial standing before its subjects and other rulers. Merchants and local leaders also dealt with it through trade, taxation and practical needs. Southern Han depended on these relationships as well as on the authority of its rulers. Its coastal position became a source of strength through the work of connecting commerce with government income.

sourceLabels.https://www11.ihp.sinica.edu.tw/storage/: Academia Sinica · Southern Han coinage and maritime evidence
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song

image.alt: The two faces of a small lead cash coin attributed to Southern Han are shown side by side.
image.caption: A lead Kaiyuan tongbao coin attributed to the Southern Han kingdom. Its modest material fits a regional monetary economy; the attribution comes from modern numismatic cataloguing rather than an inscription naming the state.

cards.name: Jingnan (Nanping (南平))
cards.description: Jingnan, also called Nanping (南平), was a small state centred on Jiangling (江陵) and important river routes. Its rulers maintained a separate court for decades while dealing with stronger neighbours.
cards.note: 924 marks the princely-title convention; the regional governorship began earlier. The state was absorbed in 963.

sections.title: The value of location
sections.text: A court on useful routes could gain influence by managing connections and exchange. Trade and diplomatic payments operated together. Jingnan’s importance came partly from its position between other states, rather than from commanding a vast territory or the largest army.

sections.title: Room to govern
sections.text: Accepting another ruler’s titles and making payments could coexist with real control at home. Jingnan’s leaders had limited bargaining power, but enough to preserve a local court for a time. Their independence rested on a changing set of relationships rather than complete freedom from outside pressure.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs: Hugh Clark · Southern kingdoms between Tang and Song

image.caption: The historic walls of Jingzhou, near Jingnan’s capital at Jiangling. The visible walls largely reflect later rebuilding, so the photograph supplies geographic context rather than tenth-century fabric.

cards.name: Later Shu
cards.description: Meng Zhixiang (孟知祥) founded Later Shu in Sichuan (四川) in 934, turning a governorship under Later Tang into an independent court. Under Meng Chang (孟昶), the state sustained regional government and literary life until Song conquered it in 965.
cards.note: 934–965 dates Later Shu; it followed the Later Tang occupation after Former Shu’s fall in 925.

sections.title: An imperial office becomes a throne
sections.text: When northern supervision weakened, a regional commander could use his existing position to seek greater independence. Later Shu grew from offices and resources already established in Sichuan (四川). The authorities these institutions answered to changed, while much of the machinery of local government continued.

sections.title: Two Shu dynasties
sections.text: Later Shu ruled much of the same region as Wang Jian (王建)’s Former Shu, but belonged to a different family. Regional culture and institutions could survive a change of dynasty and find new patrons. The shared name describes a connection to Sichuan (四川), not the return of the earlier ruling house.

image.credit: Gary Todd · National Museum of China / Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: An inscribed stone from the Later Shu Confucian Classics project is displayed in a museum.
image.caption: A surviving stone from the Confucian Classics carved in Chengdu under Later Shu. The museum photograph shows evidence of state-sponsored learning, not the complete monument as it appeared in the tenth century.

cards.name: Southern Tang
cards.description: Southern Tang inherited Wu’s regional government in 937. Its rulers claimed imperial standing and expanded into neighbouring territory before losing ground to northern powers. The last ruler, Li Yu (李煜), is especially remembered for his poetry.
cards.note: 937–975 follows the conquest-year convention. Some chronologies use 976 because of dating conventions.

sections.title: Claiming the Tang inheritance
sections.text: The dynasty used ancestry claims and the Tang name to present its rule as legitimate. That connection was politically constructed and argued over. The name alone does not prove a straightforward family line from the earlier Tang emperors.

sections.title: A court beyond its poems
sections.text: Li Yu (李煜)’s literary fame is one part of the state’s history. Its rulers also maintained armies, collected income and negotiated with rivals. Poetry and government existed in the same court, but literary achievement does not by itself explain military defeat. Southern Tang’s end came through a struggle with stronger northern power.

image.alt: A black-and-white block-print portrait of Southern Tang ruler Li Yu.
image.caption: A 1609 block-print portrait of Li Yu, Southern Tang’s final ruler and a celebrated poet. Printed more than six centuries after his death, it represents his later memory rather than a verified likeness.

cards.name: Northern Han
cards.description: Northern Han preserved a Liu-family court in Shanxi (山西) after Later Han fell in 951. It relied on Liao support while claiming imperial authority of its own. Song conquered it in 979.
cards.note: 951–979 dates Northern Han, distinct from the Earlier Han empire and the short Later Han dynasty.

sections.title: A stronger ally
sections.text: Liao ties offered protection and recognition, while limiting the court’s choices. Depending on an ally did not mean giving up every claim to authority at home. Northern Han’s rulers combined an imperial title with the practical need for support from a larger neighbour.

sections.title: The northern kingdom
sections.text: Despite its location, Northern Han is traditionally counted among the Ten Kingdoms. It also survived beyond Song’s foundation in 960. Northern Han’s location and survival past 960 make both labels imperfect.

sourceLabels.https://assets.cambridge.org/97805218/12: Cambridge History of China · Tenth-century chronology

image.alt: A modern historical map of Later Zhou and neighboring kingdoms.
image.caption: A modern reconstruction of Later Zhou and its neighbors in 951. Northern Han appears as a separate state; this is a retrospective map with approximate boundaries.

cards.name: Ten Kingdoms
cards.description: The Ten Kingdoms were regional states around the transition from Tang to Song. They began and ended at different times and did not all exist together. Northern Han, despite the common association of these kingdoms with the south, lay in the north.
cards.note: 902–979 is a broad span for the regional kingdoms, extending beyond the northern Five Dynasties period of 907–960.

sections.title: Life beyond the northern courts
sections.text: Some kingdoms lasted much longer than the rapidly changing Five Dynasties in the north. Their governments supported farming, sea trade, religious institutions and cultural life. Warfare mattered, but its effects differed across regions; political division did not make every place equally unstable.

sections.title: Different paths to Song rule
sections.text: The states varied in size and in their relationships with stronger neighbours. Some were conquered, while others negotiated submission. Each ruling house relied on its own combination of local resources, military support and diplomacy. Song reunification brought these different regional histories together over time.
