cards.name: Song paper money
cards.description: In the 1020s, the Song government took over the issuing of paper certificates in Sichuan (四川). Known as jiaozi, they developed from merchant arrangements that made payments easier than carrying heavy strings of coins.

sections.title: How paper money earned trust
sections.text: The notes depended on trust in the issuer and on rules for using and redeeming them. Government backing could make them more dependable, while issuing money also gave officials a way to fund spending. Their value came from these arrangements, not simply from the printed sheet.

sections.title: Money with boundaries
sections.text: Early notes were valid within particular regions and conditions. They did not immediately become one currency accepted everywhere. Coins, commodities and different paper issues continued side by side. Successful use depended on administration, control over how much was issued and the payments people could make with it. Paper money solved a practical problem, while creating new responsibilities for its issuer.

cards.note: 1024 is the conventional issue date; establishment of the official administration is also dated 1023. The broader official takeover belongs to the 1020s.

dateReview.note: 1024 is supported by the Reserve Bank of Australia's historical account. Columbia describes the government takeover more broadly as the 1020s; retain the note distinguishing administration in 1023 from issues in 1024.

image.alt: A reproduced paper banknote filled with Chinese writing and decorative framing.
image.caption: A reproduction of a Song banknote, often identified as jiaozi. The precise note type is uncertain; it illustrates paper currency rather than claiming to be an original 1024 issue.

cards.name: Wang Anshi (王安石)’s New Policies
cards.description: Wang Anshi (王安石) launched the New Policies in 1069 under Emperor Shenzong (宋神宗). They sought to change government finance, administration and military support. One proposal offered farmers public loans before harvest, to be repaid alongside seasonal taxes.

sections.title: Loans before the harvest
sections.text: Wang argued that public reserves could provide useful credit and reduce farmers’ dependence on private lenders. Stronger households could also support a stronger state. In practice, officials facing lending and collection targets might prioritize income over a borrower’s circumstances. The same programme could offer help or impose pressure depending on how it was carried out.

sections.title: A dispute over the state’s role
sections.text: Critics questioned whether officials could run these programmes well and whether intervention would add burdens. They were not all opponents of change. The argument concerned what good government should do with money and how far it should enter economic life. Changes at court repeatedly altered the policies’ prospects.

cards.note: 1069 marks the launch of the New Policies. The crop-loan memorial sets out the reformers’ case, rather than an independent account of its results.

dateReview.note: The translated crop-loan memorial is explicitly dated Xining 2, 1069; this is a launch marker rather than the entire reform duration.

image.alt: A printed portrait of an official in a long robe.
image.caption: Wang Anshi in Shangguan Zhou’s 1743 portrait collection. This Qing representation illustrates the reformer’s later commemoration, rather than preserving his appearance from the eleventh century.

cards.name: Shen Kuo (沈括)’s Dream Pool Essays
cards.description: Shen Kuo (沈括)’s Dream Pool Essays, also called Brush Talks, gathered observations about astronomy, geography, technology, medicine and other subjects. The work is commonly dated to about 1088, though completion is estimated between 1088 and 1095.

sections.title: Clues that challenged an explanation
sections.text: Fossil bamboo found where bamboo no longer grew suggested an earlier, different environment. The changing timing of tides challenged a simple explanation based on the sun. Shen compared ideas with observations that did not fit, then tried to explain the mismatch. His interest was in the reasoning as well as the surprising object or event.

sections.title: Knowledge for practical work
sections.text: As a scholar-official, Shen brought calculation and observation to government problems too, including how far carriers could supply an army. Some explanations were mistaken, and inherited ideas about the universe shaped his thinking. The book preserves both careful inquiry and the limits of the knowledge available to him.

cards.note: About 1088 is approximate; completion is estimated between 1088 and 1095.

sourceLabels.https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/songdynas: Columbia Asia for Educators · Shen Kuo and the compass

dateReview.note: Retain circa 1088 as a conventional anchor, but replace the assertion of a secure completion year. University of Washington Press places completion of Brush Talks/Dream Pool Essays sometime between 1088 and 1095.

image.alt: A printed technical drawing of interlocking wooden building brackets.
image.caption: A diagram from the Yingzao Fashi, the building manual of 1103. It is contextual evidence for Song technical description, not an illustration by Shen Kuo or from his Dream Pool Essays.

cards.name: Zhu Xi (朱熹) and White Deer Grotto Academy
cards.description: During his Nankang appointment beginning in 1179, Zhu Xi (朱熹) revived White Deer Grotto Academy. His rules connected learning with the effort to improve one’s character and conduct toward others, rather than treating study only as preparation for office.

sections.title: Learning as daily practice
sections.text: Teachers, students and books came together in an academy where ideas could be practised and discussed. Zhu linked moral development with understanding the patterns of the world. His influence spread through teaching routines, relationships and shared texts as well as through his own writing.

sections.title: Authority came later
sections.text: Zhu faced controversy and political hostility during his life. His interpretations of the Four Books later gained exceptional official influence, especially in examinations. A contested approach to learning became a standard against which candidates were judged. That later authority preserved his work while limiting which answers students could safely give.

cards.note: 1179 marks the academy’s revival during Zhu Xi (朱熹)’s Nankang appointment. Official adoption of his interpretations in examinations came later.

dateReview.note: 1179 is supported for the Nankang appointment and associated academy revival. Preserve the existing distinction from the later formation of examination orthodoxy.

image.caption: Zhu Xi’s 1194 letter on government affairs. An administrative document places his philosophical work beside the practical responsibilities of a scholar-official.

cards.name: Quanzhou (泉州) port
cards.description: A Maritime Trade Office was established at Quanzhou (泉州) in 1087. The Fujian (福建) port’s Song and Yuan prosperity depended on workshops, bridges, docks, officials and religious communities, connected across a landscape extending well inland.

sections.title: From workshop to ship
sections.text: Ceramic kilns and iron producers supplied goods for trade. Roads and waterways carried them toward the harbour. The port depended on workers and transport far beyond the waterfront, so its overseas connections began with local production and the journey to the docks.

sections.title: A place where communities stayed
sections.text: Religious buildings and monuments show that different communities established a lasting presence. Officials regulated trade and collected income, while merchants maintained the services and relationships that made commerce possible. Quanzhou (泉州) grew through these combined efforts. Its prosperity depended on government organization and on networks that extended beyond what officials alone could create.

cards.note: 1087 dates the trade office, not the city’s foundation. Quanzhou (泉州)’s trading system developed over centuries.

dateReview.note: ICOMOS explicitly dates the Maritime Trade Office's creation to 1087; this does not date Quanzhou's foundation.

image.alt: A long stone bridge crossing an estuary.
image.caption: Luoyang Bridge near Quanzhou, photographed in 2017. Founded in the Northern Song period and subsequently repaired, the crossing gives a physical setting for the port region’s commercial connections.

cards.name: Religion under Yuan rule
cards.description: Yuan rulers supported religious specialists from several traditions, with Tibetan Buddhism particularly influential at court. Buddhist, Daoist, Muslim and Christian communities took part in an empire that moved people and knowledge across great distances.

sections.title: What rulers and clergy offered each other
sections.text: Religious specialists could provide learning, rituals and claims to sacred authority. Rulers could grant resources, privileges and protection. Communities competed for access to this support, and imperial favour could change. The presence of several religions did not give all of them equal standing or an independent right to the same treatment.

sections.title: Art across long distances
sections.text: Artisans and patrons brought styles and techniques into new settings. Some travelled for opportunity; others moved because of conquest or forced service. The resulting works reflect skilled labour and particular commissions. Their variety reveals the empire’s far-reaching connections, along with the unequal conditions under which people contributed to them.

cards.note: 1271–1368 is a thematic Yuan range, not a single tolerance decree. Mongol religious policies differed by ruler, region and community.

dateReview.note: 1271–1368 is correctly described as a thematic dynastic range, not a universal tolerance decree. Columbia documents selective patronage and restrictions.

image.alt: A stone archway carved with Buddhist reliefs.
image.caption: The Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass, a Yuan Buddhist monument completed in 1345. Its multilingual inscriptions make religious patronage and the empire’s languages part of the same architectural object.

cards.name: David Vases
cards.description: An inscription on the David Vases records Zhang Wenjin (张文进)’s donation to a Daoist temple in 1351. Made at Jingdezhen (景德镇), the vessels carry blue decoration beneath the glaze. They show that highly accomplished blue-and-white porcelain existed before the Ming dynasty.

sections.title: A date written on the object
sections.text: Ceramics without dates are often compared through their shapes, materials and decoration. These vases provide a firm reference point. They helped overturn an older belief that porcelain of this mature kind belonged only to Ming times. A securely dated object can change how many other surviving pieces are understood.

sections.title: A gift for a family’s protection
sections.text: Zhang Wenjin (张文进) requested protection and blessings for his family. The vases began as a religious gift, bringing skilled manufacture into a relationship between a household and a temple. They later became famous under a collector’s name. Their inscription preserves the earlier donor and purpose, long before they entered the modern art market.

cards.note: 1351 is the inscription’s dedication date, not the invention of blue-and-white porcelain. Earlier examples exist; these vases securely date an accomplished work.

dateReview.note: 1351 is directly attested by the David Vases' dedicatory inscription; it is not the invention date of blue-and-white porcelain.

searchAliases: A dated offering changes ceramic history

image.credit: Freer Gallery of Art / Wikimedia Commons · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A blue-and-white porcelain dish decorated with fish and aquatic plants.
image.caption: A mid-fourteenth-century Yuan porcelain dish in the Freer Gallery. This is a comparable blue-and-white object, not one of the David Vases dated 1351.

cards.name: Wang Yangming (王阳明)’s Philosophy
cards.description: Wang Yangming (王阳明) argued that moral knowledge and action belong together. He traced this teaching to a breakthrough during his exile at Longchang in 1508. His later work challenged influential interpretations of how people should learn to live well.

sections.title: Knowing through action
sections.text: For Wang, repeating a correct moral statement was not enough. Real understanding had to appear in how a person responded and behaved. This challenged the gap between success in scholarly learning and conduct in everyday life. He also warned that selfish desires could obstruct good judgment; his teaching did not simply tell people to trust every impulse.

sections.title: Debate within Confucian learning
sections.text: Wang questioned parts of Zhu Xi (朱熹)’s teaching while drawing on the same inherited texts and concerns. Their disagreements show how much argument existed within Confucian thought. Later followers took Wang’s ideas in different directions. The date 1508 comes from the traditional account of his experience at Longchang; his ideas developed further through teaching and debate.

cards.note: 1508 marks the traditionally narrated Longchang breakthrough. The doctrines developed through subsequent teaching and debate; a conversion narrative is not a transcript of a single moment.

dateReview.note: Stanford's scholarly account places Wang's Longchang awakening in 1508; its narrated character is appropriately acknowledged.

image.alt: A painted portrait of a scholar wearing a dark cap.
image.caption: A Ming representation of Wang Yangming attributed to Shen Junhui. The portrait accompanies a philosophy transmitted through teaching and texts, rather than depicting the Longchang realization itself.

cards.name: Journey to the West
cards.description: Journey to the West turns the pilgrimage of the Tang monk Xuanzang (玄奘) into an adventure filled with religious challenges, comedy and fantasy. Its earliest surviving complete, hundred-chapter edition was printed in Nanjing (南京) in 1592. The stories behind it had developed over centuries.

sections.title: From storytelling to print
sections.text: Oral tales, performances and earlier writings had already transformed the historical journey. The printed novel gathered this material into a long narrative that later readers could encounter in a durable form. Illustrations and chapter divisions helped shape that experience. The book is traditionally attributed to Wu Cheng’en (吴承恩), although its authorship remains debated.

sections.title: Adventure with a satirical edge
sections.text: The pilgrims meet powerful figures whose claims invite fear, laughter and criticism. Religious discipline appears alongside appetite and the Monkey King’s unruly energy. The novel offers a view of late Ming literary culture, rather than a factual record of Xuanzang (玄奘)’s travels or religious life in the Tang dynasty.

cards.note: 1592 identifies the earliest surviving complete edition. Attribution to Wu Cheng’en (吴承恩) is traditional and debated; the story cycle and other versions are earlier.

dateReview.note: Scholarly studies identify the 1592 edition. The card correctly limits its claim to the surviving complete edition and qualifies author attribution.

searchAliases: Journey to the West reaches print

image.credit: Shidetang Hall of Jinling · National Library of China
image.alt: Two facing pages of a woodblock-printed novel with illustrated scenes.
image.caption: Pages from the 1592 Shidetang edition of Journey to the West, held by the National Library of China. The printed object makes the novel’s commercial and visual presentation visible.

cards.name: Li Shizhen (李时珍)’s Compendium of Materia Medica
cards.description: Li Shizhen (李时珍)’s Bencao gangmu, often called the Compendium of Materia Medica, brought together knowledge about medicinal substances. It appeared in print in 1596, after his death. Li compared inherited writings and tried to correct how substances were named, identified and classified.

sections.title: Checking knowledge passed down in books
sections.text: Older descriptions could acquire errors as writers copied them. Li examined this inherited material and reorganized it to make distinctions clearer. His work involved more than collecting additional remedies. It asked how reliable existing descriptions were and how a reader could tell one substance from another. A draft had been completed in 1578, before the first printed edition.

sections.title: Plants, animals and materials
sections.text: The book reached beyond remedies into descriptions of the natural world. Its circulation in East Asia supported further study and adaptation. It does not establish that every treatment it records is effective. The work records how people of its time gathered and evaluated knowledge about substances.

cards.note: 1596 is the first printed edition; a draft had been completed in 1578. This is a history-of-knowledge card, not advice to use historical remedies.

dateReview.note: The National Diet Library confirms the 1596 publication milestone; this is distinct from composition and should not imply publication during Li's lifetime.

searchAliases: Li Shizhen’s Compendium of Materia Medica
cards.linkTitle: Li Shizhen’s Compendium of Materia Medica

image.credit: Li Shizhen ( 李時珍 ) · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A woodblock-printed page with botanical drawings and explanatory text.
image.caption: An illustrated page from the Compendium of Materia Medica associated with Li Shizhen. The text’s arrangement turns accumulated observations and inherited authorities into a usable reference work.

cards.name: Qing Conquests in Inner Asia
cards.nameZh: 清朝征服准噶尔与回部
cards.description: Between 1755 and 1759, Qing campaigns destroyed the Dzungar state and conquered the Tarim Basin. The victories greatly expanded the empire. They also brought mass killing, disease and flight, with devastating consequences for Dzungar communities.

sections.title: The people behind the map
sections.text: These regions already contained states, communities and traditions of government. Qing conquest destroyed a rival power and imposed new forms of military control, settlement and administration. Court accounts celebrated expansion, but the history also includes the people killed or displaced. The mass killing of the Dzungars is commonly described as genocide; precise population and death totals remain uncertain.

sections.title: Governing the conquered regions
sections.text: The Qing used military and local arrangements that differed from those in the inner provinces. A claim on a map, a garrison and a provincial government could mean different levels of control. The conquests had a lasting territorial legacy, but rule continued to develop after the campaigns. Xinjiang (新疆) became a province much later, in 1884.

cards.note: 1755–1759 covers linked campaigns. Mass killing of the Dzungars is commonly analyzed as genocide; precise demographic totals remain uncertain. Xinjiang (新疆)’s later provincial establishment was in 1884.

dateReview.note: 1755–1759 is supported for the linked Dzungar and Tarim conquests. The interval groups campaigns and is not an exact duration for all Qing activity in Inner Asia. Do not add the demographic estimates quoted in the recent article as settled numbers.

image.credit: 禹之鼎 (Yu Zhiding) 范承烈 (Fan Chenglie) · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: An imperial encampment beside a river with mounted attendants.
image.caption: A late-seventeenth-century painting of the emperor at the Kherlen River, attributed to Yu Zhiding and Fan Chenglie. This is an earlier Qing Inner Asian setting, not a depiction of the 1755 Dzungar campaign.

cards.name: The Siku Quanshu (四库全书) Book Collection
cards.description: In the 1770s, the Qianlong (乾隆) court began assembling the Siku quanshu, a vast manuscript collection of Chinese writings. Its four divisions covered classics, histories, philosophical works and literature. Books came from the imperial library and collections across the empire.

sections.title: Preserving and organizing books
sections.text: Scholars compared texts, wrote descriptions and decided which works to include. Their work preserved books and created a guide that later readers could use to explore the collection. The choices of editors also shaped which authors and texts received official recognition. The collection reflects both extensive scholarship and the priorities of an imperial project.

sections.title: Censorship alongside preservation
sections.text: Collecting books allowed officials to inspect material they considered hostile to Manchu rule. Some texts were suppressed or altered. The same project that preserved a huge body of writing also exposed books to destruction. Its surviving volumes therefore show a selection from the past, shaped partly by political decisions. The main compilation period is usually dated 1773–1782.

cards.note: 1773–1782 covers the principal compilation period. Commissioning, individual manuscript copies and later revisions have different dates; the Library of Congress describes its Wenjin copy as 1773–1781.

dateReview.note: Berkeley explicitly supports compilation in 1773–1782. The earlier commission and differing dates for specific copies are correctly noted.

searchAliases: The Siku library: preservation and control

image.credit: Ji Yun and imperial compilers · World Digital Library / National Library of China
image.alt: An old Chinese book opened to columns of text.
image.caption: This surviving volume is part of the Siku Quanshu, compiled under Qianlong. The court project collected and ordered texts while also excluding and censoring works.

cards.name: End of the Imperial Examinations
cards.description: In 1905, the Qing court abolished the traditional civil-service examinations, discontinuing future examinations from 1906. The government wanted schools to provide different kinds of training for public service. An education ministry followed in December 1905.

sections.title: A familiar route to office closes
sections.text: For generations, the examinations had influenced how families invested in their children’s education. Students spent years preparing for a chance to gain office and status. Ending the system changed those expectations. It affected the relationship between study and a government career, as well as the value of knowledge people had already worked hard to acquire.

sections.title: Building a new system
sections.text: Schools needed teachers, teaching materials and money. These resources were unevenly available, and proposals based on foreign examples met debate and resistance. Abolition did not immediately provide education for everyone or bring classical learning to an end. Older qualifications lost their central official purpose while the institutions intended to replace them were still developing.

cards.note: 1905 is the abolition edict; discontinuation applied from 1906. The later December edict established the education ministry. These are related but separate decisions.

dateReview.note: The contemporary diplomatic report expressly dates the abolition edict to 2 September 1905. The separate December education-ministry decree is not the abolition date.

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Long rows of small examination cells in a walled compound.
image.caption: The Guangdong examination compound in 1873. This late Qing photograph shows the mature institution, not the appearance of the examinations at their much earlier beginnings.

cards.name: Lu Xun (鲁迅)’s A Madman’s Diary (狂人日记)
cards.description: Published in New Youth (新青年) in May 1918, Lu Xun (鲁迅)’s A Madman’s Diary became a founding work of modern Chinese short fiction. Its frightened narrator sees a society built on cannibalism. The disturbing image asks whether accepted morality and family obligations can conceal the destruction of individuals.

sections.title: How the narrator challenges society
sections.text: A classical Chinese preface presents the diary as evidence of illness; the diary itself uses vernacular Chinese, or baihua (白话). The narrator reads a history filled with moral teaching and finds cannibalism beneath its respectable words. His suspicions reach into his own family, and he eventually wonders whether he too has participated. The story makes social criticism uncomfortable: recognizing cruelty does not automatically place the critic outside it.

sections.title: What the narrator’s recovery means
sections.text: The preface reports that the narrator has recovered and gone elsewhere to await an official appointment. Readers can ask whether recovery means accepting the society he once condemned. This information comes before the diary, whose final appeal is to save the children. The two voices leave an unresolved question: can another generation escape inherited cruelty, or will those who recognize it also learn to fit in?

cards.note: Published in May 1918. Vernacular fiction existed centuries earlier, and the New Culture Movement was already underway. The story is a landmark of the modern short story, not the invention of vernacular writing. The preface concerns an official appointment, not civil service examinations.

dateReview.note: A Madman’s Diary was published in New Youth in May 1918. April 1918 on the translated text is its writing date. Ohio State source was available in search excerpt; direct retrieval failed.

cards.name: Chinese Civil War
cards.description: The Nationalist-Communist alliance broke apart in 1927, beginning a long civil conflict. Cooperation against Japan interrupted the struggle without resolving it. Major war resumed in 1946. In 1949, Communist forces took control of the mainland and the Nationalist government moved to Taiwan (台湾).

sections.title: Keeping armies in the field
sections.text: Both sides needed soldiers, food and supplies. Their relationships with civilians involved cooperation as well as coercion. Land policies, inflation and years of warfare affected people’s willingness and ability to support them. Military success depended partly on how well each side could organize these resources and sustain support under severe pressure.

sections.title: A conflict with lasting consequences
sections.text: The United States and Soviet Union influenced events, but Chinese leaders also pursued their own aims. The defeat of the Nationalists on the mainland did not produce a complete peace settlement. Separate governments continued on the mainland and in Taiwan (台湾), and armed confrontations continued after 1949. The dates on this card cover the principal conflict rather than every later clash.

cards.note: 1927–1949 is the conventional principal conflict; major war resumed in 1946, and armed confrontations continued after 1949.

dateReview.note: 1927–1949 marks the main civil-war sequence. Full-scale war resumed in 1946; 1949 is no comprehensive peace settlement.

searchAliases: Civil war and the division of governments

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Soldiers advancing through a built-up area.
image.caption: Communist troops at Siping in 1946. The photograph illustrates the resumed civil war after Japan’s defeat, not the earlier rupture of 1927.

cards.name: Second World War: War with Japan
cards.description: Full-scale war between China and Japan followed the Marco Polo Bridge incident in July 1937. Japanese occupation brought mass displacement and atrocities, including the Nanjing (南京) massacre. Nationalist and Communist forces resisted Japan while keeping separate political organizations. The war continued until Japan’s defeat in 1945.

sections.title: A country at war
sections.text: Institutions, industry and people moved inland from occupied areas. Keeping armies supplied while supporting displaced civilians placed enormous demands on government and communities. Schools, workplaces and family life were disrupted. Experiences differed between occupied territory, inland areas and Communist bases, even as the war reshaped all of them.

sections.title: China’s long wartime experience
sections.text: The full-scale conflict began in 1937, before the Pacific War of 1941. Japanese occupation of Manchuria had begun earlier still, in 1931. Later cooperation with the Allies changed supplies and diplomacy. Japan’s defeat ended the war in 1945, but left immense destruction and unresolved conflict between the Nationalists and Communists. Civil war soon returned on a large scale.

cards.note: 1937 dates full-scale war; Japanese occupation of Manchuria began in 1931. This distinction should not imply that aggression began only in 1937.

dateReview.note: 1937–1945 dates full-scale war from the Marco Polo Bridge fighting; Japanese occupation of Manchuria began in 1931.

searchAliases: Second World War: War with Japan
cards.linkTitle: Second World War: War with Japan

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Soldiers holding a position at a city street intersection.
image.caption: National Revolutionary Army troops defending a Shanghai street in 1937. The image records urban fighting, one component of a war that also devastated civilian and rural life.

cards.name: Land Reform
cards.description: The 1950 Land Reform Law extended redistribution in the new People’s Republic, following earlier Communist campaigns. Land and other property changed hands, and households were assigned class labels. The campaign involved coercion and killings as well as the transfer of property.

sections.title: Power changes in the village
sections.text: Land reform affected who could exercise authority locally. Campaigns recruited activists, identified enemies and changed relationships between families. Class labels could continue to affect how people were treated long after the original distribution of land. These consequences reached beyond the fields themselves into the politics and social life of villages.

sections.title: What came before collective farming
sections.text: Giving land to households and later organizing collective agriculture were separate changes. Each altered the control families had over farming and what the state could demand from them. Posters promoted official promises, but the experience of villagers also depended on local disputes and violence. The dates 1950–1953 cover the early PRC campaign; earlier reforms and later collectivization have their own chronologies.

cards.note: 1950–1953 follows the early PRC campaign. Earlier base-area reforms preceded it; later collectivization should be dated separately.

dateReview.note: 1950–1953 is the early PRC campaign covered by the source; earlier base-area reforms and subsequent collectivization have different dates.

image.credit: Artist or photographer unidentified · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A man reading a document aloud to a gathered rural audience.
image.caption: A public reading of the Land Reform Law in 1950. The photograph records legal mobilization, while the redistribution and coercion behind that process require other kinds of evidence.

cards.name: The 1950 Marriage Law
cards.description: The People’s Republic’s Marriage Law of 1950 promoted freedom to choose a spouse, monogamy and equal rights for women and men. It challenged coercive family practices and expanded grounds for divorce. Putting these principles into practice proved harder than announcing them.

sections.title: New rights inside the family
sections.text: Marriage affected property, work and authority as well as personal relationships. The law gave people new claims they could take to officials. Women’s ability to use those rights could still depend on relatives, money and the actions of local authorities. Government became more involved in domestic disputes as it offered ways to challenge established arrangements.

sections.title: The gap between law and daily life
sections.text: Official posters showed couples choosing marriage freely and living harmoniously. Those images expressed the reform’s aims. They did not prove that everyone could exercise the new rights safely or that officials enforced them consistently. The effects varied between communities and households, and unequal practices did not disappear when the law was passed.

cards.note: 1950 dates the new law. Legal equality is not evidence that unequal household practices immediately disappeared.

dateReview.note: 1950 dates the PRC Marriage Law, not completion of changes in household practices.

image.credit: National People’s Congress · National Database of Laws and Regulations
image.alt: The opening page of a Chinese legal document.
image.caption: A later official text of the PRC Marriage Law, from the National People’s Congress law database. It shows the legal tradition that followed the 1950 reform; it is not the original 1950 enactment.

cards.name: Nixon visits China
cards.description: U.S. President Richard Nixon visited China on 21–28 February 1972. He met Mao Zedong (毛泽东) and held talks with Premier Zhou Enlai (周恩来). The visit produced the Shanghai (上海) Communiqué and opened a path toward better relations after decades of hostility.

sections.title: Cold War interests brought the governments together
sections.text: China’s tensions with the Soviet Union and U.S. concerns over Vietnam helped create reasons for talks. Henry Kissinger’s visits in 1971 prepared the way for Nixon’s journey. The presidential visit made this diplomatic opening visible to the public.

sections.title: The communiqué set out agreements and differences
sections.text: Both governments supported progress toward normal relations while stating their separate positions on Taiwan (台湾). They also proposed wider contacts in trade, science, culture and sport. Formal U.S.–PRC diplomatic relations followed in 1979; the 1972 visit was an earlier step in that process.

sourceLabels.https://history.state.gov/milestones/196: U.S. Office of the Historian · Rapprochement with China, 1972

cards.note: 21–28 February 1972 is the visit itself, as recorded in the joint communiqué.

dateReview.note: The joint communiqué records the visit as 21–28 February 1972; the Office of the Historian gives the same dates.

image.alt: Richard Nixon and Zhou Enlai shake hands beside the aircraft stairs, with Pat Nixon and officials nearby.
image.caption: Nixon and Zhou Enlai shake hands on Nixon’s arrival in Beijing on 21 February 1972, the first day of his visit.
image.credit: White House Photo Office · U.S. National Archives / Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain in the United States

cards.name: China Joins the WTO
cards.description: China became a member of the World Trade Organization, or WTO, on 11 December 2001. Membership required changes to tariffs, market access and trade rules, and tied those domestic reforms to an international agreement.

sections.title: Trading under agreed rules
sections.text: More predictable access to markets could help businesses plan investment. China also had to carry out the obligations it had accepted. That required changes in rules and administration over time. Joining the organization was a formal milestone, followed by continuing work to put the agreement into practice.

sections.title: Different effects on different people
sections.text: Greater trade created opportunities for exporters, workers and consumers. It also increased competition and required some firms and regions to adjust. The results depended on circumstances beyond membership alone, including investment and the wider economy. The date on this card marks entry into the organization; it does not explain every economic change that followed.

cards.note: China became a WTO member on 11 December 2001.

dateReview.note: China became a WTO member on 11 December 2001.

searchAliases: China joins the World Trade Organization
cards.pinyin: zhōng guó jiā rù shì mào zǔ zhī

image.alt: World map distinguishing the World Trade Organization’s founding members from countries that joined later.
image.caption: A 2009 map distinguishing the WTO’s founding members from later entrants. China joined the organization in December 2001; the map is an explanatory graphic and is not current for later accessions.

cards.name: King Li (周厉王)’s expulsion and the Gonghe period
cards.description: Traditional histories place the expulsion of King Li (周厉王) of Zhou around 841 BCE, followed by a period known as Gonghe. The people involved are often called inhabitants of the capital. The ancient term guoren does not simply mean modern citizens or the whole farming population.

sections.title: Removing a king
sections.text: The king’s removal exposed conflict within the royal community, but did not abolish the monarchy. Later accounts made it a warning about oppressive rule, especially a ruler’s response to criticism. These stories reveal later ideas about government. They are not independently verified records of everything said during the confrontation.

sections.title: A useful date, disputed details
sections.text: 841 BCE became the conventional starting point for a continuous year-by-year chronology in traditional Chinese histories. Details remain uncertain, including who governed during Gonghe. Some accounts describe a regency; others identify a particular lord as ruler. The name should not be read in its much later sense of a modern republic.

cards.note: 841–828 BCE is the conventional range. Some reconstructions place the expulsion in 842. Accounts disagree over whether Gonghe was a regency or rule by a named lord.

dateReview.note: 841–828 BCE is conventional and supported by Korean academic abstract; 842 start alternative already disclosed. The named lord versus joint-regency interpretation is disputed.

searchAliases: King Li’s expulsion and the Gonghe interregnum
King Li’s expulsion and the Gonghe period
cards.linkTitle: King Li’s expulsion and the Gonghe period

image.alt: A Western Zhou bronze basin with an inscription cast inside it.
image.caption: A Western Zhou bronze basin bearing the Xiu inscription. It shows how elite memory and political relationships were recorded in bronze, but it does not directly document King Li’s expulsion or the Gonghe government.

cards.name: Fall of the Western Zhou capital
cards.description: In the traditional chronology, an attack involving the lord of Shen and Quanrong forces killed King You (周幽王) in 771 BCE. King Ping (周平王) established his court in the east in 770, the conventional beginning of Eastern Zhou. Rival claims to the throne and military alliances both shaped the crisis.

sections.title: Allies could turn against the king
sections.text: Regional lords and groups described as outsiders belonged to connected political networks. They could take sides in a royal succession struggle. Zhou power depended on alliances that might be redirected against its ruler. Losing the western centre weakened the resources supporting the monarchy, even though the royal title remained respected.

sections.title: The story of the warning fires
sections.text: Later tradition blamed the king’s favourite Bao Si (褒姒) and the misuse of warning beacons. This memorable tale turns a political breakdown into a lesson about a king misled by a woman. Its details are less secure than the conventional dates. Reconstructing the crisis also requires attention to rival rulers and military commitments, rather than relying on the anecdote alone.

cards.note: 771 and 770 BCE are conventional anchors. Details of the attack and the famous beacon-fire anecdote depend on later traditions and are not equally secure.

dateReview.note: 771 King You death/Western Zhou end and 770 eastward move are supported. Exact political narrative has greater uncertainty, as note explains.

searchAliases: Fall of the Western Zhou capital
cards.linkTitle: Fall of the Western Zhou capital

image.alt: An eighteenth-century painted portrait of a woman identified as Bao Si.
image.caption: Wang Hui’s eighteenth-century image of Bao Si, a figure later narratives linked to the fall of Western Zhou. The painting is much later than 771 BCE, and those narratives often turn a political and military crisis into a moral tale about a woman.

cards.name: Shang Yang (商鞅)’s reforms
cards.description: Reforms traditionally dated to 356 and 350 BCE link Shang Yang (商鞅) with Qin’s growing strength. They rewarded farming and military achievement, tightened supervision of households and extended direct control by officials. More of ordinary people’s work could then be directed toward the ruler’s needs.

sections.title: Rewards and punishments
sections.text: Rewards offered opportunities beyond inherited privilege. Punishments and collective responsibility, which held groups answerable for members’ conduct, tightened control. Both aimed to direct effort toward farming and war. Powerful households lost some independence. The possibility of advancement in selected activities therefore came alongside stronger restrictions on people’s lives.

sections.title: Changes that outlasted the reformer
sections.text: Shang Yang (商鞅) was executed in 338 BCE, but important changes survived him. Qin’s later conquests also depended on generations of rulers, officials and soldiers. The Book of Lord Shang (商君) contains layers of writing associated with his tradition, rather than a verbatim list of his policies. A proposal in the book does not prove it was applied everywhere in Qin.

cards.note: 356–350 BCE marks the traditional two reform phases. The dating and attribution of individual measures, and the composition of the Book of Lord Shang (商君), require caution.

dateReview.note: 356 and 350 BCE phases explicitly supported. Range connects two phases, not six continuous years of uniform reform; note is adequate.

image.alt: A modern outdoor statue representing Shang Yang in official robes.
image.caption: A modern statue commemorating Shang Yang. It shows how the reformer is remembered, not his historical appearance or direct evidence for the measures attributed to him.

cards.name: Qin’s northern walls
cards.description: After unification, Qin campaigns and construction extended control along the northern frontier. Earlier states had already built walls; Qin adapted and connected parts of them. Much of the familiar stone and brick Great Wall belongs to later periods, especially the Ming.

sections.title: Keeping a wall working
sections.text: Fortifications needed soldiers, communications and dependable supplies. People had to build them, transport provisions and serve on difficult terrain. These projects show the emperor’s ability to demand labour and resources, along with the costs for those assigned to the frontier. Communities brought under new control also faced changes in how they were governed.

sections.title: A changing frontier
sections.text: Walls could direct movement and support military occupation without stopping every exchange. Their routes changed as rulers faced different conditions and enemies. The Great Wall is therefore a long history of separate projects, not one fixed national boundary built once. Qin’s northern expansion and later defensive programmes belong to different political circumstances.

cards.note: About 215–210 BCE locates Qin’s northern campaign and construction phase. It is not the invention date of walls or the date of today’s surviving Ming masonry.

dateReview.note: 215–210 BCE is an approximate selected frontier-campaign interval, not securely dated bounds for all wall building. UNESCO instead says c. 220 BCE, so current UNESCO citation alone cannot prove 215–210. Keep note explicit and approx true; do not present as construction start/completion dates.

searchAliases: Qin’s northern walls and frontier occupation

image.alt: A modern map of the Qin empire around 210 BCE, with northern frontier areas marked.
image.caption: A modern reconstruction of the Qin empire near the end of the First Emperor’s reign. It situates the northern frontier, but its borders are schematic and it does not trace every wall segment built or reused by Qin.

cards.name: Yellow Turban Uprising
cards.description: In 184, followers associated with the religious leader Zhang Jiao (张角) rose against Han rule. Their yellow head coverings gave them their name. Healing practices, hopes for a changed world and economic hardship helped draw supporters. Government forces defeated the main leaders that year, though related armed groups continued much longer.

sections.title: Beliefs connected people
sections.text: Shared religious practices linked communities beyond a single place. They helped people explain suffering and imagine another future. The movement’s intended government is less clear than the accounts of its defeat, mostly written by opponents. Neither dismissing it as superstition nor calling it a modern democratic revolution does justice to that uncertainty.

sections.title: More power for commanders
sections.text: The court relied on commanders and local forces to fight the uprising. Mobilizing them helped armed leaders build greater independent influence. Han did not end in 184; it formally lasted until 220. The rebellion and its suppression added to existing court conflict, rural insecurity and changes in who controlled the soldiers.

cards.note: 184 dates the main coordinated uprising, not the extinction of every Yellow Turban group. Surviving narratives largely come from the movement’s opponents.

dateReview.note: 184 CE main uprising confirmed by de Crespigny's chronology and ChinaKnowledge. Later remnants do not require extending the onset marker.

image.alt: A Qing-period illustration of armed men fighting during the Yellow Turban uprising.
image.caption: A Qing-period illustration based on the Romance of the Three Kingdoms shows fighting during the Yellow Turban uprising. It is a much later literary image, not contemporary evidence for the rebels of 184.

cards.name: War of the Eight Princes
cards.description: The War of the Eight Princes groups several struggles among members of the Sima imperial family between 291 and 306. Palace takeovers grew into wider wars as princes sought control of the emperor and government. Their fighting weakened the unity Western Jin had achieved in 280.

sections.title: Family protection became rivalry
sections.text: Giving royal relatives armies could protect the dynasty from powerful ministers outside the family. It also gave those princes the means to fight each other. Competing claims and commands made succession dangerous. The arrangements meant to secure the dynasty therefore helped rivals challenge control of its centre.

sections.title: Damage beyond the court
sections.text: Campaigns disrupted communities and drew other armed groups into the contests. The later division of the north grew through civil war, recruitment, displacement and new alliances, rather than one sudden invasion. Western Jin survived beyond 306, but emerged weaker. Its later loss of the capitals formed further stages in that breakdown, ending the western dynasty in 316.

cards.note: 291–306 is a conventional grouping of distinct conflicts, not fifteen years of uninterrupted fighting between two fixed sides. Western Jin ended in 316.

dateReview.note: 291–306 is the conventional grouped conflict range; existing note correctly denies continuous fighting.

searchAliases: The wars of the Eight Princes

image.alt: A modern map of military alignments during the War of the Eight Princes in 301.
image.caption: A modern map of the coalition against Sima Lun in 301. It captures one stage of a long, shifting conflict and does not represent the alliances of the entire war.

cards.name: Northern Wei reforms
cards.description: In the late fifth century, Northern Wei changed land and household administration as well as life at court. Empress Dowager Feng (冯太后) and Emperor Xiaowen (孝文帝) both shaped the reforms. The court moved from Pingcheng (平城) to Luoyang (洛阳) in 494, followed by changes to elite names, dress, language and marriage.

sections.title: Different rules for different purposes
sections.text: Household registration and land allocation aimed to strengthen access to farm resources. Court rules changed how powerful families behaved and displayed rank. These were political choices about governing, not simply a whole people deciding to become Chinese. Families could negotiate or resist measures that affected their position.

sections.title: A move with uneven effects
sections.text: Relocating the court changed its relationship with northern military communities. Older identities did not disappear, and government did not become uniform overnight. Some groups were now better placed to share in court rewards than others. Reforms intended to strengthen imperial rule could therefore create new divisions as well as closer connections. Feng’s role also prevents attributing the whole programme to Xiaowen (孝文帝) alone.

cards.note: 485–499 is a selected reform window, beginning with the equal-field reforms and ending with Xiaowen (孝文帝)’s death. Feng’s earlier and continuing role prevents attributing every measure to one emperor.

dateReview.note: 485 equal-field reforms begin the selected window; 499 is Xiaowen’s death. Reforms involved Empress Dowager Feng and multiple stages, already stated.

searchAliases: Northern Wei reforms and the move to Luoyang

image.alt: A later illustration of Emperor Xiaowen and attendants in court dress.
image.caption: A later illustration identified with Emperor Xiaowen. It is useful for the ruler’s historical memory, but it is not a contemporary likeness and cannot show how dress or court culture changed under his reforms.

cards.name: Niu–Li court disputes
cards.description: Early ninth-century court conflicts are commonly called the Niu–Li struggle, after Niu Sengru (牛僧孺) and Li Deyu (李德裕). Officials fought over appointments and policy, rising and falling as influence at court changed. It is uncertain whether they belonged to two stable, clearly separated factions.

sections.title: Changing alliances
sections.text: A familiar explanation places examination graduates on one side and hereditary aristocrats on the other. Actual careers and personal relationships do not divide so neatly. Connections, views on policy and access to rulers shifted over time. A dispute over one appointment did not necessarily reflect the same two permanent camps as every other dispute.

sections.title: Why the label needs care
sections.text: Later accounts gave these conflicts a continuous story, sometimes presenting them as a warning about factional politics or as a struggle between social groups. The conflicts themselves were real, but their organization into one long contest is disputed. Keeping the familiar name need not imply certainty about who consistently belonged on either side.

cards.note: About 820–850 covers the principal disputes. The existence and membership of two stable factions remain contested.

dateReview.note: 820–850 is an older scholarly grouping; recent scholarship disputes the enduring two-faction interpretation. Existing description already communicates this.

searchAliases: The Niu–Li disputes and their later interpretation

image.alt: Traditional temple buildings beneath trees.
image.caption: The Five Officials Temple in Haikou, photographed in 2010. Its commemoration includes the exiled Tang minister Li Deyu; the later shrine reflects political memory rather than the original setting of the Niu–Li disputes.

cards.name: Yue Fei (岳飞)
cards.description: Yue Fei (岳飞) was a leading Southern Song commander against the Jurchen Jin. His successful campaigns, recall and execution in 1142 made him a lasting symbol of loyalty. His career unfolded amid disagreements about recovering territory, negotiating peace and controlling powerful generals.

sections.title: Campaigns and court decisions
sections.text: Recovering the north required money, supplies and continued military risk. The court also sought a settlement it could sustain and worried about its control over commanders. The court weighed those pressures when it recalled Yue, though they do not justify his execution. His death cannot be reduced to proof that victory would otherwise have been certain.

sections.title: The remembered loyal general
sections.text: Later generations found different meanings in Yue’s loyalty: service to his dynasty, personal moral courage and modern national identity. Poems, tattoo stories and family anecdotes helped carry that reputation. Their evidence is uneven, so famous stories should not all be treated as equally reliable accounts from his lifetime.

cards.note: 1127–1142 locates Yue’s Southern Song military career and death, not his lifespan. Famous poems and tattoo stories should not be treated as equally secure contemporary testimony.

dateReview.note: 1127–1142 is valid only as the Southern Song portion of his career. He joined the army in 1122; lifespan was 1103–1142. The existing card states the restricted frame, so no date change is necessary.

searchAliases: Yue Fei: warfare, execution and remembered loyalty

image.alt: Four formally dressed generals arranged across a horizontal painting.
image.caption: The Four Generals of the Restoration, attributed to Liu Songnian, includes Yue Fei. This Southern Song representation commemorates military leadership after the loss of the north.

cards.name: Gunpowder in the Wujing Zongyao (武经总要)
cards.description: The Wujing Zongyao (武经总要), a military reference work completed in 1044, recorded gunpowder recipes and military uses. It preserves knowledge developed through earlier experiments. Weapons that used fire came before the mature firearms familiar from later centuries.

sections.title: From recipe to weapon
sections.text: Ingredients, proportions and preparation all mattered. Armies also needed supplies, manufacturing and training to turn a written formula into something useful in battle. Recording instructions helped knowledge travel beyond one workshop, but the presence of a recipe does not mean every army had the equipment or experience to use it effectively.

sections.title: Knowledge crossed battle lines
sections.text: Song’s opponents also acquired weapons, engineers and techniques. An innovation could spread to rivals rather than securing a permanent advantage for its first users. Sieges and other military demands shaped which uses developed. Gunpowder warfare grew through repeated adaptations as different armies learned how to produce and deploy it.

cards.note: 1044 dates the compendium and its recorded recipes, not the first discovery of every ingredient or the invention of mature cannon. Surviving editions also have a later transmission history.

dateReview.note: 1044 dates the Wujing zongyao manual and recorded recipes; the card correctly avoids treating it as gunpowder's initial discovery.

image.alt: A Chinese technical text with formulae arranged in columns.
image.caption: A page transmitting gunpowder formulae from the Wujing Zongyao, compiled in 1044. The surviving edition is later than the compilation; it is textual evidence, not a photograph of an eleventh-century weapon.

cards.name: Red Turban rebellions
cards.description: Rebellions beginning in 1351 challenged late Yuan rule. Religious hopes for a renewed world helped bring followers together, but the groups called Red Turbans were not one unified army. Zhu Yuanzhang (朱元璋) emerged from this wider struggle and eventually founded Ming.

sections.title: From rebellion to government
sections.text: Promises of renewal could attract supporters. Holding territory then required grain, taxes and cooperation with influential local families. Leaders changed alliances and political language as they tried to build lasting governments. A movement organized for revolt could not govern simply by growing larger.

sections.title: Rivals for power
sections.text: Zhu Yuanzhang (朱元璋) had to defeat competing forces as well as overcome Yuan authority. As imperial control weakened, several leaders pursued their own projects, and military advantage shifted repeatedly. Shared symbols and connections linked Red Turban groups, but their armies could also compete. Ming’s eventual victory was the outcome of that struggle, not a destination agreed by every rebel.

cards.note: 1351–1368 groups the principal rebellions through Ming’s foundation. Fighting and Yuan political continuity extended beyond 1368; the movement’s religious affiliations and composition varied.

dateReview.note: 1351 is the documented outbreak; 1368 is the Ming-foundation cutoff for the card's grouped rebellions. This is not a claim that all insurgent activity ended simultaneously.

image.alt: Map of China showing the territories of Red Turban rebel forces and Yuan warlords during the dynasty’s final years.
image.caption: A modern map of rebel and warlord territories near the end of Yuan rule. It shows the divided political field from which Zhu Yuanzhang emerged; it is a reconstruction, not a contemporary map.

cards.name: The Tumu Crisis
cards.description: In 1449, Oirat forces defeated an expedition led by the Ming Zhengtong (正统) emperor and captured him. The court installed another emperor and organized the defence of Beijing (北京). Losing the ruler was a disaster, but the government continued to function.

sections.title: An imperial expedition goes wrong
sections.text: The emperor’s presence could not solve the army’s problems of supplies, information and command. Later accounts placed much of the blame on the eunuch Wang Zhen (王振). His decisions were part of the story, alongside the military arrangements that left the expedition vulnerable. A ruler at the head of an army could share the risks faced by the force he commanded.

sections.title: Two emperors and a lasting warning
sections.text: Zhengtong (正统) returned in 1450, while another ruler already occupied the throne. He recovered power in 1457. The defeat later became a warning in arguments over how emperors should conduct themselves. The 1449 marker identifies the capture, while the return and restoration were later events. The crisis did not end all Ming military action beyond its borders.

cards.note: 1449 dates the defeat and capture. Zhengtong (正统) returned in 1450 and recovered the throne in 1457; those later events should not be compressed into the battle itself.

dateReview.note: The Palace Museum confirms the defeat and capture in 1449. Later return and restoration are separate events.

searchAliases: The Tumu crisis: an emperor captured

image.credit: 魏煥 魏燕貽 · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: A detailed Chinese military map with fortified settlements.
image.caption: A map of the Xuanfu frontier in the Huang Ming jiu bian kao, published in 1544. It is later than the Tumu crisis and locates its strategic setting rather than reconstructing the battle.

cards.name: Ming Sea Trade and Coastal Raids
cards.description: Ming restrictions limited private overseas trade, but ships and goods continued to move along the coast. Enforcement varied. In the sixteenth century, raids associated with the name wokou involved networks of several nationalities, including many Chinese participants. Calling every raider Japanese would be misleading.

sections.title: Trade under restrictions
sections.text: Merchants still sought goods and profits. Some exchanges were official, while others evaded the rules. Armed traders, officials and coastal communities became involved in relationships that could mix commerce with violence. A ban could change the risks and rewards of trade without bringing all maritime activity to a stop.

sections.title: Fighting raids and permitting trade
sections.text: Campaigns against raiders accompanied arguments over how to regulate the coast. A partial opening in 1567 created new legal opportunities, although restrictions remained, especially on trade involving Japan. The dates 1371–1567 provide a broad policy frame. They do not describe one rule enforced uniformly throughout the period, and the major raids of the Jiajing (嘉靖) era occurred in the mid-sixteenth century.

cards.note: 1371–1567 is a conventional policy frame, not uninterrupted uniform enforcement. The principal Jiajing (嘉靖)-era raids belong to the mid-sixteenth century; wokou does not mean every raider was Japanese.

dateReview.note: The Oxford research dates the first cited maritime prohibition to 1371 and relaxation to 1567, while identifying many intervening decrees. The card's variable-enforcement qualification is necessary.

searchAliases: Ming Sea Trade and Coastal Raids
cards.linkTitle: Ming Sea Trade and Coastal Raids

image.credit: Henry Charles Seppings Wright · Hutchinson's Story of the Nations / Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Later illustration of armed raiders attacking people on the Chinese coast while ships approach offshore.
image.caption: Henry Charles Seppings Wright’s 1915 illustration of a wokou raid on China’s coast. It is a later British representation, not an eyewitness image of the sixteenth-century raids.

cards.name: Zhang Juzheng (张居正)’s Reforms
cards.description: Zhang Juzheng (张居正) was the senior grand secretary during the early years of the Wanli (万历) emperor’s reign. Between 1572 and 1582, he pushed for closer supervision of officials and more reliable tax collection. His programme included land surveys and wider use of consolidated tax payments.

sections.title: Making tax demands clearer
sections.text: Combining obligations could simplify what households owed. Paying in silver also made access to markets and silver supplies more important. A clearer tax demand did not necessarily mean a fairer burden. Local officials still determined how payments were distributed and collected, and how much money reached the government. The reforms had earlier local precedents.

sections.title: Reform depends on court support
sections.text: Zhang’s methods provoked arguments about discipline and the freedom of officials to criticize government. Accounts differ over how much criticism his reforms allowed. After his death, he fell into disgrace, showing how vulnerable his position had been to changing support at court. Some measures outlasted him; his fall did not mean every reform disappeared.

cards.note: 1572–1582 marks Zhang’s dominance and death. The Single Whip reforms had earlier local precedents and uneven implementation; Zhang did not invent silver taxation in one nationwide decree.

dateReview.note: 1572–1582 is supported for Zhang's senior-secretary dominance, not his whole official career or all origins of Single Whip reform.

searchAliases: Zhang Juzheng and the discipline of government

image.alt: A portrait of a Ming official with a beard and black hat.
image.caption: A sixteenth-century representation of Zhang Juzheng. The portrait accompanies the minister’s fiscal and administrative reforms; it does not depict their implementation.

cards.name: The Kangxi (康熙) Emperor
cards.description: Kangxi (康熙)’s long reign helped secure Qing rule through war, negotiation and support for learning and the arts. Defeating the Three Feudatories and incorporating Taiwan (台湾) were major turning points. His southern inspection tours also brought the emperor into important commercial regions.

sections.title: Different ways to exercise authority
sections.text: The Qing empire contained different political and religious traditions. Kangxi (康熙) preserved Manchu imperial identity while supporting classical Chinese learning and presenting himself as a responsible ruler. Military campaigns and cultural patronage helped him reach different groups. These activities belonged to the same effort to strengthen the dynasty’s authority across a large and varied empire.

sections.title: Looking at an imperial tour
sections.text: Paintings of inspection tours show orderly cities, landscapes and the emperor’s progress through them. They present the image the court wanted to project. Waterways and commerce also had practical importance to government. Kangxi (康熙) took the throne in 1661, while his reign era began in 1662. Regents governed during his early years, before he exercised personal rule.

cards.note: 1661 dates accession; the Kangxi (康熙) reign era began in 1662, explaining the two start dates in references. Early government operated through regents; the whole reign was not personal rule from infancy.

dateReview.note: 1661–1722 is accession-to-death; 1662 begins the Kangxi era name. The existing note correctly explains the distinction.

image.credit: Anonymous Unknown author Qing Dynasty Court Painter · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: The Kangxi emperor seated in richly decorated court dress.
image.caption: The Kangxi emperor in court dress, by an anonymous Qing court painter. The image expresses imperial authority, rather than recording any one campaign or administrative decision.

cards.name: Founding of the Chinese Communist Party
cards.description: The Chinese Communist Party’s first congress met in Shanghai (上海) in July 1921. It brought together small groups of Marxist activists. The organization developed amid labour activism, nationalist movements and arguments over China’s future, with support from international Communist networks.

sections.title: From discussion groups to a party
sections.text: A political party could coordinate members and actions beyond the circulation of books and ideas. It needed leaders, resources and links with workers. The Comintern, the international Communist organization, provided assistance and expected a role in strategy. These relationships connected Chinese political struggles with developments following the Russian Revolution.

sections.title: An uncertain beginning
sections.text: The party’s later control of the mainland was not assured in 1921. Alliances, repression and internal disputes changed its organization and strategy in the years that followed. The first congress conventionally dates to 23 July, based partly on later recollections. The party’s commemorative anniversary is 1 July. The anniversary and the reconstructed opening date should be kept distinct.

cards.note: The congress opened on 23 July 1921 in the conventional reconstruction. July 1 is the commemorative anniversary, not the documented opening date. Some details depend on later recollections.

dateReview.note: 1921 is established. 23 July is the conventional reconstructed opening date; 1 July is the commemorative anniversary.
