image.caption: The Shanghai site of the Chinese Communist Party’s First Congress, photographed in 2021. It is a preserved commemorative site, not a contemporary photograph of the 1921 meeting.

cards.name: Zhuge Liang (诸葛亮)’s northern expeditions
cards.description: Between 228 and 234, Zhuge Liang (诸葛亮) led repeated campaigns from Shu against Wei. Shu’s court in Sichuan (四川) claimed to restore Han rule, but faced a much larger rival. Mountain routes and the work of supplying soldiers limited what its armies could achieve.

sections.title: Getting food to the troops
sections.text: An army crossing difficult terrain needed provisions while leaving its home territory able to support the next campaign. A chance to win a battle mattered only if troops and supplies could reach it. Supply limits repeatedly forced the armies to withdraw. Comparing the cleverness of individual commanders cannot fully explain what Shu could sustain.

sections.title: The commander and his later reputation
sections.text: Zhuge Liang (诸葛亮) died in 234, ending his leadership of the campaigns. Shu survived until 263. Later stories made him a model of extraordinary foresight and loyalty. His historical work involved keeping a smaller state capable of pursuing a large military ambition. That sustained effort can be appreciated while keeping later fiction separate from accounts of the campaigns themselves.

cards.note: 228–234 dates the conventional northern expedition sequence. The later Romance of the Three Kingdoms elaborates events and should not be treated as contemporary military evidence.

dateReview.note: 228–234 is confirmed by John Killigrew’s dedicated scholarly study.

image.alt: A later ink painting of Zhuge Liang holding a feather fan.
image.caption: Zhang Feng’s later portrait of Zhuge Liang uses the familiar scholar-strategist image. It reflects his posthumous reputation rather than documenting the northern expeditions or his appearance.

cards.name: Battle of the Fei River
cards.description: In 383, Eastern Jin defeated Fu Jian (苻坚)’s Former Qin army at the Fei River. Former Qin had united much of the north and wanted to extend its rule south. Defeat disrupted that ambition and hastened the breakup of an alliance containing competing loyalties.

sections.title: One ruler, different interests
sections.text: Conquest had brought commanders and troops under Fu Jian (苻坚) without making all their interests the same. Their willingness to remain depended on rewards, confidence and the centre’s ability to demand obedience. Losing a battle could change those calculations. Defections and rival ambitions then made the consequences much larger than the immediate military loss.

sections.title: The south survived
sections.text: Victory allowed Eastern Jin and powerful southern families to continue developing government around the Yangtze (长江). Former Qin did not disappear that day; it lasted until 394 as its territory fragmented. Traditional accounts contain dramatic tactics and enormous troop totals that remain uncertain. The choices commanders and rulers made after the battle determined its wider effects.

cards.note: 383 is the battle year. Former Qin continued until 394; its fragmentation was a process. Received troop totals and tactical anecdotes should not be accepted without qualification.

dateReview.note: 383 is confirmed in Cambridge History of War; Former Qin did not disappear in the battle year.

searchAliases: The battle of the Fei River

image.alt: A modern map showing the opposing movements around the Battle of the Fei River.
image.caption: A modern map of the Fei River campaign between Former Qin and Eastern Jin. It summarizes reported movements and terrain rather than providing a contemporary battlefield survey.

cards.name: Li Zicheng (李自成) captures Beijing (北京)
cards.description: Li Zicheng (李自成)’s forces captured Beijing (北京) in 1644, and the Chongzhen (崇祯) emperor died as the Ming capital fell. Li had proclaimed a Shun government. His occupation was short: Qing forces joined with the Ming commander Wu Sangui (吴三桂) and defeated him at Shanhai Pass (山海关).

sections.title: Taking a capital and holding power
sections.text: The capture of Beijing (北京) removed the Ming court from its capital. Li still needed supplies, taxes and cooperation from officials and military commanders elsewhere. Winning the city did not automatically give him those resources. His new government faced the immediate challenge of turning military success into lasting control.

sections.title: Several changes in one year
sections.text: Beijing (北京) passed from the Ming to Li’s Shun government and then to the Qing in 1644. Ming princes and loyalists continued to resist in the south. This sequence included rebel armies, rival governments and alliances between former enemies. Qing control over wider territories developed through further conflict. The year marks the capture and loss of Beijing (北京), rather than the end of all Ming resistance.

cards.note: 1644 dates the capture and loss of Beijing (北京), not the beginning of Li’s uprising or the end of all Ming resistance. Accounts of his later death are disputed.

dateReview.note: 1644 is secure for Li's capture and loss of Beijing. The Qing takeover and continuing Southern Ming resistance are properly distinguished.

image.credit: Henry Charles Seppings Wright · Hutchinson's History of the Nations / Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Later illustration of armed rebels entering and setting fires in Beijing during the fall of the Ming capital.
image.caption: A 1915 British illustration of Li Zicheng’s forces taking Beijing in 1644. It was made centuries after the event and should be read as a later reconstruction.

cards.name: Imperial examinations under Sui
cards.description: The Sui period is associated with the emergence of imperial examinations, with 605 often used for the advanced-scholar examination. Written tests became one route toward government service. Recommendations, family standing and other routes remained important.

sections.title: What candidates studied
sections.text: Testing made demonstrated knowledge relevant to promotion. Over time, the subjects examined and the answers accepted shaped education and family ambitions. This influence grew gradually. Early Sui examinations did not yet have the much greater role that examinations would acquire under later dynasties.

sections.title: Opportunity with limits
sections.text: Preparation took time, teachers and material support. Rules about eligibility and nomination could also restrict participation. Examinations changed how officials were chosen without making access equal. The system lasted through repeated changes in its design, rather than following one complete plan created under Sui.

cards.note: 605 is a conventional date. Earlier recruitment tests existed, and definitions of the first imperial examination differ.

dateReview.note: 605 is a disputed conventional origin anchor; proposed alternatives include 587 and 605–607, depending on what counts as an examination. Existing note is appropriately cautious.

image.credit: Attributed to Yan Liben · Museum of Fine Arts, Boston / Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Emperor Wen of Sui seated in ceremonial robes in a detail from the Thirteen Emperors Scroll.
image.caption: Emperor Wen of Sui in a seventh-century detail from the Thirteen Emperors Scroll, traditionally attributed to Yan Liben. The ruler’s portrait provides context for Sui government; it does not depict an examination.

cards.name: Taizong (唐太宗)’s Zhenguan (贞观) era
cards.description: Taizong (唐太宗)’s Zhenguan (贞观) era, 627–649, became a famous model of imperial government. Later collections portrayed him debating policy and listening to criticism from ministers. Those texts preserved ideals of good rule as well as memories of a particular reign.

sections.title: Speaking honestly to an emperor
sections.text: Ministers were expected to point out dangers, but the emperor still held the power to appoint and punish them. Honest advice depended on a ruler’s willingness to listen within that unequal relationship. Accounts of Taizong (唐太宗) accepting criticism later gave officials examples they could use when urging other monarchs to heed advice.

sections.title: A model across East Asia
sections.text: The Essentials of Governance circulated beyond [[id:tang|Tang China]] and influenced later political debate. Its selected conversations offered lessons, rather than an unedited record of everything said at court. Taizong (唐太宗)’s authority also rested on military and administrative institutions and followed a [[id:xuanwu-gate|violent succession struggle]]. The book preserves one influential view of the reign alongside its military rise and violent succession.

cards.note: 627–649 is the Zhenguan (贞观) reign era, beginning after Taizong (唐太宗)’s accession in 626. The surviving governance compilation was produced and transmitted later, with editorial choices and variant versions.

dateReview.note: 627–649 is the Zhenguan era, distinct from Taizong’s accession in 626.

searchAliases: Zhenguan: government and its exemplary record

image.credit: Anonymous Chinese artist · Walters Art Museum / Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: Painted officials from a handscroll of Emperor Taizong’s twenty-four ministers.
image.caption: Part of a seventeenth-century handscroll portraying Taizong’s twenty-four celebrated ministers. Made about a millennium after the Zhenguan era, it records their later political reputation rather than their actual likenesses.

cards.name: Xuanzong (唐玄宗)’s Kaiyuan (开元) era
cards.description: Xuanzong (唐玄宗)’s Kaiyuan (开元) era, 713–741, is remembered as a high point of [[id:tang|Tang]] prosperity. Court support for the arts, skilled production and imperial reach contributed to its reputation. That prosperity was not shared equally by every region or household.

sections.title: The work behind fine objects
sections.text: Elite possessions reveal skilled workshops and resources drawn toward wealthy patrons. Storehouses and court commissions helped organize production. Finished objects preserve the tastes of their owners more clearly than the lives of the people who supplied materials and labour. Cultural splendour depended on this less visible work.

sections.title: Prosperity before the rebellion
sections.text: The [[id:an-lushan|An Lushan Rebellion]] began later, in 755. Comparing its destruction with Kaiyuan (开元) abundance can make the whole period look like a simple warning about luxury. Military arrangements, appointments and government demands also changed over time. The era’s achievements were real, but neither its prosperity nor the later disaster made the outcome inevitable.

cards.note: 713–741 is the Kaiyuan (开元) era, not Xuanzong (唐玄宗)’s entire reign. Shengshi means a flourishing age; the An Lushan Rebellion (安史之乱) began in 755.

dateReview.note: 713–741 is the Kaiyuan era; the Berkeley inscription catalogue uses these dates.

searchAliases: Kaiyuan: prosperity and the demands of empire

image.alt: A painted portrait of Tang emperor Xuanzong in court dress.
image.caption: A traditional portrait of Emperor Xuanzong, whose Kaiyuan reign gave the era its name. The Commons record does not identify the artist or date, so it should not be treated as a contemporary likeness.

cards.name: Sanxingdui ritual pits
cards.description: At Sanxingdui in Sichuan (四川), archaeologists found pits filled with bronze heads and masks, gold, jade, elephant tusks and other objects. Many pieces had been burned or broken before burial. The finds came from a large walled city whose ritual life differed sharply from the Shang centre at Anyang (安阳).

sections.title: A powerful centre beyond Anyang (安阳)
sections.text: Sanxingdui had advanced bronze casting and access to expensive materials, but it left no readable archive like the Shang oracle bones. Its rulers and beliefs must be studied through buildings and objects. The site prevents the written record of one court from standing in for every Bronze Age society in the region.

sections.title: The pits were not one event
sections.text: Recent excavations identify several deposits made at different times. Archaeologists still debate exactly what ceremonies produced them and whether every pit should be called sacrificial. The dates on this card cover the main deposits, not a single destruction or burial.

cards.note: The principal deposits date roughly from 1200 to 1000 BCE, with some material possibly extending to about 950 BCE. Sanxingdui lay outside direct Shang rule.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · p. 32
sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/: Antiquity · New discoveries at Sanxingdui

dateReview.note: The principal deposits date roughly from 1200 to 1000 BCE, with some material possibly extending to about 950 BCE. Sanxingdui lay outside direct Shang rule.

cards.pinyin: sān xīng duī jì sì kēng

image.alt: Large bronze mask with projecting eyes displayed in the Sanxingdui Museum.
image.caption: A bronze mask from Sanxingdui, photographed in the Sanxingdui Museum in 2010. It is an excavated ritual object, not a portrait of a known person.

cards.name: Fu Hao: Shang commander and royal consort
cards.description: Fu Hao was a consort of the Shang king Wu Ding, a military commander and a participant in court ritual. Oracle-bone inscriptions record her leading campaigns and receiving royal instructions. Her tomb at Anyang (安阳) survived unlooted, preserving weapons, ritual bronzes, jades and objects bearing her name.

sections.title: Written and archaeological evidence meet
sections.text: The inscriptions identify Fu Hao in the activities of the royal house; the tomb records the objects and sacrifices assembled for her burial. Together they provide an unusually detailed account of one Shang woman. They do not establish that other women held the same rank or authority.

sections.title: The burial displays wealth and office
sections.text: More than two hundred bronze vessels and a large collection of weapons were buried with her. The objects link military command, ritual duty and royal status. They also show how much labour and material an elite burial could command.

cards.note: Ebrey dates Fu Hao’s tomb to about 1250 BCE. Museum sources often use about 1200 BCE or the broader thirteenth century BCE. The exact year is not known.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · p. 30

dateReview.note: Ebrey dates Fu Hao’s tomb to about 1250 BCE. Museum sources often use about 1200 BCE or the broader thirteenth century BCE. The exact year is not known.

image.caption: An owl-shaped bronze zun from Fu Hao’s tomb at Anyang, displayed at the Henan Museum. The burial is dated within the thirteenth century BCE; Ebrey uses about 1250 BCE, while museum sources often use about 1200 BCE.

cards.name: Qin–Han expansion into the south
cards.description: Qin armies moved into Lingnan and created commanderies there around 214 BCE. After Qin collapsed, the kingdom of Nanyue ruled much of the region until Han conquest in 111 BCE. Military settlement, government offices and migration tied more of the south to the imperial state, often through coercion and negotiation with established communities.

sections.title: Conquest did not settle control at once
sections.text: Nanyue kept its own kings and combined institutions inherited from Qin with local and regional ties. Han victory ended that kingdom, but effective rule still depended on officials, transport, settlers and local cooperation. A boundary drawn after conquest cannot measure how deeply government reached.

sections.title: Migration changed the imperial centre of gravity
sections.text: Population moved south over many generations, bringing new land into cultivation and enlarging tax registers. Existing peoples did not simply disappear. The resulting society joined migration, intermarriage, conflict and cultural change rather than copying northern China intact.

cards.note: The range joins several developments: Qin conquest around 214 BCE, Han conquest of Nanyue in 111 BCE and continued migration through the second century. It was not one continuous war.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · pp. 85–87

dateReview.note: The range joins several developments: Qin conquest around 214 BCE, Han conquest of Nanyue in 111 BCE and continued migration through the second century. It was not one continuous war.

image.alt: Small jade seal from the tomb of Zhao Mo, king of Nanyue, displayed in Guangzhou.
image.caption: A jade seal from the tomb of Zhao Mo, the second king of Nanyue. Nanyue ruled much of Lingnan before Han armies conquered the kingdom in 111 BCE.

cards.name: Faxian’s journey to India
cards.description: The Buddhist monk Faxian left China in 399 to seek monastic rules and other texts in India. He travelled overland through Central Asia, visited places associated with the Buddha and returned by sea through Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. His written account described India as a complex and civilized society rather than a distant abstraction.

sections.title: A journey driven by missing texts
sections.text: Chinese Buddhist communities already had scriptures and institutions, but monks knew that their collections were incomplete. Faxian sought material that could settle questions about monastic discipline. The trip joined religious study to the physical work and danger of crossing deserts, mountains and seas.

sections.title: Travel writing widened the record
sections.text: Faxian noted monasteries, cities, rulers and social customs across the places he visited. His account preserves one traveller’s observations and judgments, not a neutral survey of South Asia. It also records exchange moving in more than one direction: a Chinese monk travelled abroad, selected texts and brought them home for translation.

cards.note: Ebrey dates the full journey to 399–414. Some shorter biographies give 412 for Faxian’s return to China; 414 includes the last stage before he settled at Jiankang (建康).

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · p. 106
sourceLabels.https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/te: University of Washington · The journey of Faxian

dateReview.note: Ebrey dates the full journey to 399–414. Some shorter biographies give 412 for Faxian’s return to China; 414 includes the last stage before he settled at Jiankang.

image.alt: Early twentieth-century illustration of Faxian standing among ruins attributed to Ashoka’s palace.
image.caption: Allan Stewart’s early twentieth-century illustration imagines Faxian at the ruins of Ashoka’s palace. It is not a contemporary portrait of the fifth-century monk.

cards.name: Footbinding spreads among Song elites
cards.description: Footbinding probably began among dancers or entertainers in the tenth or eleventh century, then spread among elite families. By the Southern Song, some girls had their feet tightly bound from early childhood. Small feet became associated with beauty and status, at the cost of pain and permanent physical change.

sections.title: The practice spread unevenly
sections.text: Footbinding was never universal. Region, class, labour and community customs affected whether families adopted it. Early evidence comes disproportionately from elite writing and burials, so it cannot describe every household or fix one date when the practice began.

sections.title: Bodies carried social expectations
sections.text: Binding shaped movement, clothing and ideas about respectable femininity. Families could treat it as a requirement for a suitable marriage, even when the process harmed girls. That pressure made the custom durable without requiring a law that ordered all women to follow it.

cards.note: The range marks the spread of footbinding during the Song, not a dated invention. Surviving evidence is strongest for elite women and varies by region.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · p. 160

dateReview.note: The range marks the spread of footbinding during the Song, not a dated invention. Surviving evidence is strongest for elite women and varies by region.

image.alt: A small embroidered black shoe made for a woman with bound feet, photographed against a plain background.
image.caption: A later model shoe made for a bound foot. It shows the specialized footwear the practice required; it is not a Song-dynasty shoe.

cards.name: Guan Hanqing and Yuan drama
cards.description: Commercial theatre flourished under the Yuan. Guan Hanqing wrote plays for this world, including The Injustice to Dou E, in which a young widow accepts a false murder confession to protect her mother-in-law. The story turns a corrupt legal judgment into a demand for recognition and redress.

sections.title: Drama reached audiences through performance
sections.text: A play combined sung arias, speech, gesture and familiar stage roles. Printed texts preserve scripts, but performance depended on actors, musicians and local audiences. Theatre belonged to urban commercial life as well as to later literary study.

sections.title: Dou E puts justice on trial
sections.text: Before her execution, Dou E predicts signs that will prove her innocence. The plot uses supernatural confirmation because the courts have failed her. Her father eventually reviews the case and punishes the real offenders, but official correction cannot restore the life already taken.

cards.note: Guan Hanqing’s life dates and the dates of individual plays are uncertain. The late thirteenth century is a working range for his activity, not a complete Yuan theatrical chronology.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · pp. 198–199

dateReview.note: Guan Hanqing’s life dates and the dates of individual plays are uncertain. The late thirteenth century is a working range for his activity, not a complete Yuan theatrical chronology.

image.credit: Bibliothèque nationale de France · Wikimedia Commons
image.alt: An open woodblock-printed Chinese book with an official, a kneeling figure and a group of mounted and standing figures.
image.caption: An illustrated spread from a 1615–1616 Ming anthology that preserved Yuan plays in print. It is not a portrait of Guan Hanqing or a contemporary picture of a Yuan performance.

cards.name: Hongwu abolishes the chancellorship
cards.description: In 1380, the Hongwu emperor accused his chief councillor Hu Weiyong of treason and abolished the top chancellery offices. The emperor took direct control of the ministries instead of appointing another chancellor. Later Ming emperors inherited a government with more authority concentrated at the throne.

sections.title: A purge changed the structure of government
sections.text: Hu Weiyong’s execution began a much wider purge that killed many officials and their relatives. The case removed rivals, but its institutional result lasted longer than the immediate accusations. No later Ming official formally held the old chancellor’s authority.

sections.title: More control brought more work
sections.text: Direct rule gave the emperor extraordinary access to decisions across the government. It also created a practical problem: one person could not read and decide every matter alone. Grand secretaries and palace eunuchs later gained influence by controlling documents and access, even though neither group simply recreated the abolished office.

cards.note: 1380 dates Hu Weiyong’s execution and the abolition of the Central Secretariat and chancellery. The associated purge continued afterward.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · p. 203

dateReview.note: 1380 dates Hu Weiyong’s execution and the abolition of the Central Secretariat and chancellery. The associated purge continued afterward.

image.alt: A bearded Ming gentleman sits facing forward in a broad robe and square black cap.
image.caption: A later Ming portrait of an unidentified gentleman. It represents the officials affected by Ming government, not Hu Weiyong or the events of 1380.

cards.name: Matteo Ricci prints a Chinese world map
cards.description: In 1602, the Jesuit Matteo Ricci worked with Chinese collaborators to publish the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu, a large Chinese-language map of the world. It presented the Americas and other geographical information unfamiliar to many Chinese viewers while placing China near the centre of the layout.

sections.title: The map was a collaborative translation
sections.text: Ricci drew on European geographical sources, but Chinese scholars and printers made the map readable and reproducible in China. Explanatory text and translated place names mattered as much as coastlines. The result was neither a European map merely relabelled nor a complete replacement for Chinese geographical knowledge.

sections.title: Maps could support a religious mission
sections.text: Ricci presented himself as a learned man and used mathematics, astronomy and geography to build relationships with officials. The map attracted attention without requiring viewers to accept Christianity. Knowledge exchange and missionary strategy operated together.

cards.note: 1602 dates the best-known six-panel edition. Ricci produced earlier Chinese world maps, and later copies changed details.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · pp. 224–225

cards.name: Muslim uprisings and Qing reconquest
cards.nameZh: 清末回民起义与清军收复新疆
cards.description: Muslim communities rebelled against Qing rule in Yunnan and across parts of the northwest during the 1850s and 1860s. Local violence, ethnic hostility, official abuses and struggles for political control drove conflicts that were connected in time but not directed as one national movement. Qing armies retook the affected regions at enormous human cost.

sections.title: Several wars unfolded at once
sections.text: The uprising in Yunnan produced a rebel government centred on Dali. Farther north, fighting spread through Shaanxi (陕西) and Gansu, while Yaqub Beg built a separate state in much of Xinjiang (新疆). The participants, aims and local histories differed, so one label should not erase those distinctions.

sections.title: Reconquest strengthened some regional commanders
sections.text: The Qing relied on armies organized around powerful officials rather than only on older banner and Green Standard forces. Zuo Zongtang led the campaign that restored Qing control in Xinjiang (新疆). The campaigns preserved the empire’s western territory while leaving communities devastated and local power more militarized.

cards.note: The range combines the Yunnan uprising, usually dated 1855 or 1856–1873, the northwestern uprisings of the 1860s and 1870s, and Qing reconquest completed in 1878. These were related but distinct conflicts.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · pp. 254–257

image.caption: Troops and artillery in Gansu in 1875, photographed during a Russian expedition that gathered information about the fighting in western China. The image shows Qing military presence, not a battle or every community involved in the uprisings.

cards.name: The Warlord Period
cards.description: After Yuan Shikai (袁世凯) died in 1916, no central government could command the whole country. Military commanders, provincial governors and local strongmen built competing power bases. Governments continued to sit in Beijing (北京), but cabinets changed rapidly and warlord armies fought repeated wars for territory and revenue.

sections.title: Fragmented power reached ordinary people
sections.text: Armies demanded taxes, recruits and supplies from the areas they controlled. Banditry and fighting disrupted travel and farming, and some villages organized their own defence. Political fragmentation was therefore more than a contest among generals in capital cities.

sections.title: Political and cultural change continued
sections.text: Sun Yat-sen (孙中山)’s Nationalists built a base in Guangzhou (广州) while students and writers challenged inherited authority through the New Culture and May Fourth movements. The Northern Expedition of 1926–1928 defeated or absorbed major warlords and established a Nationalist government at Nanjing (南京), though regional military power did not vanish.

cards.note: 1916–1928 is the conventional range from Yuan Shikai (袁世凯)’s death to the establishment of the Nanjing (南京) Nationalist government. Warlord power persisted after 1928.

sourceLabels.https://www.cambridge.org/highereducatio: Patricia Buckley Ebrey · The Cambridge Illustrated History of China, 3rd ed. · pp. 276–279

dateReview.note: 1916–1928 is the conventional range from Yuan Shikai’s death to the establishment of the Nanjing Nationalist government. Warlord power persisted after 1928.

image.caption: Chinese soldiers train with swords during the warlord era. The archival footage survives in a later U.S. government documentary; it illustrates military organization, not one specific battle.

cards.name: China enters the Korean War
cards.nameZh: 中国人民志愿军入朝参战
cards.description: Chinese forces entered the Korean War in October 1950 after United Nations troops advanced toward the Yalu River. Fighting pushed the front south and then settled near the dividing line. The 1953 armistice stopped the main combat without producing a peace treaty.

sections.title: The war reshaped China’s foreign position
sections.text: The new People’s Republic fought the United States less than a year after its founding. The war strengthened China’s alliance with North Korea and deepened hostility with the United States. U.S. protection of Taiwan (台湾) also made a Communist attack on the island far less likely.

sections.title: Mobilization extended inside China
sections.text: The government raised money, recruited soldiers and presented the conflict as resistance to American aggression. Wartime security campaigns targeted people accused of counterrevolutionary activity. Battlefield losses and domestic repression formed part of the same national mobilization.

cards.note: Chinese forces crossed into Korea in October 1950. The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953; no peace treaty followed.

cards.name: Agricultural collectivization
cards.description: Soon after land reform gave plots to rural households, the Communist Party began pooling farming through mutual-aid teams and cooperatives. By 1956, most farm households had entered higher-level cooperatives. Families were paid mainly for labour rather than for the land and tools they had contributed.

sections.title: Land reform and collectivization moved in opposite directions
sections.text: Land reform broke up landlord holdings and transferred property to households. Collectivization then reduced household control by placing land and production under cooperatives. Treating the two as one reform hides the speed and scale of that reversal.

sections.title: Village officials controlled more of daily farming
sections.text: Cooperative leaders assigned work, recorded work points and helped determine what crops to plant. The state purchased grain at fixed prices to support cities and industrialization. Local cadres therefore mediated between national demands and the food and income available to farm families.

cards.note: The change proceeded in stages from mutual-aid teams to lower- and higher-level cooperatives. The 1951–1956 range precedes the larger people’s communes introduced during the Great Leap Forward in 1958.

cards.name: Hundred Flowers and the Anti-Rightist Campaign
cards.description: In 1956 and early 1957, Mao Zedong (毛泽东) called for open criticism of problems within the Communist Party. Intellectuals, students, workers and some party members voiced complaints. The leadership soon reversed course, and the Anti-Rightist Campaign punished many of the people who had spoken.

sections.title: An invitation to criticize became a political trap
sections.text: People first responded cautiously, then spoke more freely as officials continued to request criticism. Complaints addressed bureaucracy, restricted speech, working conditions and party privilege. The sudden change in policy made earlier participation evidence of political disloyalty.

sections.title: The campaign narrowed public argument
sections.text: Hundreds of thousands were labelled rightists. Many lost jobs, were sent to the countryside or labour camps, and carried the label for years. The punishment also warned colleagues and families that disagreement could threaten education, employment and personal safety.

cards.note: The Hundred Flowers campaign developed during 1956 and peaked in spring 1957. The Anti-Rightist Campaign began in mid-1957 and continued through 1958.

cards.name: The one-child policy
cards.description: In 1980, China’s government began enforcing birth targets that usually limited urban couples to one child and allowed some rural couples two. The rules varied by place and population group. Fines, workplace pressure, contraception, sterilization and forced abortions were all used in enforcement.

sections.title: The policy entered family decisions
sections.text: Permission to marry or have a child could depend on work units and local officials. Enforcement differed, but some families faced severe punishment for an unauthorized pregnancy or birth. Son preference under tight birth limits also contributed to a large imbalance between male and female births.

sections.title: Ending the limit did not restore birth rates
sections.text: A nationwide two-child policy replaced the one-child rule in 2015, and the limit rose to three children in 2021. Birth rates continued to fall as housing, education, work and childcare costs shaped family choices. The long policy also left fewer working-age adults to support a growing older population.

cards.note: 1980 marks the nationwide drive for one-child families. A two-child policy replaced it in 2015, and a three-child policy followed in 2021; local rules and exceptions varied throughout.

cards.name: Confucianism and Daoism
cards.description: Confucianism and Daoism offer different answers about good government, personal conduct and living with disorder. People still debate both traditions.

sections.title: Confucius (孔子) on conduct and government
sections.text: Confucius (孔子) connected good government with learning, care for others and the example set by rulers. Practising respect in everyday relationships could help build a better society. Later followers disagreed about how to put these ideas into practice.

sections.title: Laozi (老子) on force and needless striving
sections.text: The Daodejing (道德经), associated with Laozi (老子), questions forceful control and needless striving. Wuwei (无为) describes action that avoids needless interference and force. The book developed over time; Laozi (老子)’s identity and lifetime remain uncertain.

sections.title: Keep exploring
sections.text: These are starting points within two varied traditions. Neither began on a single known day. Open the individual cards below to meet Confucius (孔子), explore the Daodejing (道德经), and discover Zhuangzi (庄子)’s questions about how we see the world.

cards.note: This is a thematic introduction, with Eastern Zhou used only to place it in the Early China collection. It does not mark the founding or full duration of either tradition. Daoism includes later religious traditions as well as the early writings introduced here.
